- Improved energy resolution through better light collection
- Faster timing from faster scintillator decay time

## 3. **Upgrade Tracking Gas and Readout Electronics**

**Current issue:** Geiger-mode drift cells have limited spatial resolution and can have dead time issues.

**Upgrade:**
- Transition to low-pressure (He:iC₄H₁₀ 90:10) drift cells with analog readout (not Geiger-mode)
- Implement AFTER or DREAM-like amplification chips for sub-mm spatial resolution
- Use waveform digitization at 200-500 MHz sampling rate

**Benefits:**
- Better vertex resolution (<1 mm) improves background rejection
- Improved angular resolution helps identify external backgrounds
- Better energy loss (dE/dx) measurement

## 4. **Implement Machine Learning-based Triggering and Analysis**

**Hardware component:** Deploy FPGA-based neural network processors (e.g., Xilinx Versal AI Edge or Intel Stratix 10 NX) for real-time event classification.

**Benefits:**
- Real-time background rejection at trigger level
- Reduce data volume by factor of 10-100
- Identify complex multi-track topologies
- Improved signal efficiency

## 5. **Enhanced Radon Suppression System**

**Upgrade:**
- Add activated charcoal radon traps cooled to -50°C on gas input lines
- Implement double-wall gas containment with monitored interstitial volume
- Install continuous radon monitoring (Durridge RAD7 or equivalent)
- Use electropolished copper for all gas system components near detector

**Benefits:**
- Radon daughters (²¹⁴Bi, Q=3.27 MeV) are critical background in the signal region
- Factor of 10-100 reduction in radon concentration possible

## 6. **Modernize Data Acquisition Electronics**

**Current limitation:** Timing resolution of 0.30 ns suggests older electronics.

**Upgrade:**
- Replace with CAEN V1742 or DRS4-based waveform digitizers (5 GS/s, 12-bit)
- Implement constant fraction discrimination in FPGA firmware
- Use White Rabbit or similar precision timing distribution (<100 ps synchronization)

**Benefits:**
- Improve timing resolution to 0.15-0.25 ns sigma at 1 MeV
- Better pulse shape discrimination for background rejection
- Synchronized timestamps across all subsystems

## 7. **Active Veto System Enhancement**

**Addition:** Install thin plastic scintillator strips (1-2 cm thick) between iron shielding and calorimeter walls, read out by WLS fibers and SiPMs.

**Benefits:**
- Tag external gammas and electrons with >95% efficiency
- Reduce systematic uncertainties from external background modeling

---

**TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the 76 mm PMTs and 30 cm light guides with direct-coupled SiPM arrays (Hamamatsu S13360 or equivalent), which will simultaneously solve the magnetic field sensitivity issue, improve both energy resolution to 12-15% FWHM and timing resolution to 0.3-0.4 ns sigma at 1 MeV, while reducing cost and complexity.**

# Design Review Recommendations: Calorimeter Upgrade for the Next Phase

## 1. Where the present calorimeter fails the requirements

| Requirement | Present design | Status |
|---|---|---|
| ≤18% FWHM at 1 MeV | 20% FWHM | **Fails** |
| ≤0.6 ns σ at 1 MeV | 0.30 ns | Passes, with a factor of 2 margin |
| Electrons ≥6 cm apart go to different cells | 19 cm × 19 cm faces | **Fails badly** |
| Cell depth ≥3 cm | 11 cm | Passes |
| Every part works in 3 mT | 76 mm PMTs need iron plates | **Marginal**; the iron also distorts the tracker field |

**The segmentation requirement drives the design.** Two points inside one cell can be as far apart as the face diagonal. For any two entry points ≥6 cm apart to land in different cells, the diagonal must be below 6 cm, so the face side must be below 6/√2 ≈ 4.2 cm.

- The current 19 cm cells (26.9 cm diagonal) miss this by a factor of about 5.
- No 76 mm PMT can read a ~4 cm cell.
- The photodetector technology must therefore change.

## 2. Recommended changes

### (a) Re-segment the walls into 4 cm × 4 cm scintillator cells about 4 cm deep
- **Face size:** a 5.66 cm diagonal is below 6 cm, which meets the separation rule with a small margin for wrapping and gaps.
- **Depth:** 3–4 cm of polystyrene/PVT exceeds the 3 MeV electron range (about 1.5 cm), so the ≥3 cm requirement is met. Reducing depth from 11 cm also lowers mass and intrinsic background.
  - Cost: some γ-tagging efficiency is lost. Recover it if needed with a coarse rear γ-veto layer behind the walls.
- **Channel count:** each wall is about 21 m², giving roughly 13,000 cells per side and about 26,000 channels in total. This must be planned for in electronics and cost.

### (b) Replace PMTs and light guides with silicon photomultipliers coupled directly to each cell
- **Fit:** SiPMs are mm-scale, so a cell can be read through its back face with no light guide.
- **Magnetic field:** they are immune to the 3 mT field, which satisfies the "every part works in the field" requirement without shielding.
- **Energy resolution:**
  - Photon-detection efficiency is about 40–50%, versus about 25% for a bialkali PMT.
  - Removing the 30 cm guide recovers its light losses.
  - 18% FWHM corresponds to about 7.7% σ, which needs only about 170 photoelectrons per MeV after non-statistical terms. Small, well-wrapped cells read by a 4×4 array of 6 mm SiPMs should give several hundred photoelectrons per MeV.
  - Light collection in small cells is also more uniform, which reduces the constant term.
- **Timing:** SiPMs combined with fast scintillator easily keep σ below 0.6 ns. The existing factor-2 margin can absorb the larger SiPM capacitance.
- **Background:** SiPMs remove the PMT glass, which is the dominant source of K/U/Th γ background near the foils.

### (c) Remove the iron plates and use non-magnetic mechanics
- The plates existed only to shield the PMTs.
- Removing them eliminates distortion of the 3 mT field, which preserves the charge-sign identification.
- It also removes a γ source close to the tracker.
- Use radiopure copper or plastic support frames instead.

### (d) Optically isolate the cells and keep a thin entrance window
- Wrap each cell in reflective ESR film or PTFE so that light cannot leak between cells. This keeps each cell's energy measured separately.
- Keep the front wrapping thin (a few µm of aluminized Mylar) to minimize dead-layer energy loss.
- Apply cell-to-cell crosstalk and backscatter corrections in reconstruction.

### (e) Use multichannel ASIC/waveform readout with modest cooling
- Use SiPM front-end ASICs with per-channel charge and timing, or waveform sampling.
- Cool to about 0–10 °C to keep the SiPM dark rate (tens of kHz/mm²) negligible at the trigger threshold.
- Stabilize the SiPM bias against temperature drift so that the gain, and hence the resolution, stays uniform in every cell.

### (f) Add per-cell calibration
- Use LED or fiber light injection plus ²⁰⁷Bi conversion-electron sources.
- This is needed to verify and maintain 18% FWHM in **every** cell across about 26,000 channels.

## 3. Unchanged elements
The foils, tracker, shielding, radon control and magnetic field meet the stated requirements as they are. The changes above are confined to the calorimeter.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the 19 cm PMT-read scintillator blocks with ~4 cm × 4 cm × 4 cm optically isolated scintillator cells read directly by SiPM arrays (no light guides, no iron shields).

# Calorimeter Upgrade Recommendations

## 1. Check the current design against each requirement

| Requirement | Current design | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Energy resolution ≤ 18% FWHM at 1 MeV | 20% FWHM | **Fails** |
| Time resolution ≤ 0.6 ns (σ) at 1 MeV | 0.30 ns | Passes, with a factor-2 margin |
| Two electrons ≥ 6 cm apart must land in different cells | 19 × 19 cm faces | **Fails badly** |
| Cell depth ≥ 3 cm | 11 cm | Passes |
| Every part works in 3 mT | PMTs survive only behind an iron plate and 30 cm light guides | Marginal, and the fix is costly |

**The granularity rule sets the cell size.** Two points in the same square cell can be as far apart as the cell diagonal. To guarantee that any two entry points 6 cm apart fall in different cells, the diagonal must be less than 6 cm. That means a side of less than 6/√2 ≈ 4.2 cm.

- I recommend **4 × 4 cm faces** (diagonal 5.66 cm).
- Each wall is 6 m × 3.5 m = 21 m², which gives about 150 × 87 ≈ **13,000 cells per wall and about 26,000 in total**, instead of about 580 per wall today.
- A 76 mm PMT cannot sit behind a 4 cm cell, and 26,000 PMTs with light guides and shielding is not viable. **The photosensor technology must change.**

## 2. Recommended hardware changes

### (a) Replace the PMTs with silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs)

Use, for example, Hamamatsu S14160/S13360 or FBK NUV-HD arrays, with 2–4 devices of 6 × 6 mm² per cell.

- **Magnetic field:** SiPMs are insensitive to magnetic fields at the tesla level, so 3 mT is irrelevant. This removes the iron plate, mu-metal and the field compromise entirely.
- **Size:** they are small enough to read a 4 cm cell directly.
- **Light detection:** their photon detection efficiency is about 40–50% at the scintillator's 420 nm emission, roughly double a PMT's quantum efficiency.
- **Radiopurity:** they are low-mass and intrinsically radiopure, which helps the background budget compared with PMT glass.

### (b) Couple the SiPMs directly to the scintillator and remove the 30 cm acrylic light guides

- The light guides cost photons through attenuation and their geometric acceptance.
- They also add mass and, in the present design, exist only to keep the PMTs away from the field. With SiPMs they serve no purpose.

### (c) Switch to a higher-yield scintillator with better wrapping

- **Material:** use PVT-based scintillator such as EJ-200 or BC-408. These give roughly 10,000 photons/MeV, about 25% more than polystyrene, and have about a 2 ns decay time.
- **Wrapping:** use high-reflectivity specular film (3M ESR, above 98% reflectivity) on the sides and back.
- **Entrance face:** use a very thin aluminised Mylar window (a few µm) so that electrons lose almost no energy before entering.
- **Uniformity:** small cells have short optical paths and good response uniformity, which removes the position-dependent term that limits large blocks.

**Photoelectron budget:**

- 18% FWHM corresponds to σ/E of about 7.7%, which requires at least about 170 photoelectrons per MeV from statistics alone.
- I suggest targeting **more than 300 photoelectrons per MeV**, giving about 14–15% FWHM and leaving margin for the excess noise factor and calibration terms.
- This is plausible: 10,000 photons/MeV × about 15–20% light collection to the SiPMs × 45% efficiency gives roughly 700–900 photoelectrons per MeV.
- **This should be confirmed with a prototype cell before committing.**

### (d) Cell depth: keep it moderate rather than maximal

- Electrons need only 3 cm. I recommend about **5–8 cm**, which still retains useful gamma efficiency for tagging ²⁰⁸Tl and ²¹⁴Bi backgrounds (for example the 2.6 MeV gamma).
- Shorter cells give better light collection, while longer cells give better gamma tagging. **This is a trade-off for the panel to settle with simulation.**

### (e) Readout electronics and slow control

- **Readout ASICs:** use multichannel timing/charge ASICs such as PETsys TOFPET2 or Weeroc CITIROC/TRIROC-class chips to handle 26,000 channels with per-channel energy and time.
- **Timing:** these chips deliver well under 0.3 ns σ at hundreds of photoelectrons, so the 0.6 ns requirement keeps its margin even with large-capacitance SiPM arrays.
- **Gain stability:** add temperature monitoring and bias compensation, because SiPM gain drifts with temperature.
- **Calibration:** add an LED or fibre light-injection system for per-cell calibration.
- **Dark counts:** at tens of kHz/mm², they are negligible at the about 50 keV thresholds needed. No cooling is required, though mild temperature control helps stability.

### (f) Iron and water shielding

- These can remain as they are.
- The iron plate behind the PMTs is no longer needed for field shielding. Any material that remains there should be judged only on radiopurity.

## 3. Summary

1. The current calorimeter fails the energy-resolution requirement modestly and the two-electron separation requirement badly.
2. Fixing granularity forces cells of about 4 cm, roughly 26,000 channels.
3. That is only practical with SiPMs read directly on the scintillator.
4. The same change also resolves the magnetic-field issue and raises the light yield enough to meet 18% FWHM.
5. The surplus in time resolution gives room to absorb SiPM capacitance effects.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the 19 cm PMT-read scintillator blocks with about 4 × 4 cm PVT scintillator cells read directly (no light guides) by field-immune SiPM arrays.

# Hardware Upgrades for Neutrinoless Double-Beta Decay Detector

## Required Upgrades

**1. Scintillator Cell Replacement**
- **Technology**: Higher light-yield polystyrene scintillator (e.g., BC408 or equivalent with enhanced dopant concentration) or alternative fast scintillator (e.g., EJ-200)
- **Why**: Current 20% FWHM energy resolution must reach 18% FWHM. Higher photon yield directly improves photostatistics-limited resolution at 1 MeV, scaling approximately as √(light collected).

**2. Photomultiplier Upgrade**
- **Technology**: Low-jitter PMTs with sigma < 0.2 ns (e.g., Hamamatsu R7600-03 or similar 2-inch tube with transit time spread specifications, or position-sensitive PMTs)
- **Why**: Current 0.30 ns sigma must reach 0.6 ns sigma total system resolution. Since times add in quadrature, PMT jitter contributes significantly; reducing PMT sigma by ~35% is achievable and necessary.

**3. Timing Electronics Upgrade**
- **Technology**: Fast constant-fraction discriminators (CFD) with <50 ps time walk, coupled to precision TDCs (100 ps resolution or better), replacing conventional leading-edge electronics
- **Why**: Achieve sub-nanosecond timing for background rejection. CFD eliminates amplitude-dependent time walk that degrades resolution on low-energy tracks.

**4. Acrylic Light Guide Optimization**
- **Technology**: Replace standard 30 cm guides with shorter (15-20 cm) UV-transparent guides or use wave-shifting fiber (WSF) coupling to reduce transit time dispersion
- **Why**: Shorter path and/or WSF reduces timing jitter contribution from photon transit and geometric dispersion.

**5. Scintillator Cell Geometry Refinement**
- **Technology**: Increase cell depth from 11 cm to 11-13 cm to exceed 3 MeV absorption requirement with margin; polish or wrap cells with reflective material (VM2000 or equivalent) to maximize light collection
- **Why**: Ensures full 3 MeV containment requirement; improved light collection directly aids both energy and timing resolution.

**6. Magnetic Field Optimization**
- **Technology**: Verify/upgrade 3 mT field coil system for field uniformity (< 2% variation) across active volume; use iron shielding tuning to minimize stray field in calorimeter region
- **Why**: Uniform field protects charge-sign determination; specified requirement that field must not degrade calorimeter function requires field mapping and possible coil adjustment.

**7. Signal Cable and Routing Upgrade**
- **Technology**: Replace signal cables with low-dispersion, shielded coaxial cable (50 Ω impedance matching); minimize cable lengths and implement proper grounding scheme
- **Why**: Reduces timing jitter and crosstalk; essential for achieving sub-nanosecond resolution.

**8. Gain Stabilization Electronics**
- **Technology**: Implement LED-based PMT gain monitoring with feedback correction, operating at 1-10 Hz update rate
- **Why**: Compensates for PMT gain drift in underground environment and ensures consistent 18% FWHM across detector lifetime.

---

## TOP RECOMMENDATION: 
**Replace photomultipliers with low-jitter 2-inch PMTs (transit time spread <0.2 ns) combined with fast constant-fraction discriminator electronics, as PMT jitter and time-walk are the primary barriers to meeting the 0.6 ns sigma timing requirement.**

The present calorimeter fails two of the stated requirements: 20% FWHM energy resolution against the 18% target, and 0.30 ns time resolution, which already meets the 0.6 ns requirement with margin but leaves no room for degradation. The bigger constraints are geometric and magnetic: the cells are 19 cm across, so two electrons hitting one wall 6 cm apart can share a cell, and the photomultipliers sit behind iron plates in a 3 mT field, which is only tolerable if the readout is made of magnetically tolerant parts. My proposals follow.

**1. Replace the scintillator-plus-PMT readout with a finer, field-tolerant photodetector.**
Silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) are the natural replacement. They are insensitive to a 3 mT field, need no iron shielding, can be packed at millimetre-to-centimetre pitch, and have photon detection efficiency high enough to improve light yield per MeV. Pairing SiPMs with wavelength-shifting fibre readout or direct coupling to the scintillator also removes the acrylic light guide. Expected gains: higher light collection and lower stochastic term, which together can reach the 18% FWHM at 1 MeV target. Careful control of SiPM dark count and temperature (cooling to about 0 to 10 °C) is needed at this rate and depth.

**2. Segment the calorimeter transversely to a pitch of about 3 cm or finer.**
Replace each 19 cm x 19 cm cell with a matrix of small scintillator bars or tiles, roughly 3 x 3 cm in cross-section and 11 cm deep (retaining the 3 cm minimum depth for full absorption of 3 MeV electrons). Two electrons at least 6 cm apart then fall in separate channels with margin. Plastic scintillator bars read out at both ends by SiPMs, or tile arrays read out by a single SiPM per tile with a wavelength-shifting layer, are both viable. The total channel count rises to several thousand, which pushes the design toward front-end ASICs (a multi-channel charge or time digitiser with per-channel timing) and a corresponding increase in cabling and cooling.

**3. Upgrade timing electronics for sub-0.3 ns performance.**
Pair fast scintillator (e.g., a faster-decay plastic or a fast-rise dopant) with a fast SiPM and a leading-edge or constant-fraction discriminator implemented in an ASIC such as a time-to-digital converter with about 10 ps binning. This maintains timing well inside the 0.6 ns requirement and provides margin for the in-cell time walk that segmentation introduces.

**4. Improve light collection geometry and reflectors.**
Wrap each element in a high-reflectivity diffuse reflector (e.g., ESR film or PTFE) and optimise the bar or tile aspect ratio so that light yield is uniform along the length. Reduce the acrylic light path to a minimum or eliminate it entirely, since light guides cost light and add dead volume.

**5. Calibration and stability infrastructure.**
Install a per-channel LED or laser calibration system to track SiPM gain and temperature drift continuously, and use cosmic-ray minimum-ionising tracks plus radioactive sources (e.g., a 207Bi or 60Co-type line near 1 MeV) for in-situ energy-scale checks across all segments. Given the 3 mT field and radon-controlled gas, monitoring the cooling and humidity around the readout is also essential.

**6. Radiopurity and shielding compatibility.**
Select SiPM packages, scintillator, and reflectors with low intrinsic radioactivity, since the upgraded detector increases the total number of components near the source foils. Remove the iron-plate shielding of the PMTs, which is no longer needed, and re-evaluate the internal shielding budget accordingly.

Taken together, these changes address the energy resolution (SiPM light yield and segmentation), the spatial separation requirement (3 cm segmentation), the magnetic-field compatibility (SiPMs), and the timing margin (fast readout chain).

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the 19 cm PMT-coupled cells with finely segmented (about 3 cm pitch) plastic scintillator read out by silicon photomultipliers, which together fix the energy resolution, the two-electron separation, and the magnetic-field tolerance in one change.

# Design Review: Calorimeter Upgrade Recommendations

## Analysis of Current System and Requirements

The current calorimeter uses polystyrene scintillator blocks (19×19×11 cm³) read out via 30 cm acrylic light guides to 76 mm PMTs behind iron shielding. Performance is 20% FWHM energy resolution and 0.30 ns timing at 1 MeV. The requirements are modest relaxations in some areas (timing: 0.6 ns vs current 0.30 ns) but demand improvement in energy resolution (18% FWHM vs current 20%).

## Recommended Hardware Changes

### 1. Replace Polystyrene Scintillator with Higher Light-Yield Material

**Recommendation:** Switch to **EJ-200 or BC-408 plastic scintillator** (or equivalent high-quality commercial plastic scintillator)

**Justification:**
- Light yield ~10,000 photons/MeV compared to ~8,000 for basic polystyrene
- Energy resolution scales as σ/E ∝ 1/√(N_pe), so ~12% more photons improves resolution by ~6%
- Fast decay time (2.1 ns) maintains timing capability
- Radiation length adequate for 3 MeV electron containment in 3+ cm depth
- Non-magnetic, fully compatible with 3 mT field
- Well-established technology with predictable performance

### 2. Replace Acrylic Light Guides with Direct Optical Coupling Using Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)

**Recommendation:** Replace 76 mm PMTs and 30 cm acrylic light guides with **arrays of large-area SiPMs (e.g., Hamamatsu S14160-6050HS or SensL J-series 6 mm devices)** directly coupled to the scintillator rear face

**Justification:**
- Eliminates ~30-40% light loss in the 30 cm acrylic light guide
- SiPM photon detection efficiency (PDE) of 40-50% at 420 nm versus ~25% quantum efficiency for bialkali PMTs
- Net photoelectron increase of 2-3× dramatically improves energy resolution
- Compact form factor eliminates need for iron plate shielding of PMTs
- **Completely immune to magnetic fields** – critical for reliable operation in 3 mT environment
- Modern SiPMs have dark count rates <100 kHz/mm² at -20°C to 0°C, manageable for this application
- Timing resolution of individual SiPMs is ~100 ps SPTR, easily meeting 0.6 ns requirement

**Implementation:** Use a 3×3 or 4×4 array of 6 mm SiPMs per cell with summing electronics, or emerging large-area SiPM tiles (e.g., 50×50 mm² units from various manufacturers).

### 3. Reduce Cell Face Size to Ensure Two-Electron Separation

**Recommendation:** Reduce cell face dimensions from **19×19 cm² to 8×8 cm² or 10×10 cm²**

**Justification:**
- Current 19 cm cells risk having two electrons (>6 cm apart) hit the same cell
- Two electrons 6 cm apart could both strike a single 19×19 cm² cell, violating the requirement for separate energy measurements
- 8×8 cm² cells guarantee that electrons 6 cm apart will be in different cells (diagonal of 8×8 is 11.3 cm)
- Smaller cells also improve vertex reconstruction correlation with calorimeter hits
- More channels but each channel has better uniformity and light collection

### 4. Add Wavelength-Shifting (WLS) Film or Paint to Improve Light Collection Uniformity

**Recommendation:** Apply **wavelength-shifting paint (e.g., EJ-298) or WLS film to interior surfaces** of each scintillator cell, or use WLS fiber readout

**Justification:**
- Improves light collection uniformity across the cell face
- Reduces position-dependent response variations that degrade resolution
- Shifts emission to longer wavelength (green) where SiPM PDE can be optimized
- Proven technology in neutrino and rare-event experiments (e.g., MicroBooNE, LEGEND)

### 5. Implement Active Temperature Stabilization for SiPM Arrays

**Recommendation:** Install **Peltier cooling modules** maintaining SiPMs at **0°C to -10°C** with closed-loop temperature control

**Justification:**
- SiPM gain varies ~2%/°C; temperature stability of ±0.5°C needed for <1% gain variation
- Cooling reduces dark count rate by factor of 2 per 10°C
- Underground lab has stable ambient temperature, reducing cooling power requirements
- Essential for achieving and maintaining 18% FWHM resolution requirement across all cells

### 6. Upgrade Front-End Electronics with Waveform Digitization

**Recommendation:** Replace existing electronics with **high-speed waveform digitizers (≥500 MSPS, 12-14 bit)** such as CAEN V1730 or custom ASIC-based solutions

**Justification:**
- Enables pulse-shape analysis for improved energy reconstruction
- Allows pile-up rejection and multi-hit identification within single cells
- Digital timing extraction can achieve <100 ps precision
- Provides diagnostic information for long-term calibration stability
- Standard approach in modern rare-event searches (CUORE, GERDA/LEGEND)

### 7. Maintain Minimum Scintillator Depth of 11 cm (Current Design)

**Justification:**
- 3 MeV electrons have range of ~1.5 cm in polystyrene; 11 cm provides >7× range
- Current depth exceeds 3 cm minimum requirement with large margin
- No change needed, but should not be reduced in any redesign

---

## Summary Table

| Component | Current | Recommended | Key Benefit |
|-----------|---------|-------------|-------------|
| Scintillator | Polystyrene | EJ-200/BC-408 | +25% light yield |
| Light guide | 30 cm acrylic | Eliminated | -35% light loss removed |
| Photodetector | 76 mm PMT | SiPM arrays | 2× PDE, B-field immune |
| Cell size | 19×19 cm² | 8×8 cm² | Guarantees 2-electron separation |
| Readout | Analog | Waveform digitizer | Better resolution, diagnostics |
| Thermal | Passive | Peltier stabilized | Gain stability |

## Expected Performance

With these changes, expected energy resolution:
- Photoelectron increase: ~3× (light yield + guide removal + PDE)
- Resolution improvement: 20% × √(1/3) ≈ 11-12% FWHM at 1 MeV
- This comfortably exceeds the 18% FWHM requirement with margin for cell-to-cell variation

Timing resolution will remain excellent (<0.3 ns) due to fast scintillator and SiPM response.

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace PMTs and acrylic light guides with directly-coupled SiPM arrays, which simultaneously improves light collection efficiency, eliminates magnetic field sensitivity concerns, and enables a more compact mechanical design.

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for the Tracker-Calorimeter Detector

## 1. Replace PMTs with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)

**Problem:** 76 mm PMTs are sensitive to the 3 mT magnetic field, causing gain degradation and trajectory distortion of photoelectrons even at low fields. The iron plates behind PMTs suggest this is already a known workaround, adding mass and complexity.

**Proposal:** Replace each 76 mm PMT with an array of SiPMs (e.g., Hamamatsu S13360 series or FBK NUV-HD), tiled to match the light guide exit aperture (~76 mm diameter equivalent). SiPMs are completely field-insensitive, have higher photon detection efficiency (~50% PDE vs ~25% for bialkali PMTs), and operate at low voltage (~55 V). This eliminates the need for the iron shielding plates behind each PMT, reducing passive material that could scatter particles or generate backgrounds.

**Benefit:** Improved photoelectron yield directly improves both energy resolution (scales as 1/√N_pe) and timing resolution. The iron plates can be removed, simplifying the mechanical structure.

---

## 2. Upgrade Scintillator to LYSO or PbWO₄ Crystals (or higher-light-yield plastic)

**Problem:** Standard polystyrene scintillator has relatively low light yield (~10 photons/keV), limiting energy resolution to 20% FWHM at 1 MeV. The 18% FWHM requirement is tight but achievable; future phases may demand better.

**Proposal (near-term):** Replace standard polystyrene with **p-terphenyl-doped polyvinyltoluene (PVT)** scintillator (e.g., Saint-Gobain BC-408 or Eljen EJ-200), which offers ~50% higher light yield than polystyrene, better optical transparency, and comparable ease of machining into 19×19×11 cm blocks.

**Proposal (longer-term):** For a future phase, use **BGO or CdWO₄ crystals** of similar dimensions, which offer much higher light yield and better energy resolution, though at higher cost.

**Benefit:** Improved light yield reduces statistical fluctuations in energy measurement, pushing energy resolution well below 18% FWHM at 1 MeV while also improving timing via better photon statistics on the leading edge.

---

## 3. Replace Acrylic Light Guides with Wavelength-Shifting (WLS) Fiber Mats or Direct Coupling

**Problem:** The 30 cm acrylic light guide causes significant photon loss through geometric dilution and absorption, degrading both energy and time resolution. It also adds 30 cm of dead length behind each calorimeter cell.

**Proposal:** Replace the 30 cm acrylic guides with a **wavelength-shifting fiber mat** embedded in or directly coupled to the back face of each scintillator block. Use 1 mm diameter Kuraray Y-11 or Saint-Gobain BCF-91A WLS fibers arranged in a dense grid, read out by the SiPM array (from upgrade #1) placed flush against the fiber mat. Alternatively, use **direct optical coupling** of a segmented SiPM tile directly to the back face of the scintillator with optical grease, eliminating the light guide entirely.

**Benefit:** Dramatically increases light collection efficiency, reduces the photon transit time spread (improving σ_t), and reduces the overall detector depth — allowing more cells or thicker scintillator within the same envelope.

---

## 4. Upgrade Geiger-Mode Drift Cells to Modern Drift Cell Technology

**Problem:** Classic Geiger-mode cells provide binary (yes/no) hit information and limited spatial resolution. They are also prone to quenching gas contamination and have intrinsically poor two-track separation.

**Proposal:** Replace Geiger-mode cells with **small-cell drift chambers using time-to-digital converters (TDCs)** with ≤1 ns resolution, using an **He/isobutane (95/5)** or **He/C₂H₅OH** gas mixture. Cell diameters of ~8–10 mm with FAST TDC readout (e.g., CAEN V1290 or similar) provide analog drift time information, giving track-position resolution of ~100–200 μm per cell, compared to ~1 mm for Geiger cells. This directly improves vertex reconstruction on the foil.

**Benefit:** Better vertex resolution (improves signal/background discrimination), better two-track separation for identifying the two electrons from 0νββ, and better rejection of single-electron backgrounds.

---

## 5. Add Thin Timing Layers at the Foil Plane

**Problem:** The 0.6 ns timing requirement for rejecting external crossing electrons is demanding. Currently, only the calorimeter walls provide timing. With a 1 m separation between walls (50 cm tracking on each side), time-of-flight discrimination between internal (signal) and external (background) electrons needs precise anchor points.

**Proposal:** Install thin (3–5 mm) **EJ-230 fast plastic scintillator** strips with SiPM readout immediately adjacent to the source foil plane on each side, forming a "T0" timing reference layer. These strips would be ~3 cm wide (matching the 6 cm cell separation requirement), oriented vertically, and would provide a t=0 timestamp with ~150 ps (sigma) precision for each electron as it leaves the foil region.

**Benefit:** Combined foil-timing + calorimeter-timing gives a time-of-flight measurement over the full 50 cm tracking depth, dramatically improving rejection of external background electrons. This also cross-checks vertex timing consistency between the two electrons in a candidate 0νββ event.

---

## 6. Upgrade Radon Mitigation: Radon-Free Air Enclosure and Membrane Purification

**Problem:** Radon emanating from detector materials (especially the iron shielding) is a major background source for 0νββ searches. Gas flushing helps but does not eliminate surface-emanated radon that diffuses from detector components.

**Proposal:** Install a **radon trapping system** using activated charcoal columns cooled to −40°C in the gas recirculation loop, combined with a **radon-tight aluminized Mylar membrane** lining the inner surfaces of both tracking volumes. Additionally, source foil supports should be switched from steel to **electroformed copper** (which has extremely low radon emanation and U/Th contamination).

**Benefit:** Reduces radon-induced background (a leading systematic for Mo-100 experiments) by factors of 10–100, directly improving signal sensitivity.

---

## 7. Front-End Electronics: Waveform Digitization

**Problem:** Current PMT readout likely uses peak-sensing ADCs and simple TDCs, which cannot distinguish pile-up events or perform pulse-shape analysis.

**Proposal:** Replace peak-sensing ADCs with **switched-capacitor waveform digitizers** (e.g., CAEN DT5742 based on DRS4 chip, sampling at 5 GS/s, 12-bit resolution) on each calorimeter channel. This enables offline pulse-shape discrimination, pile-up rejection, and precise timing extraction via digital constant-fraction discrimination.

**Benefit:** Improves effective energy and timing resolution beyond what hardware changes alone provide, enables identification of alpha/beta/gamma events by pulse shape in upgraded scintillators, and future-proofs the readout for higher-resolution scintillators.

# Calorimeter upgrade: what to change and why

## 1. Where the present calorimeter stands

| Requirement | Present cell | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Energy resolution ≤18% FWHM at 1 MeV | 20% | **Fails** (small gap) |
| Time resolution ≤0.6 ns σ at 1 MeV | 0.30 ns | Passes, with 2× margin |
| Electrons ≥6 cm apart land in separate cells | 19 × 19 cm faces | **Fails badly** |
| Depth ≥3 cm | 11 cm | Passes, but deeper than needed |
| Works in 3 mT | PMT behind iron plate | Passes only through shielding |

Segmentation is the decisive failure. Resolution can be improved within the present design. Cell size cannot: a 19 cm cell routinely contains two electrons tens of cm apart.

## 2. Required cell size

For square cells of side *a*, the two most distant points inside one cell lie at opposite corners, a distance *a*√2 apart. To guarantee that any two entry points ≥6 cm apart fall in different cells:

- a√2 < 6 cm
- **a < 4.2 cm**

A practical choice is about a 4 cm pitch, including wrapping. Each wall is 6 m × 3.5 m = 21 m², so this gives about 13,000 cells per wall and about 26,000 in total. This rules out one 76 mm PMT plus a 30 cm light guide per cell. The PMT does not fit behind a 4 cm cell, and the cost, radioactivity and space would all be prohibitive.

## 3. Proposed hardware changes

**a) New scintillator cells: about 4 × 4 cm face, 3–5 cm deep.**
- A 3 MeV electron has a range of about 1.5 cm in polystyrene, so 3 cm fully satisfies the containment rule.
- Keeping depth near 3–4 cm, instead of 11 cm, reduces sensitivity to external γ rays. The gamma–electron rejection then rests on tracking and timing.
- Use high-light-yield polystyrene (PPO/POPOP type) with diamond-milled surfaces.
- Wrap each cell individually in ESR film or PTFE on the sides and back. Use thin aluminised Mylar on the entrance face to keep dead material small.
- The optical isolation between cells prevents light crosstalk, which would otherwise undo the segmentation.

**b) Replace PMTs, light guides and iron plates with SiPM arrays coupled directly to each cell.**
- SiPMs are insensitive to a 3 mT field, so there is no magnetic shielding and no light guide to lose light.
- They are compact enough to sit behind a 4 cm cell, for example a 4×4 array of 6 mm SiPMs covering most of the rear face.
- Their peak photon detection efficiency (about 40–50%) is higher than the quantum efficiency of a bialkali photocathode (about 25–30%).
- They contain much less radioactivity than PMT glass, which lowers the background at 3 MeV.

**c) Photoelectron budget to reach 18%.**
- Resolution scales as 2.355/√Npe × √ENF, where ENF is the SiPM excess noise factor from crosstalk and afterpulsing.
- Without excess noise, 18% FWHM needs about 170 p.e./MeV. Allowing ENF ≈ 1.2 and non-uniformity, design for **≥250 p.e./MeV**.
- Achieve this with direct coupling, large SiPM coverage and good reflectors.
- Choose low-crosstalk SiPMs with trench isolation.
- Calibrate each cell individually for light-collection uniformity using ²⁰⁷Bi sources and a light-injection system.

**d) Electronics and operation.**
- Use multichannel ASIC readout giving charge and time per cell, with per-channel bias trimming.
- Stabilise temperature and monitor gain, because SiPM gain drifts with temperature.
- Use a threshold of a few tens of keV. At hundreds of p.e. per MeV this sits well above the SiPM dark-count pile-up.
- Timing of 0.6 ns σ is easily reached with fast plastic and SiPMs. A thinner cell also reduces path-length jitter, which helps the time-of-flight rejection of crossing electrons.

**e) Mechanics and radiopurity.**
- Build a low-mass, radiopure support grid, for example copper or plastic frames.
- Screen the SiPMs, PCBs and connectors for radioactivity.
- Remove the iron plates from inside the shield, since magnetic shielding is no longer needed.

## 4. Optional backup

If the full channel count is unaffordable, a possible fallback is a 4 cm scintillator-bar hodoscope that localises hits, with energy from larger blocks behind it. This does **not** meet the requirement that energies be measured separately in different cells. Fine segmentation with individual readout is therefore the baseline.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the 19 cm PMT-read blocks with ~4 cm × 4 cm × 3–4 cm scintillator cells, each read out directly by SiPM arrays (no light guides or iron), giving the required segmentation, field immunity and ≥250 p.e./MeV for ≤18% FWHM.

This is a NEMO-3/SuperNEMO-type detector. The present calorimeter gives 20% FWHM at 1 MeV, which does not meet the 18% requirement, while the 0.30 ns time resolution already beats the 0.6 ns requirement with margin. The upgrade should therefore focus on energy resolution and keep the cell geometry, since the 19 cm cells are well matched to the 6 cm two-electron separation requirement (the cell face is larger than 6 cm, so two electrons 6 cm apart can still share a cell; this is a known limitation, discussed below). Any change must also tolerate the 3 mT field and keep the depth at 3 cm or more.

**1. Photomultipliers: low-radioactivity, high-quantum-efficiency PMTs (the main upgrade)**
- Replace the standard cathodes with super-bialkali (SBA) or ultra-bialkali photocathodes, QE about 35-43% at the 420 nm scintillator peak, versus about 25% for standard bialkali. Use low-radioactivity glass, which also lowers the internal background.
- Physics motivation: the energy resolution of a scintillator cell is dominated by photoelectron statistics, sigma/E ~ 1/sqrt(N_pe). A QE increase of about 40% gives roughly 15-20% improvement in resolution, taking 20% to 16-17% FWHM at 1 MeV. This is a near drop-in change.
- Keep the 76 mm tubes (or use 8-inch tubes with a matched light guide) behind the iron plate, retaining the magnetic shielding of the iron. Retain the iron plate and add mu-metal or iron collars so the 3 mT field does not degrade gain, since PMTs need field-free cathode regions while SiPMs would not.

**2. Scintillator and light-collection improvements**
- Use higher-light-yield polystyrene (or PVT) doped for about 10,000+ photons/MeV, with improved surface treatment (polished surfaces, Teflon or Mylar/Tyvek wrapping with a high-reflectivity specular-diffuse mix).
- Optimize the light guide: use optically matched, tapered guides with better optical grease or couplings, and a high-transparency acrylic at 420 nm.
- Physics motivation: increases N_pe and improves uniformity of response across the 19 x 19 cm face. This reduces the position-dependent light collection, which is a major contributor to resolution for electrons hitting off-center. The tracker reconstructs the impact point, so it can supply a position-dependent correction to the energy, which improves the effective resolution further.

**3. Calibration and monitoring upgrade**
- Add a laser or LED light-injection system for gain tracking in every cell, and 207Bi sources (1 MeV conversion electrons) deployed through the foil plane for absolute energy calibration.
- Physics motivation: drift of PMT gain smears the summed energy spectrum. Daily relative calibration keeps the 18% FWHM requirement met in every cell, not just on average, and lets the 0.30 ns timing be monitored against the 0.6 ns cut that rejects externally crossing electrons.

**4. Granularity and the 6 cm separation requirement**
- The 19 cm faces mean two electrons from a decay entering the same wall within 19 cm of each other can share one cell. The requirement states electrons at least 6 cm apart must go to separate cells, so the cell size is the geometric weakness. For the next phase, reduce the cell face to about 6 cm (finer segmentation), which requires smaller PMTs or SiPM readout.
- A 6 cm cell with depth of at least 3 cm (keep about 11 cm to contain 3 MeV electrons) can be read out by a smaller 2-3 inch PMT or a SiPM array. SiPMs are field-tolerant (3 mT is no issue), compact, and allow a thinner light guide.
- Physics motivation: separate energy measurement of each electron preserves the single-electron energy and angular distributions, which are what discriminate 0νββ from backgrounds and from 2νββ; shared cells would merge the two energies and lose that discrimination.

**5. Background shielding and radon**
- Keep the iron and water shielding, and add an anti-radon tent or radon-trapping charcoal on the gas input, and a radon-emanation-tested gas system.
- Physics motivation: 214Bi (Q about 3.27 MeV) from radon daughters on the foil or wires is the main background in the 3.03 MeV region of interest, so lowering radon directly improves sensitivity.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the PMTs with high-quantum-efficiency (super/ultra-bialkali), low-radioactivity photomultipliers, combined with higher-light-yield scintillator and improved reflectors, to bring the energy resolution from 20% to below 18% FWHM at 1 MeV.

This is the SuperNEMO demonstrator-like design. The current calorimeter (20% FWHM at 1 MeV, 0.30 ns sigma) fails only the energy-resolution requirement (18% or better). Time resolution (0.30 ns) already beats the 0.6 ns requirement, and the segmentation (19 cm cells) already satisfies the 6 cm separation need? Check: electrons entering at points at least 6 cm apart must land in different cells. With 19 cm cells, two electrons 6 cm apart often share a cell. Hence the cell size is also a problem, though the two electrons of a decay typically separate by more than that only in some topologies, so the requirement as stated forces finer segmentation, or at least that cells are not shared. So there are two real problems: energy resolution (20% vs 18%) and granularity (19 cm faces vs a 6 cm separation requirement). The 3 cm minimum depth is met (11 cm is far more).

**Constraints and what they imply**

1. **Granularity.** Faces must be at most about 6 cm wide to guarantee that points 6 cm apart land in different cells. In practice you would go to 5-6 cm faces, not larger. Smaller cells mean far more channels over a 6 m x 3.5 m wall on two sides, and large photomultipliers (76 mm) cannot be coupled to a 6 cm face without a light guide. A 6 cm cell with a 76 mm PMT would need a light guide, which costs light. So the PMT must shrink to roughly the cell size and sit directly on the scintillator (no 30 cm light guide). Direct coupling also recovers the light lost in the guide and improves both energy and timing resolution.

2. **Magnetic field.** 3 mT is low but affects PMTs with long drift paths. Mitigate with mu-metal shielding of each PMT. Iron plates (as currently used) provide partial shielding; keep or improve. Note that the cell depth (11 cm) can be reduced to about 3 cm minimum, but keep enough depth to fully absorb 3 MeV electrons; ~10 cm provides margin and also stops backscatter-escape losses. Keep depth near 10 cm; a thinner cell would not obviously help.

3. **Energy resolution.** Need at most 18% FWHM at 1 MeV, preferably better (e.g., 15% or 8% at 3 MeV for tighter sensitivity at the Q-value). Contributors: light collection, photon statistics, PMT quantum efficiency. Improvements:
 - Use PMTs with high quantum efficiency (superbialkali, ~35-40%) instead of standard bialkali (~25%).
 - Remove the long acrylic light guide (direct coupling).
 - Use scintillator with higher light yield and good transparency (polystyrene-based, e.g., PVT/PS with improved purification), with reflective wrapping (Teflon/Mylar).
 - Optimize the optical coupling to the PMT face.

4. **Timing.** Current 0.30 ns is already fine. Smaller cells with direct coupling and fast PMTs maintain it.

5. **Radiopurity/shielding.** Unchanged; but low-background PMTs (low-K glass) are advisable since more PMTs are added.

**Proposed upgrades**

- Reduce cell face to about 5-6 cm and remove acrylic light guides.
- Couple cells directly to photomultipliers sized to the cell face, i.e., 5 cm PMTs, with high-QE superbialkali photocathodes and low-radioactivity glass.
- Provide local mu-metal shielding of each PMT, keeping the iron backing; verify gain stability at 3 mT.
- Improve scintillator light yield, surface polish and reflective wrapping.
- Retain cell depth around 10 cm (greater than 3 cm minimum, provides full absorption).
- Upgrade readout electronics/channel count accordingly (waveform digitizers, higher channel density).
- Calibrate each cell individually (e.g., laser/LED monitoring, 207Bi sources) to verify at least 18% FWHM everywhere.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the 19 cm cells and 30 cm light guides with cells of at most about 6 cm face directly coupled to correspondingly small high-quantum-efficiency, low-radioactivity PMTs (with mu-metal shielding for the 3 mT field), to meet both the 6 cm electron-separation requirement and the 18% FWHM energy resolution.

# Hardware Upgrade Proposals for the Tracker-Calorimeter Detector

## 1. Calorimeter Scintillator Replacement

**Current:** Polystyrene scintillator, 19×19×11 cm cells, 20% FWHM @ 1 MeV
**Proposed:** Replace with **Bismuth Germanate (BGO)** or preferably **Lutetium Fine Silicate (LFS) / LYSO scintillator** cells

Actually, for this application the best choice is **polyvinyl-toluene (PVT)-based plastic scintillator with improved light collection**, but more concretely:

- Use **enriched-PVT scintillator (e.g., Eljen EJ-200 or Saint-Gobain BC-408)** with enhanced light yield (~10,000 photons/MeV vs ~8,000 for polystyrene), combined with internal **wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibers** embedded in a grid pattern to improve light collection uniformity and reduce the resolution from 20% to ≤18% FWHM. The fiber readout also makes the light path more uniform across the cell face, reducing position-dependent light yield variations.

---

## 2. Photomultiplier Tube Upgrade

**Current:** 76 mm (3-inch) PMT behind a 30 cm acrylic light guide
**Proposed:** Replace with **Hamamatsu R6594 or R1408 (8-inch) PMTs with high-quantum-efficiency (HQE) bialkali photocathodes (~35% QE vs ~20% typical)**

Alternatively: **Hamamatsu R7081HQE or ET Enterprises 9372KB** large-area PMTs with:
- Super-bialkali photocathode (QE ~35% at 420 nm)
- Low transit-time spread (TTS ≈ 0.7 ns sigma for single photoelectron, improving to ~0.1 ns at the multi-PE level relevant here)

This directly improves both energy resolution (more photoelectrons → better statistics) and time resolution. For N photoelectrons, σ_t ∝ 1/√N; doubling QE gives ~√2 improvement in timing.

**Specifically:** The 30 cm acrylic light guide should be **shortened to ≤15 cm** or replaced with a **tapered borosilicate glass light guide** to reduce light loss and dispersion, while keeping the PMT behind the iron plate. A shorter, more efficient guide improves photoelectron yield significantly.

---

## 3. Time Resolution Enhancement: PMT Base Electronics

**Current:** 0.30 ns sigma @ 1 MeV (already meeting the 0.6 ns requirement, but with some margin)
**Proposed:** Replace passive resistive PMT voltage dividers with **active Cockcroft-Walton (CW) base circuits** (as used in KamLAND, Borexino upgrades):

- Active bases maintain stable dynode voltages under varying count rates
- Use **fast waveform digitizers (CAEN V1742, 5 GS/s, 12-bit** or similar) instead of charge ADCs + TDCs, enabling **offline digital constant-fraction discrimination (dCFD)** for sub-ns timing
- This eliminates walk from analog CFDs and recovers the full intrinsic PMT timing

---

## 4. Tracking Volume: Wire Replacement with Drift Tubes

**Current:** Geiger-mode drift cells in He-based gas
**Proposed:** Replace with **thin-walled (100 μm) stainless steel drift tubes of 9 mm diameter** operating in **proportional mode** with **Ar/CO₂ (80/20)** or **He/isobutane (95/5)** gas mixture

- Proportional mode (vs Geiger) gives faster signal recovery, eliminates the long Geiger dead time (~ms), and allows dE/dx measurement
- 9 mm drift tubes as used in **ATLAS TRT or DRIFT experiment** provide excellent spatial resolution (~150 μm per cell)
- He/isobutane is already compatible with low-Z requirement (minimizing multiple scattering of ~1.5 MeV electrons)
- **Key benefit:** Faster cells reduce random coincidence background from radon daughters on wires

---

## 5. Radon Rejection: Upgraded Gas System

**Current:** Gas flushed to suppress radon
**Proposed:** Install a **dedicated radon-trapping cold-trap system** (charcoal trap at −40°C, as used in SNO+ and SuperNEMO) on the gas input line, capable of reducing Rn to <0.1 mBq/m³:

- **Air liquide radon-free helium supply** with continuous radon monitoring via electrostatic radon detectors (Durridge RAD7 or custom alpha counters)
- Closed-loop gas recirculation with molecular sieve + cold trap regeneration
- Continuous radon monitoring at the gas outlet with sensitivity <1 mBq/m³

## 6. Magnetic Field: Coil Upgrade for Uniformity

**Current:** 3 mT field (charge sign only)
**Proposed:** Replace with a **segmented coil array** wound from **Rutherford-cable superconducting wire (NbTi)** running at modest current in a bath cryostat, or more practically:

- Use **water-cooled aluminum strip coils** with active current stabilization (±0.1% regulation) to achieve **field uniformity better than 1% across the tracking volume**, enabling eventual momentum measurement rather than just charge sign

## 7. Front-End Electronics: Replace Charge ADCs with SiPM-Based Readout (Long-Term)

**Proposed:** Replace PMTs + acrylic light guides with **arrays of 6×6 mm² SiPM tiles (Hamamatsu S13360-6050PE or FBK NUV-HD)** mounted directly on the scintillator face:

- SiPMs are **insensitive to magnetic fields** (critical at 3 mT, which is actually benign for PMTs, but SiPMs eliminate this concern entirely)
- PDE ~50% at 420 nm vs PMT QE ~25%, giving ~2× more photoelectrons
- Directly tile the 19×19 cm face with a **4×4 array of 4.5 cm × 4.5 cm SiPM modules**, each read by its own channel or ganged in groups
- Expected improvement: energy resolution → ~14% FWHM @ 1 MeV; timing → ~0.15 ns sigma @ 1 MeV
- This eliminates the entire light-guide + PMT + iron-plate assembly, reducing material budget

## 8. Shielding Enhancement

**Current:** Iron + water shielding
**Proposed:** Add a **15 cm layer of ultrapure water (< 0.1 ppt U/Th)** as an inner active muon veto using **8-inch HQE PMTs** in the water volume (water Cherenkov veto), replacing or augmenting the outer passive iron shield:

- Provides active tagging of muon-induced neutrons, which are a leading background near Q = 3.03 MeV
- Can be built from the existing water shielding infrastructure

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the 76 mm standard PMTs with high-quantum-efficiency super-bialkali PMTs (e.g., Hamamatsu R7081HQE, ~35% QE) combined with shortening the acrylic light guide from 30 cm to ≤15 cm and reading out with 5 GS/s waveform digitizers using digital constant-fraction discrimination — this single change simultaneously pushes energy resolution below 18% FWHM and time resolution well below 0.3 ns sigma at 1 MeV, addressing both calorimeter performance requirements with margin.

This is the NEMO-3 / SuperNEMO demonstrator situation, so the task is to bring the calorimeter to the stated requirements while keeping the tracker and shielding design.

**Requirements vs. present performance**

- Energy resolution: present 20% FWHM at 1 MeV, required ≤18% (SuperNEMO aimed at 7-8% at 1 MeV for 0νββ sensitivity, but the stated spec is ≤18% in every cell).
- Time resolution: present 0.30 ns sigma, requirement 0.6 ns, so timing is already met. Do not sacrifice it.
- Granularity: 19 cm cells are fine as long as two electrons separated by ≥6 cm hit different cells. This is the critical point, discussed below.
- Depth: ≥3 cm is required, and the present 11 cm is more than sufficient.
- Magnetic field: every component must work in 3 mT.

**Problems and fixes**

1. **Granularity vs. the 6 cm separation requirement.** With 19 × 19 cm² faces, two electrons 6 cm apart will often enter the same cell, so their energies are summed and the individual-electron energy measurement is lost. Cell faces would have to be roughly ≤6 cm, which is a major redesign. The cell face must be reduced to about 5-6 cm (e.g., 5 × 5 cm² blocks, possibly in a mosaic) so that any two electrons 6 cm apart are always in different cells. This is by far the most consequential change. It implies roughly 10× more channels (6 m × 3.5 m × 2 walls = 42 m²; at 5×5 cm² that is ~17,000 channels), and thus PMTs cannot be 76 mm per cell without light guides fanning out.

2. **Photodetector geometry.** The 30 cm light guides plus PMTs with diameters (76 mm) larger than the 5-6 cm cell face cannot be tiled. Options: (a) smaller PMTs (e.g., 25-38 mm) coupled directly or with very short guides; (b) silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs), small, compact, immune to magnetic fields, and allowing direct readout. SiPMs would let the PMT be removed from behind the iron plate, but they have dark rate, temperature sensitivity, and limited area, and there is a risk to timing and gain stability. A compact option is small-diameter, high-quantum-efficiency PMTs with short guides.

3. **Magnetic field and the iron shield.** The 3 mT field is applied across the PMTs. The iron plate behind was meant to shield them, but with a short or absent light guide, the PMTs would be inside the field region. Fix: use PMTs with mu-metal shielding, or SiPMs. Ensure the PMT axis alignment relative to the field.

4. **Energy resolution (20% → ≤18% at 1 MeV).** Sources of improvement: use scintillator with higher light yield (e.g., polystyrene doped for higher output, or PVT with good optical clarity); minimize light-guide losses (a 30 cm guide loses light; shorten it); use high-QE (super-bialkali or ultra-bialkali, ~35-40% QE) PMTs; wrap the scintillator with reflective material (e.g., Teflon/Tyvek, aluminized Mylar) and improve optical coupling (optical grease/pads). Reducing the guide from 30 cm to a few cm should markedly increase photoelectron statistics and bring resolution to the 7-8% level seen in later R&D.

5. **Depth:** keep a depth of ≥3 cm; 10-15 cm is more than enough, but with 5 cm faces a depth of ~10 cm is fine for a cell aspect ratio that keeps light collection acceptable. Reduce it somewhat (e.g., ~7-10 cm) to improve resolution and limit gamma sensitivity if desired, but not below 3 cm.

6. **Timing:** with smaller cells and shorter guides, timing will improve, giving margin below 0.6 ns.

7. **Calibration/monitoring:** add LED or laser light-injection and 207Bi source systems to keep the 18% resolution in every cell, with gain monitoring per channel.

**Summary of upgrade**

Replace 19 cm cells with finely segmented cells with faces ≲5-6 cm; shorten or eliminate the long light guides; use compact, high-QE, magnetically shielded small PMTs or SiPMs; optimize scintillator and wrapping; add per-channel calibration. Resolution and timing then meet the specs, and every electron pair separated by ≥6 cm is measured in separate cells.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Shrink the calorimeter cell faces from 19 × 19 cm² to about 5-6 cm (with correspondingly small, field-tolerant photodetectors and short light guides) so that electrons ≥6 cm apart always land in different cells and are measured individually.

# Concrete Hardware Upgrades for the Next Phase

## 1. Replace PMTs with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)

**Technology:** Arrays of SiPM tiles (e.g., Hamamatsu S13360 series or FBK NUV-HD), tiling the back face of each scintillator cell, eliminating the 30 cm acrylic light guide and iron backing plate.

**Physics motivation:** The 76 mm PMTs require the 30 cm acrylic light guide precisely because they cannot operate in the 3 mT magnetic field — even this modest field deflects the dynode-chain electrons enough to degrade gain. SiPMs are intrinsically field-insensitive solid-state devices. Removing the light guide dramatically increases light collection efficiency: a light guide of 30 cm inevitably loses photons to attenuation and geometric solid-angle losses. More photons reaching the photodetector directly improves both energy resolution (σ_E/E ∝ 1/√N_pe) and time resolution (σ_t ∝ 1/√N_pe). The current energy resolution is 20% FWHM at 1 MeV; the requirement is ≤18% FWHM. SiPFs with photon detection efficiency ~50% (vs ~25% for a bialkali PMT coupled through a long light guide) can plausibly reduce FWHM to ~14–15% at 1 MeV, comfortably meeting the specification. The time resolution requirement (≤0.6 ns σ at 1 MeV) is currently met at 0.30 ns but the existing iron plate behind each PMT creates a dead zone and additional material; removing it simplifies the structure. SiPMs also allow the cells to be made more compact in depth, freeing mechanical space.

---

## 2. Replace Polystyrene Scintillator with PVT-based or Polyvinyl-toluene Scintillator with Higher Light Yield

**Technology:** Cast PVT scintillator (e.g., equivalent to BC-408 or EJ-200) instead of plain polystyrene, maintaining the same 19×19 cm² face geometry.

**Physics motivation:** Standard polystyrene scintillator yields roughly 8,000–10,000 photons/MeV; PVT-based scintillators yield ~10,000–11,000 photons/MeV with better transparency and longer attenuation length (~380 cm vs ~250 cm). Over the 11 cm cell depth this matters less than the light guide, but once the light guide is removed (upgrade #1), cell-internal light transport becomes the dominant loss. The higher attenuation length of PVT means more photons survive the bounce path to the SiPM tiles at the back face. This directly tightens both energy and time resolution. Additionally, PVT has a faster emission time constant (~2.1 ns vs ~3.5 ns for pure polystyrene), improving the time resolution relevant for the external-background rejection cut, and enabling the ≤0.6 ns σ requirement at 1 MeV to be met with margin.

---

## 3. Increase Scintillator Cell Depth to ~15 cm

**Technology:** Recast scintillator cells with depth increased from 11 cm to ~15 cm, same face area.

**Physics motivation:** The Q-value of ¹⁰⁰Mo is 3.034 MeV. Each electron in a 0νββ decay can carry up to nearly the full Q-value. The range of a 3 MeV electron in polystyrene (density ~1.06 g/cm³) is approximately 14–15 mm in terms of CSDA range, but the practical containment length including straggling is closer to 13–14 mm. The requirement states cells must be "at least 3 cm deep so that it fully absorbs 3 MeV electrons" — 11 cm already exceeds this. However, 11 cm corresponds to only ~11.6 g/cm² of polystyrene, and shower leakage at 3 MeV causes non-Gaussian tails on the high side of the energy response, worsening the effective FWHM. Increasing depth to 15 cm (~15.9 g/cm²) better contains the electromagnetic shower and reduces energy leakage fluctuations. This tightens the energy resolution at 3 MeV where the signal electrons sit, and reduces a background from partially-contained tracks that can mimic a signal by appearing as two electrons summing to Q. The only cost is modest additional mass and mechanical re-engineering.

---

## 4. Upgrade Tracking with Drift Cells Having Stereo-angle or Longitudinal Segmentation

**Technology:** Replace the existing single-layer Geiger-mode cells with smaller-diameter, faster-drift proportional drift tubes arranged in alternating stereo layers (e.g., ±5° stereo), or add cathode-strip readout for longitudinal coordinate measurement.

**Physics motivation:** The existing Geiger-mode cells reconstruct the transverse (x–y) track projection well but have poor longitudinal (z, along the foil height) resolution. This limits vertex resolution along the foil, allowing background events whose two electrons originate from different foil locations to be misidentified as a correlated pair. The 3 mT magnetic field is used only for charge-sign determination; the track curvature carries no momentum information. With better 3D vertex resolution, one can more tightly constrain the two-electron vertex to a single point on the foil (within ~1 cm³ rather than ~1 × 1 × 10 cm³), suppressing chance coincidences between uncorrelated electrons from different radon or ²¹⁴Bi decays at different foil positions. Stereo-angle proportional tubes also provide timing information to tag delayed coincidences (e.g., ²¹⁴Bi→²¹⁴Po) used to veto radon backgrounds.

---

## 5. Add a Thin Radon-Trapping Membrane or Replace Helium Gas with He+Ar Mixture with Online Rn Monitoring

**Technology:** A continuous radon-trapping cold-trap loop (using activated charcoal at −40°C) on the gas recirculation circuit, supplemented by an online radon emanation monitor (electrostatic Rn monitor, sensitivity ~1 mBq/m³).

**Physics motivation:** The dominant background in this class of experiment is ²¹⁴Bi from ²²²Rn daughters deposited on or near the source foil. The detector already flushes gas, but dynamic flushing without trapping merely dilutes Rn rather than removing it efficiently. A charcoal cold trap on the recirculation loop can reduce Rn in the tracking volume to <0.1 mBq/m³, reducing the rate of ²¹⁴Bi→²¹⁴Po (BiPo) sequences and isolated high-energy electrons that form the main irreducible background below Q. The continuous Rn monitor allows real-time flagging of data taken during elevated Rn periods (e.g., following a gas-system opening), enabling those runs to be excluded without blinding the entire dataset.

| Upgrade | Key Gain |
|---|---|
| SiPM replacement | Energy + time resolution; removes B-field PMT problem |
| PVT scintillator | Light yield, attenuation length, faster timing |
| Deeper cells (15 cm) | Shower containment at 3 MeV |
| Stereo drift tubes | 3D vertex resolution, Rn-background tagging |
| Radon cold-trap loop | Reduction of dominant ²¹⁴Bi background |

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the 76 mm PMTs and 30 cm acrylic light guides with SiPM tile arrays coupled directly to the scintillator cell back faces, since the light guide is the primary cause of photon loss that limits both energy and time resolution, the PMTs cannot be reliably operated in the 3 mT field without the iron shielding plate that complicates the geometry, and the SiPM upgrade simultaneously addresses the energy-resolution requirement (≤18% FWHM at 1 MeV), the time-resolution requirement (≤0.6 ns σ at 1 MeV), and removes field-sensitivity constraints on the calorimeter layout.

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for Next-Phase Detector

## 1. **Upgrade: Replace PMTs with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)**
**Technology:** 6×6 mm or 8×8 mm SiPMs (gain ~10^6) with integrated active quenching circuits, temperature-stabilized readout electronics.

**Physics Motivation:** 
- Current PMTs achieve 0.30 ns time resolution; SiPMs can reach 0.15–0.20 ns with fast scintillation coupling and optimized electronics
- Meets 0.6 ns σ requirement with comfortable margin, improving external-background rejection
- SiPMs are insensitive to the 3 mT magnetic field (whereas PMTs suffer some gain loss)
- Improved photon detection efficiency (>50% vs ~25%) reduces statistical energy resolution floor
- Better single-photon time response helps reject cosmogenic backgrounds

## 2. **Upgrade: Replace Polystyrene with Plastic Scintillator Tiles + Wavelength-Shifting Fiber Readout**
**Technology:** EJ-200 or equivalent 3 cm thick tiles with embedded Y-11 WLS fibers coupled to SiPMs; multi-cell fiber bundles to reduce dead regions.

**Physics Motivation:**
- Polystyrene has slower scintillation decay (~2.7 ns) limiting time resolution; plastic scintillators achieve ~2.3 ns and couple better to SiPMs
- WLS fibers reduce light guide bulk (acrylic adds propagation time jitter), improving timing to <0.5 ns σ
- Higher light yield per MeV improves energy resolution (currently 20% FWHM) toward 18% target
- Fiber geometry allows finer lateral segmentation without increasing PMT count

## 3. **Upgrade: Increase Calorimeter Cell Segmentation to 10 cm × 10 cm**
**Technology:** Dual-readout configuration with position-sensitive SiPM arrays or position-sensitive fibers.

**Physics Motivation:**
- Current 19 cm × 19 cm cells risk energy leakage when two 1–1.5 MeV electrons enter <6 cm apart (6 cm separation requirement)
- Finer segmentation ensures each electron (whether they converge or diverge) deposits energy in distinct cells
- Improves vertex reconstruction precision and reduces pile-up ambiguity in high-activity decay signatures
- 10 cm cells remain thick enough (11 cm depth) for full MeV-scale electron absorption

## 4. **Upgrade: Add Thin Muon Veto Layer Behind Calorimeter**
**Technology:** Scintillator paddle array (5 cm × 5 cm, 1 cm thick) with SiPM readout behind iron shielding.

**Physics Motivation:**
- Underground at 3000 m w.e., residual cosmic muons (~10^−6 cm^−2 s^−1) can mimic two-electron events if they decay or create secondary showers
- Muon veto reduces this background by ~3 orders of magnitude with minimal dead time
- Achieves better discrimination than track-curvature alone for high-energy backgrounds

## 5. **Upgrade: Replace Helium Drift Gas with Helium + 5% CO₂ or Xe-based Gas**
**Technology:** Optimized gas mixture with digitized readout electronics; field-shaping wire geometry unchanged.

**Physics Motivation:**
- Current He-based gas has limited electron ionization density; CO₂ or Xe additive increases spatial resolution (~2 mm vs ~5 mm)
- Better track reconstruction improves charge-sign discrimination and vertex precision near the Mo foil
- Xe-based mixture improves energy resolution in the tracker, reducing ambiguity when electrons are close in angle

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Key Benefit |
|---------|-----------|-------------|
| 1 | SiPMs + fast electronics | Time resolution <0.4 ns σ (margin on 0.6 ns spec) |
| 2 | Plastic scintillator + WLS fibers | Energy resolution <18% FWHM; faster timing |
| 3 | 10 cm × 10 cm cells | Resolves nearby electron pairs reliably |
| 4 | Muon veto | Cosmic background rejection |
