# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for the Tracker-Calorimeter Detector

## 1. Calorimeter Photodetectors: Replace PMTs with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)

**Problem:** 76 mm PMTs are sensitive to the 3 mT magnetic field. Even this modest field can deflect photoelectrons within the dynode structure, degrading gain and resolution. Iron shielding plates behind each PMT add dead material and complicate the geometry.

**Proposal:** Replace each 76 mm PMT + iron plate assembly with an array of **SiPMs (e.g., Hamamatsu S13360 series or FBK NUV-HD, 6×6 mm² tiles)**, tiling a ~20×20 mm² active area at the end of the light guide. SiPMs are completely immune to magnetic fields, have higher photon detection efficiency (~50% PDE vs ~25% for a standard bialkali PMT), and are compact. The iron shielding plates become unnecessary, reducing passive material.

**Expected gain:** Better photoelectron yield → improved energy resolution toward the 18% FWHM target. Time resolution improves because SiPM transit-time spread is ~100 ps sigma versus ~1 ns for a 76 mm PMT, comfortably meeting the 0.6 ns requirement.

---

## 2. Scintillator Material: Replace Polystyrene with PVT-Based or LaBr₃ Scintillator

**Option A (conservative):** Switch from polystyrene (light yield ~8,000 ph/MeV, slow component present) to **EJ-200 or BC-408 PVT-based scintillator** (light yield ~10,000 ph/MeV, decay time ~2.1 ns). This is a drop-in replacement with the same machining properties but ~25% more light, directly improving both energy and time resolution. Cost is modest.

**Option B (aggressive):** Use **LaBr₃:Ce crystals** (light yield ~63,000 ph/MeV, decay time ~16 ns, energy resolution ~3% at 1 MeV). This would dramatically exceed the 18% FWHM requirement and give superb time resolution. Drawbacks: LaBr₃ is hygroscopic, expensive, and contains internal ¹³⁸La radioactivity (~0.09 Bq/g) which must be characterized as a background source. For the outer cells furthest from the foil, this background is manageable.

**Recommendation:** Adopt EJ-200/BC-408 PVT as the baseline upgrade; deploy LaBr₃ selectively in a subset of cells for cross-calibration and performance benchmarking.

---

## 3. Light Guide: Replace Acrylic with Wavelength-Shifting (WLS) Plate + Short Acrylic Coupler

**Problem:** The 30 cm acrylic light guide causes significant photon loss through bulk absorption and total-internal-reflection escape, and adds ~30 cm of non-instrumented depth per side.

**Proposal:** Replace the long acrylic guide with a **3–5 mm thick PMMA wavelength-shifting plate** (doped with Y-11 or BBQ fluorophore) bonded directly to the back face of the scintillator cell, read out by SiPM tiles on the edges of the WLS plate. This is the technology used in CALICE and CMS HGCAL prototypes. Light collection uniformity improves, the assembly depth shrinks by ~25 cm per side, and the coupling efficiency increases.

---

## 4. Tracking: Replace Geiger-Mode Drift Cells with Small-Diameter Drift Tubes (Straw Tubes)

**Problem:** Geiger-mode cells have a long dead time after firing (~ms), preventing multi-hit reconstruction if two tracks pass nearby. They also have limited two-track separation.

**Proposal:** Replace Geiger cells with **4 mm diameter aluminized Mylar straw tubes** operated in proportional mode (as used in ATLAS TRT or COMET), still using a helium-based gas mixture (He/isobutane 80/20 or He/CO₂). Straws provide:
- Sub-millimeter spatial resolution per hit
- Dead time of order microseconds rather than milliseconds
- Better two-track separation for the 6 cm vertex separation requirement
- Reduced sensitivity to the 3 mT field (proportional operation is field-tolerant at this level)

Wire diameter 25–30 µm gold-plated tungsten. Operate at ~1500 V for a gas gain of ~10⁵.

---

## 5. Front-End Electronics: Upgrade to Waveform-Sampling ASICs

**Problem:** Simple charge-integrating ADCs and leading-edge discriminators for timing do not extract the full information available from each scintillator pulse.

**Proposal:** Instrument each calorimeter channel with a **waveform-sampling ASIC** such as the **TARGET-C** (used in IACT cameras) or **DRS4** chip (PSI), sampling at 1–2 GSa/s with 12-bit depth. Benefits:
- Offline constant-fraction discrimination → time resolution improvement by factor ~2 over leading-edge
- Pulse-shape discrimination to reject alpha/neutron backgrounds
- Charge integration with configurable gate → better linearity
- Identification of pile-up events

For the tracker straws, use **AFTER/AGET ASICs** (GET electronics, used in TPCs) for shaping and digitization.

---

## 6. Radon Mitigation: Active Radon-Trapping System on Gas Flush

**Problem:** Radon daughters (²¹⁴Bi → ²¹⁴Po in particular) on tracker wires or foil surfaces mimic double-beta decay signals via the BiPo process and are a dominant background.

**Proposal:** Install a **charcoal cold-trap radon-removal unit** (liquid nitrogen cooled activated charcoal, as used by SuperNEMO) on the helium gas supply line, achieving radon activity <0.1 mBq/m³ in the tracking volume. Supplement with a **radon-tight neoprene/Tedlar inner enclosure** around the tracking volume, sealed with epoxy-glued joints. Monitor continuously with **electrostatic radon detectors** (alpha counting type, sensitivity ~1 mBq/m³) at the gas outlet.

---

## 7. Foil Upgrade: Higher-Purity, Thinner Foils with Improved Source Preparation

**Problem:** At 45 mg/cm², electron energy loss and multiple scattering in the foil degrade the energy sum measurement. Impurities in the molybdenum (²⁰⁸Tl, ²¹⁴Bi) contribute background.

**Proposal:** 
- Reduce foil thickness to **30–35 mg/cm²** (still mechanically self-supporting if alloyed with a small fraction of PVA binder, as in NEMO-3/SuperNEMO technique)
- Use **zone-refined / ICP-MS certified ¹⁰⁰Mo** with ²²⁸Ra < 10 µBq/kg and ²²⁶Ra < 10 µBq/kg
- Apply **electrodeposition** rather than powder pressing for uniform density and minimum pinhole fraction

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Addresses | Technology Readiness |
|---|---|---|
| SiPM array replacing PMT | B-field immunity, time & energy resolution | TRL 8–9 |
| EJ-200 PVT scintillator | Energy & time resolution | TRL 9 |
| WLS plate light guide | Light yield, compactness | TRL 7–8 |
| Straw tube tracker | Two-track separation, dead time | TRL 8–9 |
| Waveform-sampling ASICs | Timing, pile-up, PSD | TRL 8 |
| Cold-trap radon removal | BiPo background | TRL 8 |
| Thinner, purer foils | Energy resolution, background | TRL 7–8 |

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the 76 mm PMTs (and their iron shielding plates) with SiPM tile arrays, since this simultaneously eliminates the magnetic-field sensitivity of the photodetectors, removes the need for the iron shielding plates, increases photon detection efficiency by roughly a factor of two, and directly enables both the 18% FWHM energy resolution and sub-0.6 ns time resolution requirements to be met without any other changes to the scintillator or light guide geometry.

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for the Planar Tracker-Calorimeter Detector

## Analysis of Current Limitations

The detector currently achieves 20% FWHM energy resolution but must meet 18% FWHM—a modest but non-trivial gap. The time resolution target of 0.6 ns sigma is already being met (0.30 ns current vs 0.6 ns required), but the energy resolution is the binding constraint.

## Specific Hardware Upgrade Recommendations

### 1. **Replace PMTs with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)**
- **Current:** 76 mm PMTs with ~25% quantum efficiency in blue region
- **Upgrade:** 8-12 SiPMs (6×6 mm each) per cell in parallel configuration
- **Rationale:** SiPMs offer 40-50% QE, lower dark noise when cooled to -20°C, insensitivity to 3 mT magnetic field (unlike PMTs), and intrinsically faster timing. This directly improves light collection statistics, reducing energy resolution by ~15% relative.
- **Implementation:** Mount SiPMs on ceramic substrate directly behind scintillator; use active temperature stabilization and preamplifiers integrated into the light guide.

### 2. **Upgrade Scintillator to Higher Light-Yield Material**
- **Current:** Polystyrene (typical 10,000 photons/MeV)
- **Upgrade:** Polyvinyltoluene (PVT) or doped polystyrene with higher wavelength shifter concentration (15,000-18,000 photons/MeV)
- **Rationale:** Increased photon yield directly reduces statistical fluctuations in energy reconstruction. Combined with SiPM upgrade, this could achieve 16-17% FWHM.

### 3. **Reduce Cell Optical Losses**
- **Current:** 30 cm acrylic light guide introduces ~15% transmission losses
- **Upgrade:** Replace with black-walled wavelength-shifting (WLS) fiber bundle (BCF-91A fibers, 2-3 mm diameter) or direct coupling with air gaps and reflective surfaces
- **Rationale:** Fewer photons lost before SiPM means higher light collection efficiency and better energy linearity.

### 4. **Implement Active Magnetic-Field Compensation for PMTs (if PMTs retained)**
- **Alternative to SiPM upgrade:** Use Helmholtz coil structures around each PMT to locally null the 3 mT field
- **Rationale:** PMTs experience gain shift and dark current degradation in magnetic fields; local compensation improves stability. However, this is less elegant than switching to SiPMs.

### 5. **Upgrade Readout Electronics**
- **Current:** Likely conventional charge-to-digital conversion
- **Upgrade:** Waveform digitization at 1-2 GS/s with 14-bit ADCs + real-time pulse shape analysis
- **Rationale:** Allows baseline subtraction, pile-up rejection, and correction for non-linearity in the photon detection chain. Can improve effective energy resolution by 10-15%.

### 6. **Thicker Scintillator Cells for Better Light Collection Geometry**
- **Current:** 11 cm depth
- **Upgrade:** Increase to 13-15 cm depth (still absorbs 3 MeV electrons)
- **Rationale:** Improved light collection geometry reduces dependence on edge-of-cell response. Combined with SiPMs, reduces energy resolution variance across cell volume.

---

## Integration Strategy

The most cost-effective path achieving 18% FWHM:
1. **Primary:** Replace PMTs with SiPM arrays (immediate ~20→18% improvement alone)
2. **Secondary:** Upgrade to PVT scintillator with higher photon yield
3. **Tertiary:** Implement waveform digitization for corrections

This combination should reliably achieve **17-18% FWHM** while improving magnetic-field immunity and timing resolution as a bonus.

---

**TOP RECOMMENDATION:** Replace the 76 mm PMTs with parallel arrays of temperature-controlled Silicon Photomultipliers (8-12 units per cell, 6×6 mm each) coupled directly or via short WLS fiber bundles to the scintillator cells—this single change eliminates magnetic-field sensitivity issues, increases quantum efficiency from ~25% to ~45%, and directly improves energy resolution to meet the 18% FWHM requirement.

# Proposed hardware upgrades for the calorimeter walls

## What the present calorimeter does and does not meet

| Requirement | Present cells | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Energy resolution ≤18% FWHM at 1 MeV | 20% FWHM | **Fails** |
| Time resolution ≤0.6 ns σ at 1 MeV | 0.30 ns | Passes, with margin |
| Electrons ≥6 cm apart land in separate cells | 19 × 19 cm faces | **Fails badly** |
| Depth ≥3 cm | 11 cm | Passes, with excess depth |
| Works in 3 mT | Needs PMTs behind iron | Only with shielding |

The 6 cm separation rule sets the cell size:

- For square cells of side s, two points 6 cm apart can still fall in the same cell if the cell diagonal exceeds 6 cm.
- A guaranteed split therefore needs s√2 ≤ 6 cm, so s ≤ 4.2 cm.
- A 19 cm face fails by almost a factor of 5.

The calorimeter must therefore be rebuilt with much finer cells, not tuned.

## 1. Re-segment each wall into ~4 × 4 cm scintillator cells

- **Cell size:** use polystyrene (or PVT) cells with 4.0 × 4.0 cm faces, giving a 5.7 cm diagonal (under 6 cm).
- **Depth:** about 3.5–4 cm. This is still above the 3 cm full-absorption requirement for 3 MeV electrons, which have a range of about 1.5 cm in plastic. It also gives a compact, cube-like cell with good light-collection uniformity, which the 11 cm depth does not.
- **Channel count:** each 6 × 3.5 m wall needs about 150 × 88 ≈ 13,000 cells, or about 26,000 for both walls.
- **Wrapping:** wrap each cell individually in specular reflector (3M ESR or PTFE) so cells are optically isolated and light does not leak into neighbours.
- **Entrance face:** use a thin aluminized Mylar window (a few µm) so the electron loses as little energy as possible before entering the scintillator.

## 2. Replace the PMTs and light guides with directly coupled SiPMs

At this granularity, 76 mm PMTs physically cannot fit. A light-guide-plus-PMT layout would also be far too massive and too radioactive at 26,000 channels.

**Photosensor**
- Glue an array of 6 × 6 mm SiPMs directly to the rear face of each cell. Examples are Hamamatsu S14160 or FBK NUV-HD, with photon detection efficiency of about 45–50%.
- A 2×2 array per cell is a reasonable starting point.

**Magnetic field**
- SiPMs are unaffected by 3 mT.
- This removes the iron plates, the 30 cm light guides and mu-metal, satisfying the field requirement without any shielding.

**Energy resolution**
- The resolution goal of 18% FWHM corresponds to 7.6% σ. Photostatistics alone then require more than about 170 photoelectrons per MeV, and about 300 or more to leave headroom for non-uniformity.
- Polystyrene emits about 10⁴ photons per MeV. Direct coupling, short light paths and good optical coverage should reach several hundred photoelectrons per MeV. That target is about 10–12% FWHM.

**Timing**
- SiPM single-photon timing plus high photoelectron counts keeps σ well below 0.6 ns. Below 0.3 ns is likely.

**Radiopurity**
- Silicon has much lower ²¹⁴Bi and ²⁰⁸Tl content than PMT glass, and the sensor mass near the source drops by orders of magnitude. This directly reduces background near the 3.03 MeV Q-value.

**Dark counts**
- Room-temperature dark rates are about 50 kHz/mm², or a few MHz per cell. A modest threshold of about 50 keV handles this.
- Mild cooling to about 10 °C, using the existing water shield as a heat sink, gives extra margin.

## 3. Front-end electronics

- Use a low-power multichannel ASIC for SiPM readout, such as Weeroc CITIROC/PETIROC or a TOFPET2-class chip. These provide charge plus sub-100 ps time-to-digital conversion for each cell.
- For calibration samples, add waveform sampling on a subset of channels with a SAMPIC-type chip.
- Provide per-channel bias trimming and temperature compensation of the SiPM gain.
- Run in-situ calibration with an LED or laser fibre fan-out to each cell, and with ²⁰⁷Bi sources for the absolute energy scale.

## 4. Supporting items

- **Mechanics:** use low-background mechanical frames of radiopure copper or PTFE, replacing the iron and PMT supports.
- **Material screening:** screen all SiPM boards, glue and cables by HPGe counting.
- **Surface events:** use cell-edge hit sharing with neighbouring cells to identify electrons that strike near cell boundaries and are back-scattered. Event reconstruction combined with tracker extrapolation can handle these.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Rebuild each calorimeter wall as ~4 × 4 × 4 cm polystyrene cells read directly by SiPM arrays (no light guides, no PMTs), which meets the 6 cm two-electron separation, improves resolution below 18% FWHM, and is immune to the 3 mT field.

# Hardware Upgrades for the Next-Phase Planar Double-Beta-Decay Detector

## 1. Diagnosis: which requirements the present calorimeter fails

| Requirement | Present cells | Status |
|---|---|---|
| ≤18% FWHM at 1 MeV | 20% FWHM | **Fails** |
| ≤0.6 ns (σ) at 1 MeV | 0.30 ns | Passes with margin |
| Electrons ≥6 cm apart land in different, separately read cells | 19 cm × 19 cm faces | **Fails badly** |
| Depth ≥3 cm, full absorption of 3 MeV electrons | 11 cm | Passes |
| Every part works in 3 mT | PMTs work only behind iron shields | Marginal |

**The granularity condition.** To guarantee that two points 6 cm apart never share a cell, no cell may contain two points 6 cm apart. So the largest dimension of a cell face (its diagonal) must be below 6 cm.

- For square faces this means a side below 6/√2 ≈ 4.2 cm.
- A practical choice is 4 cm × 4 cm faces, with a 5.7 cm diagonal.

**Channel count.** Each wall is 6 m × 3.5 m.

- With 4 cm cells that is about 150 × 88 ≈ 13,000 cells per wall, or roughly 26,000 cells in total.
- This compares with about 550 cells per wall today.

A 76 mm PMT cannot physically serve a 4 cm cell, and 26,000 PMTs with light guides and iron shields would be impractical. Granularity therefore forces a change of photosensor.

## 2. Upgrade A (core): finely segmented scintillator read out by SiPMs

**Technology**

- **Cells:** 4 × 4 cm² polystyrene or PVT scintillator tiles, about 4 cm deep.
  - This exceeds the 3 cm needed to stop 3 MeV electrons (range about 1.5 cm).
  - It keeps some gamma efficiency.
- **Wrapping:** each tile is wrapped in a reflector (ESR or Teflon) to optically isolate it.
- **Readout:** each tile is directly coupled, with no light guide, to a silicon photomultiplier array.
  - Examples are a 2×2 array of 6×6 mm² devices, or larger-area SiPM tiles.
  - High photon-detection efficiency (about 40–50%) is needed.

**Physics motivation**

- **Field immunity.**
  - SiPMs are insensitive to a 3 mT field, and in fact to fields of tesla scale.
  - This removes the iron plates and the magnetic dependence of PMT gain and timing.
  - It satisfies the "every part works in 3 mT" requirement by construction.
- **Energy resolution.**
  - Removing the 30 cm acrylic light guide eliminates its attenuation losses.
  - A small, well-reflecting tile gives more uniform light collection.
  - High-PDE SiPMs give a photoelectron yield comparable to or above the present PMT readout.
  - Resolution is limited by photostatistics plus non-uniformity, so the 18% FWHM target becomes reachable. This must be verified with prototypes before committing.
  - Better resolution narrows the 2νββ tail under the 3.03 MeV peak, which is the irreducible background.
- **Two-electron separation.**
  - Each electron's energy is measured in its own cell.
  - This enables single-electron energy spectra and angular-correlation studies that can discriminate the 0νββ mechanism, such as light neutrino exchange versus right-handed currents.
- **Timing.**
  - SiPMs with fast scintillator easily reach about 0.3–0.5 ns at 1 MeV.
  - This keeps the time-of-flight rejection of crossing electrons from outside.
- **Radiopurity.**
  - SiPMs contain far less mass than PMT glass, which is a major source of ⁴⁰K, U and Th.
  - This lowers the gamma background reaching the foils and trackers.

**Implementation points**

- **Dark counts.** SiPM dark rate per channel is acceptable with a threshold of about 30–50 keV. Mild cooling, to about 0–10 °C, plus a time coincidence with the tracker can reduce it further.
- **Electronics.** Multichannel ASICs (Citiroc/TOFPET-type) provide charge and timing per channel. Their low mass keeps the front-end radiopure.
- **Calibration.** Each channel needs LED or laser gain monitoring, temperature compensation of the SiPM bias, and in-situ ²⁰⁷Bi sources.
- **Edge effects.** With small cells, electrons back-scatter or exit sideways into neighbouring tiles. Two steps handle this:
  - Associate each extrapolated track with its tile cluster.
  - Sum the energy of a cluster when only one track points to it.
  
  The 6 cm separation rule keeps two-electron clusters distinguishable.

## 3. Upgrade B: tracker–calorimeter matching and timing electronics

**Technology:** finer-pitch drift-cell readout near the wall, or a thin plane of position-sensitive detectors in front of the calorimeter.

**Motivation:** with about 26,000 small cells, the track-to-cell association must be unambiguous. Better impact-point extrapolation reduces mis-association and improves the measurement of each electron's individual energy.

## 4. Upgrade C: source and background improvements

These support the calorimeter upgrade.

- **Purer, thinner or more uniform foils.** Material purified by distillation or chromatography reduces ²¹⁴Bi and ²⁰⁸Tl in the source. Thinner, uniform foils also reduce energy loss and straggling, which complements the better calorimeter resolution.
- **Radon control.** Use a radon-tight tracker envelope with an anti-radon air supply and a radon trap on the gas flush. This cuts ²¹⁴Bi deposited on the wires and foils.

## Summary

The decisive change is replacing the 19 cm PMT-read cells with finely segmented scintillator tiles of 4 cm or smaller, directly read by SiPMs. This one change addresses four requirements at once:

- the 6 cm separation requirement, which is impossible to meet with the present cells;
- operation in the 3 mT field;
- the energy-resolution target, by removing the light guides;
- radiopurity.

It does so while preserving the sub-nanosecond timing.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the 19 cm PMT-read scintillator cells with ~4 cm × 4 cm (≤4.2 cm side), ≥3 cm-deep scintillator tiles each directly read out by magnetic-field-immune SiPMs.

This is the SuperNEMO-type demonstrator. The current cell gives 20% FWHM against a requirement of 18% FWHM or better, while timing (0.30 ns against 0.6 ns required) already passes with margin. The upgrade should therefore target energy resolution first, without breaking the other constraints.

**Key observations**

1. Energy resolution is the only failing spec. The requirement is 18% FWHM or better at 1 MeV, and the present cells give 20%. Timing has a factor of 2 of margin, so the time resolution can be traded for light collection.

2. The 3 mT field is not negligible for a 76 mm PMT, and the iron plate behind it helps only partially. The field-parallel orientation (parallel to the foil, so perpendicular to the PMT axis) is the worst case for the dynode chain, so shielding is needed. Magnetic sensitivity can degrade gain and resolution.

3. The 6 cm separation requirement means cell faces should be no larger than about 6 cm × 6 cm in any case where two electrons could enter the same cell. With 19 cm × 19 cm faces, two electrons 6 cm apart can enter the same cell. The face must be reduced (about 6 cm × 6 cm, or at most a few cm more with careful design), or, equivalently, the cells must be segmented so that any two entry points at least 6 cm apart land in different, separately read-out cells. This is a granularity change, and it matters more than the resolution fix because it is a hard physics requirement for using each electron's energy individually.

4. Depth must be at least 3 cm (to absorb 3 MeV electrons). The existing 11 cm depth is much more than needed, and thinner scintillator reduces the light path, attenuation, and the Compton-like gamma sensitivity. A depth of about 10 cm is not needed for electrons, so a depth of around 3–5 cm is sufficient, improving light collection. The 30 cm light guide is a big loss factor, and removing it (direct coupling) greatly improves light yield, hence resolution.

**Proposed hardware upgrades**

1. **Reduce cell face to about 6 cm × 6 cm (or equivalent finer segmentation)**, so any two electrons separated by at least 6 cm hit different, separately instrumented cells. This directly meets the individual-energy requirement. Keep walls contiguous with minimal dead material (thin reflective wrapping, e.g., Teflon/Mylar).

2. **Cut scintillator depth to about 3–5 cm** (above the 3 cm full-absorption minimum for 3 MeV electrons), reducing the light path and gamma sensitivity.

3. **Remove the long acrylic light guide.** Couple the PMT directly or through a very short guide (a few cm, or none) so that light collection rises substantially. This is the main lever for getting from 20% to better than 18% FWHM, and a well-designed direct-coupled cell can reach roughly 7–8% FWHM at 1 MeV.

4. **Use a matched, smaller-diameter, high-quantum-efficiency PMT** (e.g., 5-inch/3-inch or smaller, with a bialkali photocathode of super-bialkali, 35–40% QE) matched to the new cell face, fixed with optical gel/cement. A cell of 6 cm face matches a roughly 2–3 inch tube. Choose low-radioactivity glass to protect the ultra-low background goal, since the detector searches for a rare decay.

5. **Use a higher light-yield, fast scintillator.** Switch from the base polystyrene to high-quality PVT or polystyrene with optimized dopants (higher yield and short decay time), giving both better statistics and good timing, which is easily within 0.6 ns.

6. **Magnetic compatibility**: surround each PMT with a mu-metal shield plus the iron plate/shielding, and choose tubes with low sensitivity to transverse field (or reduced gain loss, using a gain-stable base, if necessary a low-dynode-count design). Ensure the 3 mT field leaves resolution and gain within spec, and calibrate gains periodically with a light-injection or source system.

7. **Calibration and monitoring**: install a light-injection system (LED/laser fibers) and use 207Bi sources (1 MeV conversion electrons) to check each cell's resolution and timing in situ.

**Expected result**: with a 6 cm face, 3–5 cm depth, direct coupling, and high-QE PMTs, resolution should be about 8% FWHM at 1 MeV (well under 18%), timing about 0.2 ns sigma or better (under 0.6 ns), full containment of 3 MeV electrons, and operation in 3 mT. The sacrifice of the larger 19 cm face is compensated by a higher channel count, which is acceptable.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the 19 cm × 19 cm cells and long acrylic light guides with much smaller (about 6 cm face), thinner (3–5 cm) scintillator cells directly coupled to small, high-QE, magnetically shielded PMTs, so every electron is individually measured with better than 18% FWHM resolution.

# Concrete Hardware Upgrades for the Next Phase

## 1. Calorimeter: Replace PMTs with Large-Area SiPMs (Silicon Photomultipliers)

**Technology:** Tile the 76 mm PMT face with an array of 6 mm × 6 mm SiPM tiles (e.g., Hamamatsu S13360 series or FBK NUV-HD), read out in groups, coupled directly to the scintillator block without the 30 cm acrylic light guide.

**Physics motivation:**
- SiPMs are insensitive to the 3 mT magnetic field, whereas PMTs with 76 mm dynodes suffer gain drift and trajectory distortion of photoelectrons even in weak fields; removing the iron backing plate (currently needed to shield the PMT from the field) reduces passive material and thus back-scattering that degrades energy resolution.
- Eliminating the 30 cm acrylic light guide reduces photon transit-time spread; the guide currently contributes ~0.15–0.20 ns (σ) to the time resolution budget. Shorter light path and faster SiPM response (rise time < 1 ns, no transit-time spread from dynode chains) can push the time resolution well below the required 0.6 ns (σ) at 1 MeV, helping reject crossing-electron backgrounds more efficiently.
- SiPM photon detection efficiency (PDE ~ 50–60% at 420 nm) exceeds that of a standard bialkali PMT (~25%), roughly doubling photoelectron yield. Since energy resolution scales as σ_E/E ∝ 1/√N_pe, doubling N_pe improves the statistical term by √2, pushing σ_E/E from 20% to ~14% FWHM at 1 MeV — comfortably meeting the 18% requirement with margin.
- The 3 cm minimum depth requirement is unaffected; the gain in light collection relaxes the need for thick scintillator to compensate light losses in the guide.

---

## 2. Scintillator: Replace Polystyrene with PVT-Based or Polyvinyl-Toluene Scintillator with Higher Light Yield

**Technology:** Cast cells from EJ-200 (PVT base, light yield ~10,000 photons/MeV) or BC-408, replacing the existing polystyrene (BC-400 equivalent, ~8,000 photons/MeV). Alternatively, use LAB-based plastic scintillator loaded with enriched ¹⁰⁰Mo as a future step, but as an immediate upgrade simply improve the base plastic.

**Physics motivation:**
- Higher intrinsic light yield directly increases N_pe collected at the photodetector, improving both energy and time resolution — both constrained by the problem statement.
- PVT scintillators have longer attenuation lengths (> 4 m vs. ~2 m for some polystyrene formulations), reducing self-absorption losses over the 11 cm depth + light guide path and improving cell-to-cell uniformity, which is critical when every cell must independently meet the 18% specification.
- Better uniformity reduces the spread in energy calibration constants across the ~hundreds of cells, lowering the systematic floor on energy resolution relevant for the 3.03 MeV signal region.

---

## 3. Tracking: Replace Geiger-Mode Drift Cells with Thin-Gap Small-Cell Drift Tubes or Straw Trackers with 3D Hit Reconstruction

**Technology:** Replace Geiger cells with 1 cm diameter drift tubes (e.g., Mylar straws, anode wire at 20 µm gold-plated W) in a He/isobutane (90/10) gas, arranged in crossed stereo layers (axial + ±5° stereo).

**Physics motivation:**
- Geiger-mode cells give only a hit/no-hit per tube and a drift time, reconstructing 2D projections. Stereo straw tubes give a full 3D space point per hit without ambiguity, improving the vertex position resolution on the foil. A better-reconstructed vertex allows tighter angular and spatial coincidence cuts between the two electrons, suppressing the dominant background from two single-β decays in adjacent foil regions.
- The 6 cm minimum separation requirement between two electron entry points on the calorimeter wall relies on track extrapolation precision; smaller cell diameter (1 cm vs. several cm for Geiger cells) improves spatial resolution from ~1 cm to ~200 µm per cell, reducing mis-assignment of two electrons to one calorimeter cell.
- Straw tubes are robust against the 3 mT field (Lorentz angle at 3 mT is negligible at the drift velocities in He-based gas), and the He-based fill gas is preserved, minimising multiple scattering for the low-energy (< 3 MeV) electrons. The radiation length of He/iC₄H₁₀ at atmospheric pressure is ~700 m, so a 50 cm tracking volume corresponds to only ~0.07% X₀ per radiation length, preserving track curvature measurement.
- Faster drift velocity in isobutane-doped He reduces dead time per event, improving efficiency for pile-up rejection without sacrificing the radon-flush gas architecture.

---

## 4. Radon Mitigation: Active Radon-Trapping Cold-Trap Recirculation System

**Technology:** Insert a zeolite or activated-charcoal cold trap (cooled to −40 °C) in the gas recirculation loop, with a redundant radon monitor (electrostatic collection PIN-diode detector, sensitivity < 0.1 mBq/m³).

**Physics motivation:**
- At 3000 m w.e., the dominant background for neutrinoless double-beta decay searches is ²¹⁴Bi (a ²²²Rn daughter) on or near the foil, which produces electrons mimicking the signal topology. Even trace Rn levels (mBq/m³) in the tracking gas produce background events at the 3.03 MeV endpoint region.
- A cold trap with continuous monitoring reduces Rn activity in the gas by factors of 10–100 compared to simple flushing, directly cutting the background index in the region of interest.
- This upgrade is straightforward to implement without opening the detector and complements all other upgrades.

---

## 5. Source Foil: Increase ¹⁰⁰Mo Mass Using Thinner, Wider Foils of Higher Isotopic Enrichment

**Technology:** Increase enrichment from the present level to > 97% (via centrifuge cascade), and thin the foils to ~30 mg/cm² while increasing lateral area; alternatively stack two foil planes 10 cm apart within the same tracking volume.

**Physics motivation:**
- The signal rate scales as N_Mo × T_{1/2}^{−1} (the quantity being measured), so maximising source mass directly improves sensitivity. Currently 9 kg of Mo is used; moving to 15–20 kg through higher enrichment and additional foil area within the existing mechanical frame would improve the half-life sensitivity proportionally.
- Thinner foils (30 mg/cm² vs. 45 mg/cm²) reduce electron energy loss and scattering in the source, sharpening the reconstructed sum-energy peak at Q = 3.03 MeV. # Concrete Hardware Upgrades for the Next Phase

## 1. Replace PMTs with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)

**Technology:** Arrays of SiPM tiles (e.g., Hamamatsu S13360 series or FBK NUV-HD), tiling the back face of each scintillator cell, replacing the 76 mm PMT + 30 cm acrylic light guide assembly.

**Physics motivation:** PMTs are sensitive to even weak magnetic fields; at 3 mT the dynode chain can be significantly affected by field orientation. SiPMs are intrinsically field-insensitive. Eliminating the 30 cm acrylic light guide removes the dominant source of photon loss and time smearing (light travel time dispersion ~1–2 ns across 30 cm). SiPMs have photon detection efficiency ~40–50% vs ~25% for a typical bialkali PMT, directly improving both energy and time resolution via √N photon statistics. The energy resolution scales as 1/√(N_pe), so doubling PDE roughly improves resolution by ~√2, taking 20% FWHM toward ~14% FWHM, comfortably meeting the 18% requirement. The single-photon time resolution of SiPMs (~100 ps) with higher photon yield pushes timing well below the 0.6 ns requirement, strengthening rejection of external crossing electrons. The iron plate behind the PMT (magnetic shielding) becomes unnecessary, reducing passive material that could scatter or absorb electrons.

---

## 2. Replace Polystyrene Scintillator Cells with PVT-Based or Lanthanum Bromide (LaBr₃) Scintillator Cells

**Technology (preferred intermediate option):** PVT (polyvinyl toluene) scintillator with higher light yield (~10,000 photons/MeV vs ~8,000 for polystyrene), or for a more ambitious upgrade, inorganic scintillator crystals such as LaBr₃:Ce (~63,000 photons/MeV, decay time ~16 ns).

**Physics motivation:** The energy resolution requirement of 18% FWHM at 1 MeV with the current 20% performance leaves very little margin. Higher light yield directly improves resolution. LaBr₃ would give intrinsic resolution ~3–4% FWHM at 1 MeV, far exceeding the requirement. Even upgraded PVT with better optical coupling brings meaningful improvement. For the double-beta decay search, the sum energy of the two electrons must peak sharply at Q = 3.03 MeV; better per-cell energy resolution narrows the signal window and suppresses background from 2νββ tail and other sources. The 11 cm depth already satisfies the ≥3 cm requirement for 3 MeV electrons in polystyrene (radiation length X₀ ~43 cm, but range of 3 MeV electron ~1.5 cm in plastic), so depth can be maintained. LaBr₃ cells would need careful engineering due to crystal hygroscopicity.

---

## 3. Upgrade Geiger-Mode Drift Cells to Low-Mass Drift Cells with He/isobutane and Increased Cell Granularity

**Technology:** Replace current Geiger cells with small-diameter (≤5 mm) drift tubes or thin-wall proportional tubes, maintaining helium-based gas (He/isobutane 95/5) but increasing the number of cells or using a full drift-chamber geometry with individual wire readout and fast TDCs.

**Physics motivation:** Better track position resolution improves vertex reconstruction on the foil, discriminating true ββ vertices from background events where two separate single-electron tracks (e.g., from Compton scattering of external γ-rays) fake a two-electron topology. The 3 mT magnetic field curves the tracks, but with Q = 3.03 MeV the electron momenta are ~1–1.5 MeV/c; at 3 mT the sagitta for a 50 cm track is only ~a few mm, so momentum resolution is limited—the field is used only for charge sign determination, not momentum measurement. Improved spatial resolution therefore helps vertex quality and topological rejection rather than energy. This also helps identify internal background from ²¹⁴Bi (a major ββ decay background) by detecting the delayed alpha from ²¹⁴Po following the beta.

---

## 4. Add a Radon-Trapping Cold Trap and Online Radon Monitor with ²²²Rn Daughter Tagging

**Technology:** Activated-charcoal cold trap (cooled to −40°C) on the inlet gas line plus an electrostatic radon monitor (e.g., AlphaGUARD or custom electrostatic collection counter) on the outlet, combined with offline tagging of ²¹⁴Bi-²¹⁴Po delayed coincidences in the tracking data.

**Physics motivation:** Radon is the dominant internal background in this detector class. ²²²Rn daughters (specifically ²¹⁴Bi) undergo beta decay with endpoint 3.27 MeV > Q(¹⁰⁰Mo) = 3.03 MeV, directly contaminating the signal region. The ²¹⁴Bi→²¹⁴Po delayed coincidence (τ ~237 μs, α energy 7.69 MeV) can tag and veto Bi events, but only if the tracking volume has sufficient alpha detection efficiency and the data acquisition captures the delayed signal. Cold trapping suppresses bulk radon activity; online monitoring provides a data-quality metric. Even at 3000 mwe depth, radon from rock emanation and detector materials remains the limiting background. A factor of 10 radon reduction can translate directly into a factor of ~3 improvement in sensitivity (since background B scales the half-life sensitivity as T₁/₂ ∝ 1/√B for background-dominated experiments).

---

## 5. Increase Molybdenum Source Mass via Thinner, Wider Foils with ¹⁰⁰Mo-Enriched Composite

**Technology:** Replace 45 mg/cm² foils with composite foils of ¹⁰⁰Mo powder mixed in a PVA binder at reduced areal density (~30 mg/cm²), extending the foil array to cover the full 6 m × 3.5 m plane with additional foil modules, targeting ~15–20 kg total ¹⁰⁰Mo mass.

**Physics motivation:** The ββ decay signal rate scales linearly with source mass. Reducing areal density from 45 mg/cm² decreases electron energy loss and straggling within the foil (self-absorption), improving the accuracy with which the calorimeter measures the true electron energy—this is crucial because the two-electron sum energy is the primary signal discriminant at Q. Thinner foils also reduce the probability that one electron re-scatters before reaching the tracker, which can fake a vertex shift. More ¹⁰⁰Mo mass directly extends the half-life sensitivity as T₁/₂ ∝ M·t for signal-limited operation.

This is a description of the SuperNEMO demonstrator-style tracker-calorimeter. The current calorimeter uses 19 cm square polystyrene scintillator blocks read by 76 mm PMTs behind iron plates, which gives 20% FWHM at 1 MeV and 0.30 ns time resolution. The requirements are 18% FWHM or better, 0.6 ns or better (so the present time resolution already exceeds the need, which is a useful margin), cells at least 3 cm deep (the present 11 cm is fine), 6 cm minimum separation between particles entering a wall, and full operation in a 3 mT field. The main gap is energy resolution, and the main constraint is that the PMTs must work in a magnetic field.

Proposed upgrades:

1. **Replace the PMTs with magnetic-field-tolerant photodetectors.** Conventional PMTs are sensitive to 3 mT fields through electron trajectory deflection, lowering gain and degrading resolution. Options are:
   - Silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs), which are immune to magnetic fields, but need care with dark noise and radiation damage at this low background level; cryogenic or temperature-controlled operation and low-noise readout help.
   - Fine-mesh or magnetic-shielded PMTs, with mu-metal shielding and a fine-mesh dynode structure, as a fallback if SiPM noise proves unacceptable.
   The SiPM option is the stronger choice for resolution because it improves light collection uniformity and avoids the iron plates that currently limit geometry.

2. **Improve light collection to raise photostatistics.** Energy resolution at 1 MeV is dominated by photoelectron statistics. Upgrades include:
   - Wrap the scintillator blocks in a high-reflectivity diffuse reflector (e.g., PTFE or enhanced specular films) to increase collected light.
   - Replace the 30 cm acrylic light guides with shorter, optically optimized guides or direct coupling, reducing light losses.
   - Use a higher light-yield scintillator (e.g., a plastic with higher light output or a PSF-based wavelength shifter fibre readout) to increase photoelectron count per MeV.

3. **Segment or redesign cell geometry to meet the 6 cm separation rule.** A 19 cm cell face is too large for two electrons separated by 6 cm to be resolved in separate cells. Reduce the face size to roughly 6 cm or below (with cells ≥3 cm deep, keeping depth at 11 cm or so), giving a segmented wall of many small cells. Smaller cells also reduce the light path and improve uniformity, but increase channel count, so readout must be compact (SiPM arrays with multichannel front-end ASICs).

4. **Multichannel readout electronics.** With many small cells, adopt integrated front-end ASICs for SiPM readout that provide per-channel charge and timing, supporting the 0.6 ns time-of-flight requirement and keeping cabling manageable inside the shielding. Timing of 0.3 ns or better per cell is achievable with fast SiPM signals and leading-edge discrimination with time-walk correction.

5. **Calibration and stability.** Add an LED or laser calibration system per channel and temperature monitoring, since SiPM gain drifts with temperature, to maintain the 18% resolution over the run.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the magnetic-field-sensitive 76 mm PMTs with SiPM readout of finer scintillator cells (about 6 cm faces) with high-reflectivity wrapping, which addresses the energy resolution, the 6 cm separation requirement, and field tolerance together.

# Calorimeter Upgrade Proposal

## 1. Check the present design against each requirement

| Requirement | Present cells | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Energy resolution ≤ 18 % FWHM at 1 MeV | 20 % FWHM | **Fails** |
| Time resolution ≤ 0.6 ns σ at 1 MeV | 0.30 ns | Passes, with 2× margin |
| Two electrons ≥ 6 cm apart land in different cells | 19 × 19 cm faces | **Fails badly** |
| Cell depth ≥ 3 cm | 11 cm | Passes |
| All parts work in 3 mT | PMTs need iron plates and light guides | Marginal |

**Granularity is the hardest requirement.** Any two entry points ≥ 6 cm apart must fall in different cells. So no two points inside one cell can be 6 cm or more apart. The cell face diagonal must therefore be under 6 cm, giving a square side below 4.24 cm. Choose a **4 × 4 cm pitch**, with a diagonal of 5.66 cm.

About 26,000 cells is too many for 76 mm PMTs, light guides and iron plates. The photosensor technology itself has to change.

## 2. Proposed hardware changes

### A. Re-segment the walls into small cells read by SiPMs (main change)
- **Cells:** 4 × 4 cm face, about 4–5 cm deep (≥ 3 cm required). A 3 MeV electron's range in polystyrene is about 1.5 cm, so absorption is ensured. Fewer than ~5 cm reduces gamma sensitivity (see section 4).
- **Channel count:** each 6 × 3.5 m wall is about 21 m², or about 13,000 cells per wall and about 26,000 in total.
- **Readout:** silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) coupled directly to the back face of each cell.
  - SiPMs are insensitive to 3 mT, so the iron plates and 30 cm light guides can go.
  - This removes the light-guide light loss.
  - It also removes the most radioactive components: the PMT glass and the bulk iron next to the scintillator.
- **Photosensor size:** about 4 × (6 × 6 mm) SiPMs per cell, ganged or summed.

### B. Raise light yield to meet 18 % FWHM
- 18 % FWHM corresponds to σ = 7.65 %.
- Including the SiPM excess noise factor and non-statistical terms, this needs **≥ 250–300 photoelectrons per MeV**.
- Measures to reach it:
  - High-yield PVT or polystyrene scintillator.
  - Specular reflector (ESR) or PTFE on all faces.
  - A thin aluminized-Mylar entrance window of a few µm, to keep energy loss in dead material low.
  - High-PDE SiPMs (> 40 % at about 420 nm).
  - Optical grease or glue coupling.
- Small cubes also give better light-collection uniformity than the large 19 cm cells, which improves the constant term.

### C. Preserve timing (≤ 0.6 ns σ)
Large ganged SiPM capacitance slows pulses. To counter this:
- Use parallel/series hybrid ganging or per-SiPM preamps feeding a fast summing ASIC.
- Use fast-decay scintillator (about 2 ns).
- Timing of about 0.3–0.5 ns σ at 1 MeV is achievable with several hundred photoelectrons.

### D. Electronics and operation
- **Front end:** multichannel ASIC (charge plus time) mounted on the wall back-plane, using low-background PCBs and cables.
- **Temperature:** stabilise or cool to about 15–20 °C, ±0.1 °C. This controls SiPM gain drift and dark rate, which is about 100 kHz per cm² at room temperature. Use a coincidence threshold of about 50 keV.
- **Calibration:** LED or laser light injection per cell, plus the existing Bi-207 deployable sources.
- **Radiopurity:** screen the SiPMs, reflectors and electronics. They sit right behind the scintillator.

### E. Mechanics
- Use thin inter-cell reflector walls (≤ 0.1 mm) to keep dead area below a few percent.
- Use a lightweight radiopure support frame, such as copper or carbon fibre.
- Keep the walls gas-tight, or separate them from the tracker, to preserve radon control.

## 3. Optional or secondary changes
- **Tracker association:** improve vertex/track-to-cell matching so that two electrons in neighbouring cells are assigned correctly. The 4 cm pitch is much finer than the present cells, so this is mostly software plus the tracker's existing resolution.
- **Retain the external shielding.** The iron in the outer shield remains useful as gamma shielding. It is only the magnetic shielding plates behind the PMTs that are removed.

## 4. Trade-offs to flag
- **Gamma detection:** thinner cells (4–5 cm instead of 11 cm) reduce gamma detection efficiency. This weakens the Tl-208 and Bi-214 background-channel tagging, which uses e–γ topologies. It also lowers the rate of external gamma background in the walls. Mitigation is either a deeper back layer or retaining some deeper cells on the edges.
- **Cost and complexity:** going from about 1,000 PMT channels to about 26,000 SiPM channels is a large increase. ASIC readout keeps the cost per channel low.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the 19 cm PMT-read scintillator cells with ~4 × 4 cm scintillator cells read directly by SiPMs (no light guides or iron plates), which meets the 6 cm separation requirement, works in 3 mT, and raises light collection to reach ≤18 % FWHM.

Cells with ~13 cm faces ensure that 6 cm separation guarantees different cells are hit, allowing independent energy measurements.

## 4. Replace Acrylic Light Guides with Shorter, Higher-Efficiency Coupling

**Technology:** Short tapered light guides (~5-10 cm) with wavelength-shifting (WLS) plates, or direct optical coupling with WLS fibers embedded in the scintillator edges

**Why:** The current 30 cm acrylic light guides cause significant light loss (~30-40%). Shorter guides with optimized geometry dramatically improve light collection, directly improving energy resolution and timing. WLS technology can efficiently concentrate light onto compact SiPM arrays.

## 5. Upgrade Readout Electronics for SiPM Operation

**Technology:** Low-noise, temperature-compensated preamplifiers with waveform digitization (e.g., 500 MHz+ FADCs)

**Why:** SiPMs require different front-end electronics than PMTs—lower gain requires lower noise amplification, and temperature compensation is essential for stable energy calibration. Waveform digitization enables optimal timing extraction and pile-up rejection.

## 6. Maintain or Increase Scintillator Depth

**Technology:** Retain 11 cm depth (already exceeds 3 cm minimum; sufficient for 3 MeV electron range of ~1.5 cm in polystyrene)

**Why:** The current depth is adequate. The 3 cm minimum is easily satisfied, ensuring full energy containment for the Q-value electrons.

3. **Light collection efficiency:**

This is a NEMO-3/SuperNEMO-type tracker-calorimeter. The tracker is fine, so the weak point is the calorimeter. The present cells give 20% FWHM and 0.30 ns, which already beats the 0.6 ns timing requirement, so the main shortfall is energy resolution (20% vs. ≤18%). Everything else (granularity, depth, B-field tolerance) must be preserved while the resolution is improved.

**Where the current resolution is limited**

- Large (19 cm) polystyrene blocks with 30 cm light guides lose a lot of light in transport (poor light collection, attenuation, multiple reflections). Photoelectron statistics at 1 MeV is the main contributor to the 20% FWHM.
- Light-guide plus 76 mm PMT coupling gives poor optical efficiency, since the square 19 cm face is matched to a round photocathode.
- The PMT's quantum efficiency (~25% bialkali, standard) is a further limit.
- Surface/wrapping quality and the scintillator's intrinsic light yield matter too.

**Proposed hardware upgrades**

1. **Replace the PMTs with high-quantum-efficiency, low-radioactivity 8" (or 5") hemispherical PMTs with super-bialkali photocathodes** (QE ~35–40% at 400 nm, e.g. Hamamatsu R5912-MOD / R5912-HQE-type), with radiopure glass. Higher QE directly raises photoelectron yield by ~35–50%, giving resolution ~ 1/√N improvement. This is the single biggest gain. Keep the PMT tubes large enough to cover the cell face; 8" tubes match the 19 cm block better than the existing 76 mm tubes.

2. **Remove or shorten the light guides by direct coupling.** Couple the 8" PMT directly to the scintillator block via a shaped (hemispherical-recess) entrance window machined in the scintillator, with optical grease or optical pad. Eliminating the 30 cm guide removes attenuation and reflection losses. For the 11 cm deep cell, a PMT bulb recess also improves light collection. Where a short guide remains, make it a thin (<~5 cm) tapered acrylic guide.

3. **Use higher-light-yield scintillator.** Switch to polystyrene (or PVT) doped for ~10,000+ photons/MeV with long bulk attenuation length and fast decay (~2 ns), such as PS with p-terphenyl/POPOP-type dopant or Eljen EJ-200/EJ-204-class material, with polished surfaces, and wrap in Teflon (PTFE) tape/ Tyvek or aluminized Mylar for high diffuse reflectivity. Optimizing the 11 cm depth (still ≥3 cm requirement) can further reduce position-dependent light collection variation.

4. **Magnetic shielding and field tolerance.** PMTs sit in the 3 mT field. Retain the iron plate behind the cells and add mu-metal shielding around each PMT so gain and timing hold in the field. The large bulb must tolerate the field (the iron plate and mu-metal shield make 3 mT acceptable).

5. **Optimize readout electronics for resolution and timing.** Use stable HV with gain monitoring, and digitize with fast waveform samplers (1–2.5 GS/s, e.g. SAMLONG/DRS4-type) for charge integration and constant-fraction timing. Add a light-injection (LED/laser fibre) calibration and monitoring system plus ²⁰⁷Bi source calibration to correct gain drifts and nonuniformity. Timing will stay near or better than 0.3 ns because bigger, faster, higher-QE tubes sharpen the pulse leading edge.

6. **Keep the granularity.** Preserve the 19 cm × 19 cm cell face (the 6 cm separation requirement means cells smaller than ~19 cm would not be necessary, but anything larger would violate it), and keep the depth ≥3 cm (retain ~11 cm). Do not replace the cells with large monolithic scintillator slabs.

**Expected result**: ~35–40% higher QE plus ~20–30% better light collection from removing the light guide gives ~1.5× more photoelectrons, so FWHM at 1 MeV falls from 20% to about 15–16% (SuperNEMO-type 8" HQE PMT designs reach ≈7–8% FWHM at 3 MeV, i.e. ~14% at 1 MeV), safely under 18%. Timing remains ≤0.3 ns sigma, well within 0.6 ns.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the 76 mm PMTs and 30 cm acrylic light guides with directly coupled, magnetically shielded 8-inch high-quantum-efficiency (super-bialkali) low-background PMTs on higher-light-yield polystyrene cells to raise photoelectron yield and bring the energy resolution below 18% FWHM

# Hardware Upgrade Recommendations for the Neutrinoless Double-Beta Decay Detector

## Current Performance Gap
The detector currently achieves 20% FWHM energy resolution but must meet 18% FWHM—a modest but critical shortfall given the Q-value is only 3.03 MeV. The time resolution (0.30 ns sigma) already exceeds the 0.6 ns requirement, so timing is adequate.

## Proposed Concrete Upgrades

### 1. **Replace PMTs with Magnetic-Field-Tolerant Photodetectors** (HIGH PRIORITY)
- **Current issue**: 76 mm PMTs are severely compromised in the 3 mT field (Lorentz deflection of electron trajectories), degrading light collection uniformity and pulse-height linearity.
- **Upgrade**: Install **Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)** (e.g., Hamamatsu S13360 or Fondazione Bruno Kessler NUV-SiPMs) mounted directly on the scintillator cells or at the end of light guides.
  - SiPMs are immune to magnetic fields
  - Achieve ~15% energy resolution at 1 MeV with proper gain matching and temperature compensation
  - Lower afterpulsing with modern devices
  - Compact form factor eliminates need for long acrylic light guides

### 2. **Upgrade Scintillator Material**
- **Current issue**: Standard polystyrene has ~3% intrinsic energy resolution limit; 20% observed resolution suggests light collection losses.
- **Upgrade**: Switch to **BC-418 or EJ-200 scintillator** with improved light yield (~10,000 photons/MeV vs. ~10,000 for PS) combined with **wavelength-shifting fiber readout** or reflective wrapping.
  - Improves photo-electron statistics
  - Expected resolution: 17–18% FWHM at 1 MeV

### 3. **Implement Individual Cell Electronics Redesign**
- **Current issue**: Shared readout electronics or impedance mismatches degrade pulse shape and energy linearity.
- **Upgrade**: Deploy **dedicated low-noise charge-integrating preamplifiers** (e.g., Cremat CR-200 series or custom ASIC) per cell with:
  - Input-referred noise <1 keV (RMS) for 1 MeV signals
  - Temperature-compensated gain (critical with SiPM)
  - Shaping time optimized for 1 MeV electrons (~1 µs)

### 4. **Add Temperature Stabilization System**
- **Current issue**: SiPM and PMT gains drift ~0.3–0.5% per °C; underground labs have ±1–2°C variations.
- **Upgrade**: Install **active Peltier cooling** on calorimeter modules with ±0.5°C setpoint stability.
  - Reduces gain drift contribution to resolution from ~3% to <0.5%

### 5. **Improve Light Collection Geometry**
- **Current issue**: 30 cm acrylic light guides introduce internal scattering losses.
- **Upgrade**: Replace with **shorter guides (10–15 cm)** or **direct SiPM coupling** with:
  - Polished cell cavity surfaces (diamond polish)
  - White reflective paint (e.g., Spectralon, 95% reflectivity)
  - Reduces photon loss from ~15% to ~5%

### 6. **Cross-Talk Mitigation (Cell Isolation)**
- **Current issue**: Scintillation photons cross boundaries between cells, degrading 6 cm separation requirement.
- **Upgrade**: Insert **0.5 mm lead-backed reflective barriers** between cells to eliminate optical cross-talk while maintaining uniform field response.

---

## Expected Performance After Upgrades
- Energy resolution: **17.5–18% FWHM** (meets requirement)
- Time resolution: **~0.35 ns sigma** (maintains margin)
- Charge separation: Improved due to reduced cross-talk and better energy linearity

---

**TOP RECOMMENDATION:** Replace 76 mm PMTs with temperature-stabilized Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) mounted directly on scintillator cells, paired with dedicated low-noise charge preamplifiers per cell. This single upgrade eliminates magnetic-field degradation, improves intrinsic light collection efficiency, and is the dominant factor limiting the 18% FWHM requirement.

# Design Review: Calorimeter Upgrade Recommendations

## 1. Where the current design stands against each requirement

| Requirement | Current calorimeter | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Energy resolution ≤ 18% FWHM at 1 MeV | 20% FWHM | **Fails** |
| Time resolution ≤ 0.6 ns (σ) at 1 MeV | 0.30 ns | Passes with a factor-2 margin |
| Hits ≥ 6 cm apart go to different cells | 19 cm × 19 cm cells | **Fails badly** |
| Cell depth ≥ 3 cm | 11 cm | Passes |
| Works in 3 mT | PMTs need iron shielding and long light guides | Marginal, and a driver of the bulk |

The granularity requirement drives the whole design.

- Two points in the same cell can be as far apart as the cell's diagonal.
- To guarantee that two hits ≥ 6 cm apart always land in different cells, the diagonal must be shorter than 6 cm.
- For square cells this means a side below 6/√2 ≈ 4.2 cm. A practical choice is a pitch of about 4 cm, including wrapping.
- Each wall covers 6 m × 3.5 m = 21 m². At a 4 cm pitch that is about 13,000 cells per wall, or roughly 26,000 cells in total.

A 76 mm photomultiplier cannot physically sit behind a 4 cm cell. Even 1-inch PMTs would be impractical, expensive and sensitive to the magnetic field at this density. **The photodetector technology must change.**

## 2. Recommended hardware changes

### (a) Re-segment the scintillator walls into ~4 × 4 cm² cells
- Use polystyrene-based plastic scintillator, a familiar and radiopure material.
- Either cast or machine individual cells, or groove large blocks into optically isolated cells.
- This is the only way to meet the 6 cm separation rule, and it is not negotiable.

**Cell depth:**
- Keep the depth at 3 cm or more for full containment of 3 MeV electrons.
- I suggest about 4–5 cm rather than 11 cm. This:
  - reduces the scintillator mass and its efficiency for external gamma rays (a background reduction);
  - improves the cell aspect ratio for light collection;
  - still exceeds the 3 cm floor with margin.

### (b) Replace PMTs and light guides with directly coupled silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs)
- Use SiPM arrays, for example 2×2 tiles of 6 × 6 mm² devices from Hamamatsu, FBK or Broadcom.
- Couple them directly to the back face of each cell with optical grease or silicone pads.

**Why SiPMs:**
- **Field immunity:** SiPMs are insensitive to magnetic fields far above 3 mT. The magnetic iron shielding and the 30 cm acrylic guides can be removed.
- **Space:** removing the guides frees about 30 cm per side. This space can go to extra passive shielding or a more compact layout.
- **Light collection:** removing the guide's transport losses improves light collection. Combined with high photon detection efficiency (about 40–50% at the scintillator peak), this raises the photoelectron count.
- **Radiopurity:** SiPMs are low-mass, silicon-based devices. They are typically more radiopure than PMT glass, which is a known source of the K, U and Th gammas that matter at Q = 3.03 MeV.

**Photoelectron budget for the energy goal:**
- 18% FWHM corresponds to σ ≈ 7.6%.
- That needs roughly 170 photoelectrons per MeV, or more once SiPM excess noise and non-uniformity are included. I recommend targeting about 250 photoelectrons per MeV or more.
- This is achievable in small, well-wrapped cells.

### (c) Improve the optical finish of every cell
- Wrap each cell in a specular reflector, such as 3M ESR or another enhanced specular film, or in diffuse PTFE.
- Polish or diamond-mill the faces.
- Small cells with high-reflectivity wrapping give much better light-collection uniformity. Uniformity is a major contributor to the constant term of the resolution, so this helps reach the ≤ 18% target in **every** cell.
- Consider a scintillator formulation with higher light yield and an emission spectrum matched to the SiPM sensitivity peak.

### (d) Manage SiPM dark noise and thresholds
- Room-temperature dark rates of about 50–100 kHz/mm² can affect low-energy thresholds and accidental coincidences.
- Mitigations:
  - modest cooling, about 10–20 °C below ambient, using the existing cavern infrastructure;
  - a coincidence requirement between the SiPMs within a cell;
  - choosing low-dark-count, low-crosstalk device generations.

### (e) Adopt ASIC-based multichannel front-end electronics
- About 26,000 channels requires integrated readout, such as TOFPET2-type or similar SiPM ASICs.
- Each channel should provide charge integration plus time stamping, with per-channel bias trimming and temperature compensation of SiPM gain.

**Timing:**
- The 0.6 ns specification leaves ample margin over the present 0.30 ns.
- So the time budget can be traded against SiPM capacitance and slower shaping when that helps energy resolution.
- Even ~0.4–0.5 ns at 1 MeV still allows rejection of crossing electrons.

### (f) Calibration and clustering provisions
- Add an LED or laser light-injection system with fibers to every cell to monitor gain.
- Retain the radioactive-source deployment system for absolute energy calibration.
- With small cells, a single electron will often share energy between neighboring cells. Reconstruction should cluster each electron's cells using the tracker's impact point. The ≥ 6 cm rule then guarantees the two decay electrons never share a cell.

### (g) Keep iron for gamma shielding, not for magnetic shielding
- Retain or reposition the iron plate purely as passive gamma shielding.
- Screen every new component (SiPMs, PCBs, connectors, wrapping) for radiopurity.

## 3. Summary

Moving to about 4 cm cells forces the abandonment of PMTs. Directly coupled SiPMs on small, well-reflected cells then solve, together:
- the granularity requirement;
- the energy-resolution requirement, through better light collection;
- magnetic-field robustness;
- radiopurity and space.

All of this stays within the timing requirement.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Re-segment both calorimeter walls into ~4 × 4 cm² plastic scintillator cells read out by directly coupled SiPM arrays, replacing the 19 cm cells, 30 cm light guides and 76 mm PMTs.

This detector is clearly inspired by NEMO-3/SuperNEMO. Here are concrete hardware upgrades for the next phase:

## 1. **Replace PMTs with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)**

**Technology:** Tile the scintillator cell faces with 6mm × 6mm SiPM arrays (e.g., Hamamatsu MPPC or FBK NUV-HD SiPMs), eliminating light guides and PMTs.

**Physics motivation:** 
- SiPMs are insensitive to the 3 mT magnetic field (unlike PMTs which suffer gain variations)

- Reduces background from external gamma rays via better shielding

**Technology:** Install 1-2 mm thick wavelength-shifting plastic strips between adjacent scintillator cells to create optical isolation while maintaining hermeticity.

**Physics motivation:**

- Maintains the 6 cm separation requirement for two-electron topology
- Improves position resolution and energy containment corrections
- Reduces systematic uncertainties in energy reconstruction

**Technology:** Replace standard drift cells with plasma-panel design Geiger cells (10-100 kΩ anode resistance) and 1 GHz digitization electronics.

- Factor of 10 faster signal development improves time resolution to <100 ps per hit
- Better pattern recognition for high-occupancy events
- Improved track-calorimeter time matching for external background rejection
- Enhanced α-particle identification for ²¹⁴Bi backgrounds on source foils

**Technology:** Use polystyrene scintillator made from ¹²C-depleted carbon and deuterated solvents to reduce ¹³C and ²H content.

**Physics motivation:**

- Neutrons create correlated backgrounds mimicking 0νββ through (n,n'γ) and capture reactions
- Deuterium has large (n,γ) cross-section creating detector-wide signals
- Factor of 5-10 reduction in neutron-related backgrounds

**Technology:** Install LN₂-cooled activated charcoal traps in the gas recirculation system, targeting <0.1 mBq/m³ ²²²Rn.

**Physics motivation:**
- ²¹⁴Bi (from ²²²Rn decay) on foils is the dominant internal background
- ²¹⁴Bi β-decay (Q=3.27 MeV) directly overlaps with ¹⁰⁰Mo signal region
- Even with e⁻e⁻ topology selection, ²¹⁴Bi-²¹⁴Po delayed coincidence creates irreducible background
- Factor of 10-100 reduction in radon concentration is achievable

**Technology:** Replace some ¹⁰⁰Mo foils with ⁸²Se enriched to >95%, fabricated as selenium-loaded organic foils (40-50 mg/cm²).

**Physics motivation:**
- ⁸²Se has Q=2.996 MeV (nearly identical to ¹⁰⁰Mo)
- Different nuclear matrix elements provide complementary physics
- Observation in both isotopes would confirm 0νββ discovery
- ⁸²Se has lower 2νββ rate (T₁/₂=0.87×10²⁰ yr vs 7×10¹⁸ yr), reducing this background by ~100×
- Hedges against unknown systematic effects in single-isotope searches

## 8. **Thin Resistive Plate Chambers for Particle ID**

**Technology:** Install 5 mm thick timing RPCs between tracking volume and calorimeter (250 ps time resolution).

**Physics motivation:**
- Provides additional time-of-flight measurement to reject externals
- Distinguishes electrons from positrons independent of magnetic field through dE/dx + TOF
- Validates magnetic charge determination, crucial for 0νββ topology (e⁻e⁻ not e⁻e⁺)
- Acts as additional trigger layer with ~1 mm position resolution

---

**TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace PMTs with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)**

This single upgrade addresses both calorimeter specifications (energy and time resolution), eliminates magnetic field sensitivity issues, reduces radioactive backgrounds, and enables the most significant improvement in detector performance for isolating the 0νββ signal from backgrounds.

# Design Review Recommendations for 0νββ Decay Detector

## Analysis of Current Specifications vs. Requirements

The present scintillator cells achieve 20% FWHM energy resolution and 0.30 ns time resolution at 1 MeV. The requirements are 18% FWHM and 0.6 ns sigma. While the energy requirement is tight, the **time resolution is already adequate** (0.30 ns sigma corresponds to ~0.71 ns FWHM, well below the 0.6 ns sigma requirement when accounting for the ~2.4× conversion factor).

However, several critical issues emerge under detailed scrutiny:

## Critical Issues and Recommendations

### 1. **Energy Resolution Degradation in Magnetic Field** (HIGH PRIORITY)
**Issue:** The 3 mT field, while modest, creates a challenging environment. Standard PMT designs suffer from magnetic field effects above ~100 G in the photomultiplier tube itself, causing:
- Electron trajectory deflection in the PMT
- Reduced collection efficiency
- Gain variation across the PMT face
- Energy resolution degradation of 10-30%

**Recommendation:** **Replace 76 mm standard PMTs with magnetic-field-compensated PMTs or SiPMs (Silicon Photomultipliers)**
- **SiPMs** are inherently insensitive to magnetic fields and would eliminate this degradation mechanism entirely
- Modern SiPMs (e.g., Hamamatsu S13360, Ketek PM3350) achieve 15-18% energy resolution with adequate gain
- SiPMs enable compact detector geometry and provide superior timing (~100 ps intrinsic resolution)
- Disadvantage: higher dark count rates require temperature stabilization (~20°C ±0.5°C), which is manageable underground

**Alternative:** If PMTs are retained, use **mu-metal magnetic shielding** around each PMT to reduce field at the photomultiplier to <50 G. This adds complexity but preserves the proven PMT technology.

### 2. **Energy Resolution at Cell Boundaries** (HIGH PRIORITY)
**Issue:** The requirement that electrons separated by ≥6 cm deposit energy in different cells, combined with the 19 cm×19 cm cell size, creates edge effects where ~30% of the cell area lies within 6 cm of a boundary. Energy sharing and position-dependent response degrade resolution near boundaries.

**Recommendation:** **Implement reflective sidewall segmentation with wavelength-shifting (WLS) fiber collection**
- Replace direct PMT coupling with individual WLS fibers from the cell interior
- WLS fibers (e.g., BCF-92) collect scintillation light uniformly across the cell
- Light is transported to a single SiPM or compact PMT positioned outside the magnetic field volume
- This improves:
  - Uniformity of response across the cell face
  - Rejection of boundary-sharing events through timing discrimination
  - Tolerance to the 3 mT field

### 3. **Timing Resolution Verification** (MEDIUM PRIORITY)
**Issue:** While 0.30 ns sigma appears adequate, background rejection requires timing discrimination at the nanosecond level to identify cosmogenic backgrounds. The stated 0.6 ns sigma requirement may be insufficient for rejecting correlated events.

**Recommendation:** **Upgrade to fast scintillators and SiPMs for sub-0.5 ns sigma timing**

- Replace rigid acrylic guides with **bonded WLS plates** (e.g., EJ-280) that couple directly to the scintillator
- Couples light from the full cell area into a smaller SiPM positioned remotely
- Eliminates dead zones behind iron plate

## TOP RECOMMENDATION: **Replace the 76 mm PMTs with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) and implement wavelength-shifting fiber or plate light collection.**

**Justification:** This single change addresses the dominant limitation (magnetic field sensitivity of PMTs), simultaneously improves both energy and timing resolution to comfortable margins above specification, eliminates the complexity of magnetic shielding, and provides the uniformity needed to achieve 18% FWHM at all cell positions. The additional cost (~$5-10k for the collaboration) is modest compared to the physics gain and operational simplification.

This description matches the SuperNEMO demonstrator calorimeter. The current design uses 19 cm x 19 cm polystyrene scintillator blocks read by 76 mm PMTs through acrylic light guides, with PMTs behind iron plates. The requirements call for roughly 18% FWHM at 1 MeV (versus 20% now), 0.6 ns sigma timing (versus 0.30 ns, which is already better than needed, so timing is not the bottleneck), a 6 cm minimum separation between electron hits (so cell granularity must be finer than the current 19 cm faces), and full operation in a 3 mT field, which rules out ordinary PMTs unless shielded.

Concrete upgrade proposals:

1. **Replace the 76 mm PMTs with magnetic-field-tolerant photodetectors.** Options include Hamamatsu R5912-type PMTs with mu-metal shielding and a fine-mesh dynode arrangement, or, better, silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) read out at the cell face. SiPMs are insensitive to a 3 mT field, remove the iron plates, and allow a more compact geometry. Their photon detection efficiency at scintillator wavelengths (~400 nm) is high, and cross-talk and dark-count corrections can be handled in the readout electronics.

2. **Improve light collection and uniformity to reach 18% FWHM.** Use a higher-light-yield scintillator (e.g., a PVT-based plastic with a wavelength shifter, or a different scintillator with higher photon yield) and replace the acrylic light guide with a tapered, specularly reflective (e.g., ESR or VM2000 film-wrapped) guide. Wrapping the scintillator with a diffuse reflector such as Tyvek plus a specular film and coupling the SiPM directly with optical grease minimizes losses. Calibrate per-cell light yield with a laser or LED system and apply position-dependent corrections.

3. **Increase granularity.** Subdivide the 19 cm faces into cells of roughly 5 to 6 cm, or use a scintillator-fiber or small-tile matrix behind each tracking volume. This meets the 6 cm separation requirement directly, which the current cells cannot do.

4. **Keep depth at 11 cm or greater** (already above the 3 cm minimum) so 3 MeV electrons are fully absorbed; no change is needed here.

5. **Maintain timing performance** with fast SiPM readout and waveform digitization (e.g., 1 GS/s or higher flash ADCs), which should comfortably deliver sigma below 0.6 ns.

Overall, the combination of SiPM readout with fine segmentation and better light collection addresses all the stated requirements, with the granularity change being the most constraining one.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the large 76 mm PMTs and iron-shielded geometry with finely segmented (~5 to 6 cm) scintillator cells read out by SiPMs coupled through reflective light guides.

This is the NEMO-3 / SuperNEMO demonstrator-type design. The existing performance is 20% FWHM at 1 MeV, while the requirement is 18% or better in every cell. Time resolution is already adequate at 0.30 ns against the 0.6 ns requirement. The main work is therefore energy resolution, with the other requirements acting as constraints that any change must preserve.

**Analysis of the constraints**

- Segmentation: electrons entering at least 6 cm apart must land in different cells. The present 19 x 19 cm faces do not meet this, because two electrons from a single decay would often share a cell and be summed. Cells with a face of about 6 cm or less would be required in principle, or the requirement must be met by other means. In practice, with only 3 cm minimum depth and 3 MeV full absorption, the cell must be small in the transverse dimension, so the face has to shrink to roughly 5-6 cm or less. Smaller cells also mean many more channels, so the photodetector must be compact.
- Depth: at least 3 cm (polystyrene scintillator stops 3 MeV electrons in about 1.5 cm, plus margin). The present 11 cm depth is wasteful, and a thinner cell reduces gamma efficiency and scattering. A depth of 10 cm is no longer needed.
- Light guide: the 30 cm acrylic guide plus 76 mm PMT on a 19 cm face loses light. A direct-coupled, small-face cell removes the guide and its attenuation, boosting photoelectron statistics and hence resolution.
- Magnetic field: a 3 mT field requires PMTs with magnetic shielding, or a photodetector insensitive to field. Silicon photomultipliers would tolerate it but are noisy and radiation-sensitive; low-background, 3 mT-compatible small PMTs with mu-metal shielding are the safe choice. The iron plate behind the cells already helps shield.
- Time resolution: smaller cells and shorter light paths improve timing, so the 0.6 ns requirement stays easily met.

**Proposed upgrades**

1. **Replace the scintillator blocks with smaller, finely segmented cells.** Use cells with faces of at most about 6 x 6 cm (matching the 6 cm separation rule) and depth of about 10 cm reduced toward 5-6 cm where gamma background allows, never below 3 cm. This directly satisfies the individual-energy-measurement requirement.
2. **Use a higher-light-yield scintillator.** Switch from polystyrene to a PVT-based plastic with high light yield and good optical transparency, or to an organic scintillator with about 10-20% more light, wrapped in a high-reflectivity wrap such as Teflon/PTFE or Tyvek with aluminised Mylar.
3. **Remove the long acrylic light guides.** Couple the photodetector directly to the scintillator with optical grease or a short, tapered light guide, which raises photoelectron yield.
4. **Use high quantum efficiency photodetectors.** Select ultra-bialkali PMTs (QE about 40% at the peak) matched to the cell face, with low radioactivity glass, mu-metal shielding for the 3 mT field, and an iron plate behind.
5. **Improve electronics and calibration.** Keep waveform digitisers, and apply a laser or radioactive source (such as 207Bi) calibration for gain stability per cell, to ensure every cell, not just the average, meets 18% FWHM.
6. **Maintain radiopurity and radon control.** Keep low-background materials in the new cells, since more channels introduce more PMT-borne activity.

These changes together lift photoelectron statistics and bring the 1 MeV resolution below 18% in each cell, while the timing stays well under 0.6 ns, the depth stays above 3 cm, the cells work in 3 mT, and the segmentation separates electrons 6 cm apart.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the 19 cm x 19 cm scintillator blocks with finely segmented cells of about 6 cm or smaller face, directly coupled (no long light guide) to high-quantum-efficiency, magnetically shielded photomultipliers.

# Hardware Upgrades for the Neutrinoless Double-Beta Decay Detector Calorimeter

## 1. Photomultiplier Replacement with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)

**Technology:** Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs), also known as Multi-Pixel Photon Counters (MPPCs)

**Why:** The current 76 mm PMTs sit behind iron plates specifically because conventional PMTs cannot operate in magnetic fields. SiPMs are solid-state devices completely immune to the 3 mT magnetic field, eliminating the need for iron shielding plates. They offer:
- Higher photon detection efficiency (40-50% vs ~25% for bialkali PMTs)
- Compact form factor allowing better optical coupling
- Excellent timing resolution (<100 ps possible)
- The improved light collection will directly enhance both energy and time resolution

## 2. Scintillator Material Upgrade to Plastic Scintillator with Higher Light Output

**Technology:** Modern high-light-output plastic scintillators (e.g., EJ-200, EJ-204, or Saint-Gobain BC-408)

**Why:** Energy resolution in scintillator calorimeters scales with √(photoelectrons). The current 20% FWHM at 1 MeV needs to reach ≤18% FWHM. Higher light yield scintillators (~10,000 photons/MeV vs older ~8,000) provide ~25% more photons, improving energy resolution by ~10% and easily meeting the 18% requirement. Time resolution also improves with more photoelectrons.

## 3. Light Guide Redesign or Elimination

**Technology:** Direct SiPM coupling with wavelength-shifting (WLS) plates or shortened/removed light guides using SiPM arrays

**Why:** The current 30 cm acrylic light guides lose significant light through absorption and incomplete internal reflection. Since SiPMs are field-immune, they can be placed directly on or very near the scintillator. This dramatically increases light collection, improving both energy resolution (more photoelectrons) and timing resolution (less photon path-length variation).

## 4. Cell Geometry Reconfiguration

**Technology:** Smaller cross-section scintillator cells (e.g., 5 cm × 5 cm faces) with individual SiPM readout

**Why:** The requirement that electrons 6 cm apart deposit energy in different cells cannot be reliably met with 19 cm × 19 cm cells. Reducing cell face dimensions to ≤6 cm ensures spatial separation requirement is satisfied. The depth should remain at or exceed 11 cm (well above the 3 cm minimum) to contain 3 MeV electron showers.

## 5. Improved Optical Interface

**Technology:** Optical grease or silicone pads with matched refractive index; enhanced surface wrapping (ESR reflector film)

**Why:** Fresnel losses at optical interfaces reduce light collection. Modern ESR (Enhanced Specular Reflector) films like 3M Vikuiti provide >98% reflectivity versus ~95% for older materials. Better optical coupling between scintillator, any remaining light guide, and photodetector maximizes photoelectron yield for both resolution requirements.

## 6. Multi-Channel Readout Electronics

**Technology:** Multi-channel waveform digitizers or dedicated SiPM readout ASICs (e.g., CITIROC, TOFPET2)

**Why:** Smaller, more numerous cells require cost-effective multi-channel readout. Modern ASICs provide per-channel timing resolution <50 ps and energy measurement in compact, low-power packages. This supports the 0.6 ns timing requirement while handling the increased channel count from smaller cells.

## 7. Temperature Stabilization System

**Technology:** Active cooling/heating with Peltier elements or temperature-controlled water circulation for SiPM arrays

**Why:** SiPM gain varies ~2-4% per °C. To maintain consistent energy calibration meeting the 18% FWHM requirement across all cells, temperature must be stabilized to better than ±1°C throughout the calorimeter.

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace PMTs with SiPMs to enable direct optical coupling without iron shielding, dramatically improving light collection and thus both energy and timing resolution while ensuring magnetic field compatibility.
