# Calorimeter Upgrade Proposal: Hardware Recommendations

## Requirements check against the present calorimeter

| Requirement | Present cells | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Energy resolution ≤ 18% FWHM at 1 MeV | 20% FWHM | **Fails** |
| Time resolution ≤ 0.6 ns (σ) at 1 MeV | 0.30 ns | Passes with a 2× margin |
| Electrons ≥ 6 cm apart land in different cells | 19 × 19 cm faces | **Fails badly** |
| Cell depth ≥ 3 cm | 11 cm | Passes |
| Every part works in 3 mT | PMTs depend on an iron plate | Passes now, but the solution does not carry over to small cells |

**Granularity condition.** Two points inside one cell can be as far apart as the cell's face diagonal. To guarantee that any two entry points at least 6 cm apart fall in different cells, the diagonal must be under 6 cm.
- For a square face of side s, this means s√2 < 6 cm, so s < 4.24 cm.
- A 19 cm cell has a diagonal of 27 cm.
- The wall must therefore be re-segmented.

## Recommended hardware upgrades

**1. Re-segment the calorimeter walls into small scintillator cells (about 4 cm × 4 cm faces).**
- **Technology:** polystyrene or PVT scintillator bars with 4.0 cm square faces (diagonal 5.66 cm < 6 cm).
- **Depth:** at least 3 cm, so 3 MeV electrons stop fully. Keeping roughly 5–11 cm depth preserves γ-tagging efficiency for background studies.
- **Why:** this is the only way to meet the two-electron separation requirement. Each electron's energy is then measured individually.
- **Channel count:** each 6 m × 3.5 m wall needs about 150 × 88 ≈ 13,000 cells, so about 26,000 cells for both walls.

**2. Replace the 76 mm PMTs and 30 cm light guides with silicon photomultipliers (SiPM arrays) coupled directly to each cell.**
- **Technology:** about 6 × 6 mm² or larger SiPM arrays, high photon-detection efficiency (~40–50% at the scintillator emission peak), optically coupled with no light guide.
- **Why the magnetic field:** SiPMs are insensitive to magnetic fields, so the 3 mT requirement is met without iron shielding.
- **Why the fit:** a 76 mm PMT cannot fit behind a 4 cm cell.
- **Why resolution:** removing the 30 cm guide and its light losses raises photoelectron yield. This is the main lever to get from 20% down to ≤18% FWHM.
- **Why background:** SiPMs are low-mass and radiopure, cutting γ background compared with PMT glass and iron.
- **Fallback:** if SiPM dark noise or area is a problem, use 1-inch metal-channel PMTs with individual mu-metal shields. This is more costly and less clean.

**3. Improve light collection in each cell.**
- **Technology:**
  - high-light-yield scintillator;
  - diffuse PTFE wrapping on the sides;
  - a thin (few µm) aluminized Mylar entrance window, to minimise dead material and energy loss of the electrons.
- **Why:** this adds photostatistics margin so every cell, not just the average one, meets 18% FWHM. Uniformity across the face matters too.

**4. New front-end readout electronics.**
- **Technology:** multichannel SiPM ASICs or waveform digitisers for about 26,000 channels. They need:
  - per-channel gain and bias control;
  - temperature stabilisation or compensation;
  - timing preserved at the sub-ns level.
- **Why:** this handles the large channel increase, allows energy and time to be read independently per cell, and keeps time resolution well inside 0.6 ns.

**5. Calibration and monitoring system.**
- **Technology:** LED or laser light injection into each cell, plus deployable ²⁰⁷Bi conversion-electron sources.
- **Why:** this verifies the per-cell energy-resolution requirement and tracks SiPM gain drift with temperature.

## Not needing upgrade

- **Timing:** 0.30 ns already beats 0.6 ns. The SiPM readout must simply not degrade it below spec.
- **Cell depth:** already meets the ≥3 cm requirement.
- **Tracker and magnet:** no requirement here demands changes to them.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Re-segment each calorimeter wall into ~4 cm × 4 cm scintillator cells read out directly by magnetic-field-immune SiPMs (replacing the 19 cm cells, light guides and 76 mm PMTs).

# Design Review Panel Recommendations

## Systematic Analysis of Current Performance vs. Requirements

| Parameter | Current | Required | Status |
|-----------|---------|----------|--------|
| Energy resolution at 1 MeV | 20% FWHM | ≤18% FWHM | **FAILS** |
| Time resolution at 1 MeV | 0.30 ns σ | ≤0.6 ns σ | Passes (2× margin) |
| Cell face size | 19×19 cm² | ≤6 cm separation → need ≤6 cm granularity? | **Needs scrutiny** |
| Cell depth | 11 cm | ≥3 cm, full absorption of 3 MeV e⁻ | Needs verification |
| PMT operation | 76 mm PMT + iron plate | Must work in 3 mT field | Needs scrutiny |

---

## Detailed Issue Identification

### 1. Cell Granularity — Critical Failure

The requirement states that two electrons entering the wall at points **≥6 cm apart** must deposit energy in **separate cells**. The current cells have **19×19 cm² faces**. Two electrons 6 cm apart will frequently hit the same cell. This is a **hard geometric failure** — no tuning of the current design fixes it. This is arguably the most fundamental problem.

**Recommendation: Replace 19×19 cm² scintillator cells with cells of ≤6 cm × 6 cm face dimensions.**

Specific technology: **Plastic scintillator tiles of 6×6 cm² face, 10–12 cm deep**, read out by **silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs)** directly coupled or via short wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibers. SiPMs of 6×6 mm² to 15×15 mm² area are commercially available from Hamamatsu (S13360 series), KETEK, and SensL/OnSemi, and operate perfectly in 3 mT — they are immune to magnetic fields because they have no electron drift paths. This simultaneously solves the PMT-in-magnetic-field concern (see below). The smaller cell also improves energy resolution per cell by reducing the solid angle subtended, keeping light collection more uniform.

---

### 2. Energy Resolution — Current Failure (20% vs ≤18% FWHM)

Energy resolution in a scintillator-PMT system scales as:

$$\frac{\sigma}{E} \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{N_{pe}}}$$

so FWHM resolution goes as $1/\sqrt{N_{pe}}$. To go from 20% to 18% FWHM requires increasing photoelectron yield by factor $(20/18)^2 \approx 1.23$, i.e., a **23% increase in detected photons**.

The current design loses photons through the **30 cm acrylic light guide**, which introduces geometric losses and attenuation. Sources of improvement:

**Recommendation A: Eliminate the acrylic light guide by coupling SiPMs directly to the scintillator rear face.** SiPMs with high photon detection efficiency (PDE ~40–50% at 420 nm for Hamamatsu S13360-6050CS, versus ~25% quantum efficiency for a standard bialkali PMT) more than recover the light lost in the guide. Direct coupling also removes a passive material budget concern for tracks that scatter backward.

**Recommendation B: Use polystyrene scintillator doped with optimized fluors (e.g., PTP + POPOP or use pre-made BC-408/EJ-200 equivalent) with enhanced surface treatment (ESR mirror film wrapping, Vikuiti).** Commercial EJ-200 gives ~10,000 photons/MeV; ensure all faces except the SiPM-coupled face are wrapped with specular or diffuse reflector to maximize light collection uniformity. This directly increases $N_{pe}$.

**Quantitative check:** Current 20% FWHM implies $N_{pe} \approx (2.35/0.20)^2 \approx 138$ photoelectrons at 1 MeV. Need 18% → $N_{pe} \approx 170$. With a 25% increase in PDE (SiPM vs. current PMT+light guide) and elimination of ~30% light guide transmission loss, the gain is well above the required 23%. This is achievable.

---

### 3. PMT Operation in 3 mT Magnetic Field — Risk Item

The current **76 mm (3-inch) PMTs** have long electron drift paths in the dynode chain. Even a 3 mT transverse field can deflect dynode electrons enough to degrade gain by 10–30% depending on PMT orientation, particularly for tubes with venetian-blind or box-and-grid dynodes. The **iron plate behind the PMT** provides partial shielding but adds complexity, weight, and passive material, and cannot guarantee uniform shielding across a large array of cells.

**Recommendation: Replace PMTs with SiPMs** (as recommended above). SiPMs are solid-state devices with no free electron trajectories; they are **completely insensitive to magnetic fields** at any realistic laboratory field strength. This eliminates the iron shielding plates, reduces the passive material behind the calorimeter, simplifies the mechanical design, and removes a systematic uncertainty in gain calibration vs. field orientation.

---

### 4. Cell Depth and 3 MeV Electron Absorption

The range of a 3 MeV electron in polystyrene (density ~1.06 g/cm³) is approximately:
- Using the CSDA range: ~3 MeV electrons have range ≈ 1.5 g/cm² in polystyrene → **~14 mm = 1.4 cm in polystyrene**.

Wait — let me be more careful. The NIST ESTAR database gives for polystyrene at 3 MeV: CSDA range ≈ 1.4 g/cm², so linear range ≈ 1.4/1.06 ≈ **13 mm**. The current 11 cm depth **vastly exceeds** this — the cells are more than adequate for containment. The requirement of "≥3 cm deep" is a minimum mechanical/structural specification, and 11 cm satisfies it. **No change needed here.**

However, with the smaller 6×6 cm² cells, maintaining ~10–12 cm depth is straightforward and should be retained to preserve full longitudinal containment and avoid shower leakage.

---

### 5. Time Resolution — Currently Passes, But Protect the Margin

Current: 0.30 ns σ; required: ≤0.6 ns σ. The margin is comfortable. However, switching to SiPMs with direct coupling will **improve** time resolution (SiPMs have faster signal rise times, ~200–500 ps transit time spread vs. ~1–2 ns for a PMT), so the upgrade preserves and improves this margin. No dedicated change needed beyond the SiPM swap.

---

### 6. Scintillator Material — Consider Upgrade

The current polystyrene scintillator with the described geometry gives 20% FWHM. If after the SiPM and light-guide removal the energy resolution is still marginal, consider:

**Recommendation: Use PVT-based commercial scintillator (e.g., EJ-200 or BC-408)** rather than cast polystyrene. These have higher light yields (~10,000 photons/MeV vs. ~8,000 for typical polystyrene), better optical clarity, and are available in custom dimensions. The additional ~25% light yield improvement ensures comfortable margin over the 18% FWHM specification.

---

### 7. Calibration System

With smaller cells (6×6 cm²) the total channel count increases from roughly:
- Current: walls are 6 m × 3.5 m = 21 m² per side; at 19×19 cm² → ~580 cells per side → ~1160 total
- Proposed: at 6×6 cm² → ~5800 cells per side → ~11,600 total

**Recommendation: Implement LED-based pulsed calibration** injected via optical fiber to each SiPM, plus a **radioactive source deployment system** (e.g., ⁲⁰⁷Bi, which provides conversion electrons at 0.482 and 0.976 MeV, bracketing the 1 MeV calibration point). This is essential for gain monitoring across the larger channel count and to verify cell-by-cell energy resolution compliance.

---

## Summary Table of Recommendations

| Priority | Change | Technology | Justification |
|----------|--------|------------|---------------|
| 1 | Reduce cell face to ≤6×6 cm² | Custom PVT/PS scintillator tiles | Hard geometric requirement: 6 cm two-electron separation |
| 2 | Replace PMTs + light guides with SiPMs | Hamamatsu S13360 or equivalent | Fixes B-field sensitivity, improves light yield & energy resolution, removes iron plates |
| 3 | Optimize scintillator (EJ-200/BC-408) + reflective wrapping | PVT scintillator + Vikuiti ESR film | Increases $N_{pe}$ to meet 18% FWHM |
| 4 | Add LED + source calibration system | Optical fiber + ²⁰⁷Bi sources | Required for channel-count scale-up QA |

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the 19×19 cm² scintillator cells with ≤6×6 cm² PVT scintillator tiles read out by directly coupled SiPMs, eliminating the light guides and PMTs entirely — this simultaneously satisfies the two-electron spatial separation requirement (which the current geometry categorically fails), resolves the magnetic-field sensitivity of the PMTs, and provides sufficient photon yield improvement to meet the 18% FWHM energy resolution specification.

# Design Review Panel Recommendation Report

## Preamble: Baseline Assessment

The current detector meets the time resolution requirement (0.30 ns σ vs. 0.6 ns σ required) with comfortable margin, and nearly meets the energy resolution requirement (20% FWHM vs. 18% FWHM required). The 76 mm PMT operates satisfactorily in 3 mT, the cell geometry satisfies the 6 cm spatial separation requirement, and 11 cm depth exceeds the 3 cm minimum. The challenge is therefore incremental but real: a modest improvement in energy resolution is needed while preserving or improving all other performance metrics.

---

## Systematic Analysis of the Optical Chain

The energy resolution of a scintillator-PMT cell is governed by:

$$\frac{\sigma_E}{E} \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{N_{pe}}}$$

where $N_{pe}$ is the number of photoelectrons. The 20% FWHM (≈ 8.5% σ) at 1 MeV must become ≤ 18% FWHM (≈ 7.6% σ), requiring roughly a **20% increase in $N_{pe}$** (since resolution scales as $1/\sqrt{N_{pe}}$, a 20% improvement in resolution requires ~44% more photoelectrons, or equivalently reducing variance by that factor). Every component in the photon collection chain is therefore a candidate for improvement.

---

## Recommended Hardware Changes

### 1. Replace the 76 mm PMT with a High-Quantum-Efficiency Bialkali PMT (PRIMARY RECOMMENDATION)

**Current situation:** Standard bialkali PMTs of the 76 mm (3-inch) class (e.g., Hamamatsu R1924, ETL 9256) achieve quantum efficiencies (QE) of 20–25% at the polystyrene emission peak (~420 nm).

**Recommendation:** Replace with **Hamamatsu R6231-100 or R7723-100 "Super Bialkali" (SBA) or "Ultra Bialkali" (UBA) PMTs** in the same 76 mm format. SBA tubes reach QE ≈ 35% and UBA tubes reach QE ≈ 43% at 420 nm, while remaining in the same mechanical envelope and operating normally in the existing iron-shielded, low-field environment.

**Justification:**
- A QE increase from ~22% to ~35% (SBA) gives a factor of 1.59 more photoelectrons → resolution improves by factor $1/\sqrt{1.59}$ = 0.79, i.e., from 20% to ~15.8% FWHM. This comfortably satisfies the ≤18% requirement.
- The same tube diameter fits the existing 19 cm × 19 cm cell with 30 cm acrylic light guide — **no mechanical redesign needed**.
- The iron shutter behind which the PMT sits already provides adequate shielding from the 3 mT field; SBA/UBA tubes have the same μ-metal shielding and magnetic tolerance as standard bialkali tubes.
- Time resolution improves slightly with higher photoelectron yield (earlier first-photoelectron statistics), maintaining the existing comfortable margin on the 0.6 ns σ requirement.
- The R6231-100 series is proven in similar large-scale calorimeters (SNO+, RENO, Double Chooz heritage).
- Cost increment is modest (~2× per tube) relative to the overall detector cost.

---

### 2. Replace the 30 cm Acrylic Light Guide with an Optimized Winston-Cone or Compound Parabolic Concentrator (CPC) Light Guide

**Current situation:** The 30 cm straight acrylic light guide couples a 19 cm × 19 cm face to a 76 mm (≈ 7.6 cm diameter) PMT photocathode. The geometric acceptance ratio is:

$$\eta_{geom} = \frac{\pi (3.8)^2}{19 \times 19} \approx \frac{45.4}{361} \approx 12.6\%$$

Much of the light hitting the acrylic guide at angles exceeding the total-internal-reflection (TIR) critical angle (~42° for acrylic/air) is lost through the sides, and even reflected photons undergo many bounces, losing intensity.

**Recommendation:** Replace the straight acrylic light guide with a **tapered compound parabolic concentrator (CPC) light guide** machined from UV-transmitting acrylic (e.g., Plexiglas XT) with **diffuse-reflective white paint (e.g., Lumirror or EJ-510) on the outer surface** to recapture leaked photons, or alternatively a **square-to-round tapered guide with specularly polished inner surface**. The taper angle should be optimized for the 19 cm → 7.6 cm transition over 30 cm.

**Justification:**
- A well-designed CPC or adiabatic light guide can improve light collection efficiency by **15–30%** compared to a straight guide in this geometry, by reducing total internal reflection losses and guiding more photons onto the photocathode at acceptable angles.
- This is geometrically compatible with the existing iron plate and PMT mounting structure.
- Combined with the SBA PMT above, total improvement in $N_{pe}$ exceeds 50%, ensuring robust compliance with the energy resolution requirement.
- Timing is improved by reducing the spread in photon transit times through the guide, which modestly helps the time resolution already well within spec.

---

### 3. Apply High-Reflectivity Specular Reflector Wrapping to Scintillator Cells

**Current situation:** Polystyrene scintillator cells are typically wrapped in Tyvek (diffuse reflector, R ≈ 95–97%) or thin aluminized mylar, with significant variation cell-to-cell.

**Recommendation:** Wrap each scintillator block in **3M Vikuiti Enhanced Specular Reflector (ESR) film** (specular reflectance > 98% at 400–500 nm) on all five non-PMT faces, with a thin layer of optical coupling grease at the light guide interface.

**Justification:**
- ESR film increases average photon survival per reflection from ~96% (Tyvek) to ~99%, which over the multiple bounces occurring in an 11 cm deep cell with 19 cm × 19 cm face makes a significant cumulative difference (e.g., for 5 average reflections: $0.99^5/0.96^5$ = 0.951/0.815 = +17% more photons reaching the guide).
- Specular reflection also reduces transit time spread, benefiting time resolution.
- ESR film is chemically inert, easy to apply during assembly, and costs ~$5–10/cell — negligible at the scale of this detector.
- This is a proven technique in KamLAND, CUORE, and NOvA calorimetry.

---

### 4. Improve Optical Coupling Between Scintillator and Light Guide

**Current situation:** Standard optical coupling (likely dry contact or thin optical cement) between the polystyrene scintillator (n ≈ 1.59) and acrylic light guide (n ≈ 1.49) introduces a refractive index mismatch and possible air gaps.

**Recommendation:** Use **Saint-Gobain BC-630 silicone optical grease** (n ≈ 1.46) or, preferably, cast a **thin layer of EJ-560 silicone rubber optical interface pad** (n ≈ 1.43, flexible, permanent) between each scintillator cell and its light guide.

**Justification:**
- Eliminating the air gap at the polystyrene/acrylic interface removes a TIR loss mechanism: without coupling medium, photons hitting the interface at angles > arcsin(1.49/1.59) = 69.6° undergo TIR back into the scintillator and may be lost. The silicone pad raises this critical angle significantly.
- EJ-560 pads are mechanically robust, temperature-stable, and can be installed during cell assembly without changing any other mechanical structure.
- Gain in light collection: typically 5–10% for well-designed cells, adding incrementally to the other improvements.

---

### 5. Implement Single-Cell Gain Calibration with an LED Pulser System

**Current situation:** The 20% FWHM already includes cell-to-cell gain non-uniformity. Any systematic spread in PMT gain or light yield across cells degrades the ensemble resolution.

**Recommendation:** Install **one blue LED (420 nm) optical fiber per cell**, fed from a central pulsed LED calibration system (e.g., a Kapustinsky circuit at 1 kHz), with a **PIN photodiode monitor** on each fiber bundle to track LED intensity. Supplement with periodic **electron source calibration** using a deployable $^{207}$Bi source (1.06 MeV conversion electrons) adjacent to representative cells.

**Justification:**
- LED calibration allows continuous gain monitoring and correction at the analysis level, reducing the contribution of gain drift and inter-cell non-uniformity to the effective energy resolution.
- $^{207}$Bi provides a monoenergetic electron line at nearly exactly the 1 MeV benchmark, enabling direct resolution measurement cell-by-cell.
- This is not a hardware replacement but an additional subsystem; it is standard practice in NEMO-3 and SuperNEMO and is low-cost relative to its impact on certified resolution compliance.
- Particularly important because the requirement is that **every cell** must achieve ≤18% FWHM — a statistical tail of under-performing cells could cause failures that only calibration monitoring would catch.

---

## Summary Table

| Change | Estimated $N_{pe}$ Gain | Resolution Improvement | Timing Impact | Difficulty |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SBA PMT (76 mm same format) | +55–60% | 20% → ~16% FWHM | Small improvement | Low — drop-in replacement |
| CPC/tapered light guide | +15–25% | Additional ~6% | Modest improvement | Medium — requires new guide tooling |
| ESR specular reflector | +10–17% | Additional ~4% | Modest improvement | Low — rewrapping |
| Silicone optical pad | +5–10% | Additional ~2% | Negligible | Low — assembly change |
| LED + $^{207}$Bi calibration | Monitors uniformity | Ensures cell-by-cell compliance | N/A | Medium — new subsystem |

The SBA PMT replacement alone is likely sufficient to meet the 18% FWHM requirement. The other measures provide margin and robustness, ensuring every cell complies.

---

## Notes on Constraints

- **Magnetic field compatibility:** All recommended PMTs (SBA/UBA bialkali in standard 76 mm metal envelope with internal μ-metal shield) operate within spec at 3 mT when the existing iron plate is in place. No change to shielding geometry is needed.
- **Cell size:** No change to cell dimensions is proposed; the 19 cm × 19 cm face and 11 cm depth are retained, satisfying the 6 cm separation and ≥3 cm depth requirements.
- **Time resolution:** With higher $N_{pe}$, time resolution only improves. The existing 0.30 ns σ already exceeds the 0.6 ns σ requirement by a factor of 2; none of the proposed changes risk degrading this.

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the existing 76 mm PMTs with Hamamatsu R6231-100 Super Bialkali PMTs of identical form factor, raising quantum efficiency from ~22% to ~35% and increasing photoelectron yield by ~55%, which alone improves energy resolution from 20% to approximately 16% FWHM — meeting the ≤18% requirement in every cell with margin, at low mechanical risk and modest cost.

# Calorimeter Upgrade Proposal

## 1. Check the present calorimeter against the requirements

| Requirement | Present cells | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Energy resolution ≤ 18 % FWHM at 1 MeV | 20 % FWHM | **Fails** |
| Time resolution ≤ 0.6 ns (σ) at 1 MeV | 0.30 ns | Passes, with margin |
| Electrons ≥ 6 cm apart land in different cells | 19 × 19 cm cells | **Fails badly** |
| Depth ≥ 3 cm | 11 cm | Passes |
| Every part works in 3 mT | PMTs need iron plates and long light guides | Works only with mitigation |

**Granularity is the main problem.** With square cells of side *s*, two points in the same cell can be up to the diagonal *s*√2 apart. To guarantee that any two entry points at least 6 cm apart fall in different cells:

*s*√2 < 6 cm, so *s* < 4.2 cm.

A 19 cm cell can hold two electrons up to about 27 cm apart, so no change to the PMT or light guide can fix this. The wall must be re-segmented by a factor of about 20 in area.

## 2. Proposed hardware changes

### (a) Re-segment the scintillator wall
- Use a cell pitch of about 4.0 cm, including the reflector. The diagonal is 5.7 cm, which is below 6 cm.
- Make each block about 4 × 4 cm in face and 4–5 cm deep. This exceeds the 3 cm needed to stop 3 MeV electrons (range about 1.5 cm in plastic).
- Use PVT or polystyrene scintillator.
- Wrap each block individually in a specular reflector (ESR or PTFE).
- Keep optical cross-talk between neighbouring cells below about 1 %, so that each cell's energy is measured separately.
- Cell count: each wall is about 6 m × 3.5 m = 21 m², giving about 13,000 cells per wall and about 26,000 in total.

### (b) Replace PMTs and light guides with SiPM arrays
- Couple one SiPM array (for example 4 × 4 or 6 × 6 mm devices, about 1–2 cm² of total area) directly to the back face of each block.
- **Magnetic field:** SiPMs are insensitive to 3 mT. The iron plates and 30 cm acrylic guides can be removed, which frees depth and mass.
- **Fit:** 76 mm PMTs cannot physically sit behind 4 cm cells.
- **Energy resolution:**
  - Meeting 18 % FWHM (σ ≈ 7.7 %) needs at least about 170 photoelectrons per MeV, before allowing for non-uniformity.
  - Expected light: about 10⁴ photons/MeV produced × about 25–30 % collection × about 40 % photon detection efficiency gives roughly 1,000 photoelectrons/MeV.
  - This should give about 8–12 % FWHM.
  - Removing the long guides also reduces light loss and position non-uniformity.
- **Timing:** small cells with direct coupling should keep σ_t at or below 0.3–0.4 ns, well inside the 0.6 ns limit.

### (c) Readout and electronics
- Use multichannel ASIC front-ends (SiPM readout chips with timing and charge measurement), so that each cell has its own energy and time.
- Stabilise temperature (about ±0.5 °C) or use gain-tracking bias compensation. This keeps calibration stable for 1–3 MeV energy measurements.
- Use a per-cell threshold of about 50 keV. SiPM dark counts are negligible at this level with a coincidence time window.
- Use low-background, radiopure PCBs, connectors and cables (Kapton/copper). The far smaller sensor mass, compared with PMT glass, reduces ²⁰⁸Tl, ²¹⁴Bi and ⁴⁰K backgrounds.

### (d) Calibration and integration
- Add an LED or laser fibre light-injection system to every cell.
- Retain in-situ ²⁰⁷Bi sources for absolute 0.5 and 1 MeV calibration of each cell.
- Use the tracker track extrapolation to associate energy deposits with tracks and to treat electrons that share an edge between two cells. Electrons that scatter into a neighbouring cell can be summed using the track; electrons from separate tracks at least 6 cm apart stay in separate cells.
- Mount everything on a non-magnetic frame (copper or aluminium) and keep the walls sealed against radon.

## 3. Summary

The present 19 cm PMT cells fail the 6 cm separation requirement by geometry and are marginal on energy resolution. Changing to about 4 cm scintillator blocks read directly by SiPMs:
- satisfies the separation requirement;
- improves resolution to about 10 % FWHM;
- keeps timing well below 0.6 ns;
- works natively in 3 mT;
- lowers the radioactive background.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Re-segment each calorimeter wall into ~4 cm × 4 cm × ~4 cm scintillator cells, each read out directly by its own SiPM array, replacing the 19 cm cells, light guides and 76 mm PMTs.

- Superior photon detection efficiency (40-50% vs 20-25%)

# Concrete Hardware Upgrades for the Next Phase

## 1. Calorimeter Scintillator: Replace Polystyrene with Yttrium-Doped Plastic Scintillator or Lyso-Based Composite

**Technology:** High-light-yield plastic scintillator (e.g., EJ-280 or PTP/bis-MSB doped polyvinyltoluene) achieving ~10,000 photons/MeV, or thin LYSO tiles at the front face of plastic blocks.

**Physics motivation:** Energy resolution scales as σ_E/E ∝ 1/√N_pe. The current 20% FWHM at 1 MeV (≈8.5% σ) is already close to the 18% FWHM requirement. Any degradation (PMT aging, light-guide yellowing) fails the spec. Higher light yield directly reduces photoelectron statistical fluctuations. Improving to ~15% FWHM at 1 MeV sharpens the signal peak near Q = 3.03 MeV against the dominant background from 2νββ decay, whose spectrum extends up to Q. Even a few percent improvement in energy resolution substantially increases signal-to-background in the region of interest.

---

## 2. Photosensor: Replace 76 mm PMTs with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)

**Technology:** Large-area SiPM tiles (e.g., Hamamatsu S13360 series or FBK NUV-HD), tiled to match the 19×19 cm² scintillator face, with low-noise readout ASICs.

**Physics motivation:**
- **Magnetic field immunity:** The 3 mT field (even if small) requires careful PMT orientation and iron shielding behind each cell. SiPMs are entirely insensitive to magnetic fields, simplifying mechanical design and removing the iron plate that currently sits between the light guide and PMT — that iron is dead material that could also generate backgrounds.
- **Timing:** SiPMs achieve single-photon time resolutions of ~100–200 ps, enabling calorimeter time resolution well below the 0.6 ns σ requirement for crossing-electron rejection, potentially reaching ~0.3 ns σ even at lower energies.
- **Quantum efficiency:** SiPMs have PDE ~40–50% vs. ~25% for bialkali PMTs, boosting photoelectron yield by nearly a factor 2, directly improving energy resolution by ~√2.
- **Compactness:** Eliminating the 30 cm acrylic light guide (a major source of photon loss and chromatic dispersion) becomes feasible if SiPMs tile directly onto the scintillator face, since SiPMs do not need the standoff distance required by PMTs for field shielding.

---

## 3. Light Guide: Eliminate or Shorten the 30 cm Acrylic Light Guide

**Technology:** Direct coupling of SiPM tiles (or wavelength-shifting (WLS) fiber readout) to the scintillator rear face.

**Physics motivation:** The 30 cm acrylic guide introduces ~30–40% photon loss through bulk absorption, surface reflections, and geometric dilution. This is one of the largest single contributors to poor photoelectron statistics. Removing it and tiling SiPMs directly recovers those photons. Alternatively, embedded WLS fibers (e.g., Kuraray Y-11) routed to SiPMs allow compact, uniform light collection. Either approach improves N_pe by a factor ~1.5–2, translating to ~20–30% better energy resolution — pushing well inside the 18% FWHM target with margin.

---

## 4. Tracking: Replace Geiger-Mode Drift Cells with Small-Diameter Drift Tubes or Micromegas

**Technology:** 5 mm diameter drift tubes (straw trackers) or bulk Micromegas planes with 150 μm pitch strips.

**Physics motivation:**
- **Vertex resolution:** Better spatial resolution (~100 μm vs. ~1 mm for Geiger cells) sharpens the measurement of the electron emission vertex on the foil. This improves rejection of background events where two single-electron tracks from different origins accidentally reconstruct to a common vertex.
- **Hit efficiency and dead time:** Geiger-mode cells have long dead times (~ms) after a discharge, creating inefficiency during high-rate conditions. Straw tubes or Micromegas recover within microseconds.
- **Background rejection via track quality:** Improved dE/dx resolution (from pulse-height measurement impossible in Geiger mode) helps identify alpha tracks and distinguish electrons from other particles, especially near the foil where internal background contamination (²¹⁴Bi, ²⁰⁸Tl on the foil surface) produces the dominant background.
- **Radon sensitivity:** Micromegas with sealed gas recirculation are more tolerant of small radon contamination because they do not have the large sensitive volume per cell that Geiger mode detectors have.

---

## 5. Molybdenum Source: Increase Mass and Reduce Foil Thickness

**Technology:** Composite foils — molybdenum powder (enriched ¹⁰⁰Mo) in a polyvinyl alcohol binder, reducing areal density to ~30 mg/cm² while increasing total mass to ~15 kg by adding foil planes.

**Physics motivation:**
- **Signal rate** scales directly with source mass: T_{1/2} sensitivity ∝ √(M·t/B). Going from 9 kg to 15 kg improves half-life sensitivity by ~√(15/9) ≈ 1.3.
- **Self-absorption and energy loss:** Thinner foils reduce the energy lost by electrons traversing the foil before reaching the tracker, sharpening the reconstructed sum-energy spectrum and reducing the low-energy tail that contaminates the signal region.
- **Multiple foil planes** can be served by the same calorimeter walls if the tracking volume geometry is preserved, making this mass increase relatively low-cost.

---

## 6. External Shielding: Add Liquid-Scintillator Active Veto

**Technology:** A 50 cm thick layer of Gd-loaded liquid scintillator (e.g., 0.1% Gd by mass in linear alkylbenzene) surrounding the iron shielding, read out by 8" PMTs.

**Physics motivation:** At 3000 m.w.e., the dominant surviving external backgrounds are muon-induced fast neutrons and residual high-energy gamma rays. The current passive iron + water shielding attenuates but does not tag these. A liquid-scintillator veto:
- Tags muons and their showers with >99% efficiency.
- Captures thermal neutrons via ²⁵⁷Gd(n,γ) with ~8 MeV prompt gamma cascade, vetoing neutron backgrounds with ~90 μs coincidence window.
- Reduces accidental coincidence backgrounds that mimic two-electron events when a gamma from outside converts in the calorimeter and a foil electron fires simultaneously.

---

## 7. Radon Mitigation: Radon-Free Air Enclosure and Emanation-Low Materials

**Technology:** Sealed detector hall supplied with radon-stripped air (<1 mBq/m³ Rn) produced by activated-charcoal columns at low temperature, combined with replacing any high-emanation plastics in the tracker with low-emanation polyethylene.

**Physics motivation:** ²¹⁴Bi (from ²²²Rn chain) on the source foil surface produces single electrons near Q(¹⁰⁰Mo) = 3.03 MeV through beta decay followed by alpha emission (the "BiPo" background). The current gas flush suppresses radon inside the tracker, but emanation from materials and diffusion from the hall atmosphere deposits ²¹⁴Pb on foil surfaces, building up ²¹⁴Bi. Measurements in similar experiments (NEMO-3) show this is the single largest background source at high energies. A radon-free enclosure reduces this by an order of magnitude.

---

| Upgrade | Technology | Primary Gain |
|---|---|---|
| Scintillator | High-yield plastic or LYSO composite | Energy resolution → <15% FWHM |
| Photosensor | SiPM tiles | B-field immunity, timing, QE |
| Light guide | Direct SiPM coupling / WLS fiber | +50% photoelectrons |
| Tracker | Straw tubes / Micromegas | Vertex resolution, background rejection |
| Source foil | Thinner, more mass | Signal rate, energy resolution |
| Active veto | Gd-loaded liquid scintillator | Muon/neutron background tagging |
| Radon control | Rn-free air enclosure | BiPo background reduction ×10 |

**TOP RECOMMENDATION:** Replace the 76 mm PMTs and 30 cm acrylic light guides with direct-coupled SiPM tile arrays, as this simultaneously solves the magnetic-field shielding problem, nearly doubles the photoelectron yield to comfortably satisfy the 18% FWHM energy resolution requirement with margin, improves timing resolution below 0.3 ns σ for crossing-electron rejection, and removes the iron backing plates that add dead material and complicate the mechanical design.

**TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace PMTs with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)**

This upgrade simultaneously addresses multiple technical requirements (magnetic field immunity, time resolution, energy resolution) while enabling other improvements and directly impacts the detector's ability to reach next-generation sensitivity for neutrinoless double-beta decay searches.

This is the NEMO-3/SuperNEMO situation. The constraints in the brief show which parts of the present instrument already meet the requirements, which do not, and where the real upgrade leverage lies. The specification is satisfied on time resolution (0.30 ns against 0.6 ns required) and marginally exceeded on energy (20% against 18% required). Everything else (foil, tracker, magnet, shielding) is a strong baseline, so the proposal should be targeted.

**1. Photomultipliers: replace the 76 mm tubes with low-radioactivity, high-quantum-efficiency PMTs (the main change)**

- Use a bialkali photocathode with "super-bialkali" quantum efficiency of about 35% or more, in place of the standard ~25%. Photoelectron statistics dominate the stochastic term of the resolution (about 1/sqrt(N_pe)), so about 40% more photoelectrons gives roughly 15-17% FWHM at 1 MeV, which meets the 18% requirement with margin.
- Choose a low-radioactivity glass (low K-40, U, Th) so the tubes do not become a background source near the foils. This was a key lesson of NEMO-3 (PMT glass contributed background).
- Choose a tube with a high-gain, fast first dynode structure, good timing (transit-time spread of about 1.5 ns FWHM or better), and good single-photoelectron response. This preserves the 0.6 ns time-resolution margin.
- Keep the 3 mT field compatible: the existing iron plate and mu-metal shield can stay, but the new tube should be validated for gain stability in the field.

**2. Scintillator: switch to a better, radiopure PVT or PS scintillator**

- Use a high-light-yield, low-self-absorption PVT (e.g. Eljen EJ-200-class) or equivalent polystyrene with optimised dopants, with a long bulk attenuation length.
- Wrap or coat the scintillator with a high-reflectivity diffuse layer (e.g. Teflon, Mylar, or Tyvek), leaving the entrance face thin so electron energy loss before the scintillator is minimised.
- Rationale: a larger fraction of light reaching the photocathode directly lowers the stochastic term of the resolution.

**3. Cell geometry: keep cells about 19 x 19 cm with at least 3 cm depth and optimise the optical coupling**

- The brief requires electrons at least 6 cm apart to land in different cells, which sets the lateral cell size, so the 19 cm pitch must not be coarser than needed. At least 3 cm depth is needed to fully absorb 3 MeV electrons. Reducing the 11 cm depth toward about 10 cm (never below 3 cm) shortens the optical path, lowers the gamma-ray background in the calorimeter, and improves light collection, but the depth must not be pushed to the minimum because 3 cm leaves no margin in light collection or containment of showering electrons.
- Replace the 30 cm acrylic light guide, which is the main light loss, with a short or tapered guide, or remove it altogether by coupling the PMT directly to the block. The latter requires a PMT with an optimised, curved-window photocathode matched to the scintillator face. A shorter guide cuts path-dependent light loss and time jitter, which improves both energy and timing.
- Use optical grease or a pad with matched refractive index at both interfaces to cut Fresnel losses.

**4. Magnetic-field compatibility**

- Retain the iron plate and add a mu-metal shield around each tube to preserve gain, since the 3 mT field would otherwise degrade the PMT response. Check that the new, possibly larger-cathode PMT keeps the same gain stability in the field.

**5. Calibration and electronics (supporting changes)**

- Install a light-injection system (LED/laser through optical fibres) for continuous gain and timing monitoring, plus periodic calibration with electron sources (e.g. Bi-207 at about 1 MeV) to verify the 18% and 0.6 ns targets cell by cell. The requirement applies to every cell, so cell-by-cell verification is needed.
- Use fast waveform digitisation (about 1 GS/s or better) to extract timing and charge, and to reject pile-up.

**What to leave unchanged**

- The foil, Geiger-cell tracker, helium gas mix, radon flushing, and shielding already deliver the stated performance; the upgrade is a calorimeter project.
- The 3 mT field only needs to tell electrons from positrons, so no change to the magnet is needed.

**Summary of why:** the energy-resolution target is the binding requirement, and it is limited chiefly by photoelectron statistics (PMT quantum efficiency, light-guide loss, and scintillator light yield). Timing has headroom, so changes should be made without degrading it.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the 76 mm PMTs with low-radioactivity, high-quantum-efficiency (super-bialkali) tubes, together with a shorter or removed light guide, to bring every cell's energy resolution below 18% FWHM at 1 MeV.

I'll treat this as a detector design problem and work through what the current calorimeter cannot do and what would fix each shortfall.

**Diagnosis of the current calorimeter against the requirements**

- Energy resolution: 20% FWHM at 1 MeV now; target is 18% or better in every cell. The gap is small but the current cells are also limited by light collection through a 30 cm acrylic guide and a 76 mm PMT, which gives low photoelectron statistics and nonuniform response.
- Time resolution: 0.30 ns sigma now, which is already better than the 0.6 ns requirement. This is a margin to keep, not a problem to solve.
- Granularity: 19 cm faces mean two electrons 6 cm apart can land in the same cell. This is the most serious failure. The 6 cm separation rule demands cells of roughly 5 cm or less lateral size, or some form of position-resolved readout within each block.
- Depth: 11 cm of polystyrene is adequate for 3 MeV electrons (the requirement is only 3 cm), so depth is not a constraint to change.
- Magnetic field: a 3 mT field is weak, but standard PMTs still lose gain and suffer timing and collection-efficiency changes in any field. Vacuum-tube PMTs are the component most likely to fail this requirement.

**Proposed upgrades**

1. Fine segmentation with position readout. Replace each 19 x 19 cm block with an array of scintillator bars or tiles of about 4 to 5 cm pitch, each cell at least 3 cm deep. Plastic scintillator bars read out at both ends, or a dense pixelated array, would let the position of each hit be reconstructed to better than 6 cm, so simultaneous electrons are assigned to separate cells. This is the change that addresses the core failure.

2. Silicon photomultiplier readout in place of the PMTs. SiPMs (or MPPC-type devices) are insensitive to the 3 mT field, compact enough to couple directly to small cells without a long light guide, and offer high photon detection efficiency. Coupling a SiPM directly to each small tile removes the 30 cm acrylic guide, improves light yield and uniformity, and should bring energy resolution comfortably under 18% FWHM at 1 MeV. Temperature stabilization and dark-count management (cooling or thresholding) are needed given the low-background environment.

3. Higher light yield scintillator. Replace or supplement polystyrene with a higher-light-output plastic (for example a PEN- or PVT-based formulation with optimized wavelength shifters) or with a fast inorganic crystal where its density and cost are justified. Better light yield directly improves the resolution term that dominates at 1 MeV.

4. Timing electronics. Keep the existing time performance by using fast front-end electronics with waveform sampling or constant-fraction discrimination matched to the SiPM pulse shape. This preserves sub-0.5 ns timing for the rejection of externally entering electrons.

5. Radiopurity and gas/cell materials. Select low-activity SiPMs, optical couplings, and wrapping materials, since the calorimeter sits in a low-background environment and the 100Mo signal region is sensitive to internal contamination.

6. Mechanical integration. Lay out the fine-pitch array so that each cell is individually accessible for calibration, use a light-tight housing with a reflector wrap, and provide per-cell gain monitoring with LED or radioactive-source calibration so that the 18% requirement holds across all cells, not only on average.

**Expected outcome**

Fine segmentation fixes the granularity requirement; SiPM readout with direct coupling and better scintillator fixes the energy resolution and the field-compatibility requirement; the existing fast-timing approach carries over to satisfy the 0.6 ns requirement with margin.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the 19 cm PMT-read polystyrene blocks with finely segmented (about 4 to 5 cm) scintillator cells read out by silicon photomultipliers, so that individual electrons 6 cm apart are separately measured and the calorimeter is insensitive to the magnetic field.

# Hardware Upgrades for Neutrinoless Double-Beta Decay Detector

## Required Upgrades

**1. Scintillator Cell Replacement**
- **Technology**: Upgrade from polystyrene to fast plastic scintillators (e.g., EJ-200 or equivalent with shorter decay times ~2.7 ns)
- **Why**: Current 20% energy resolution meets the 18% requirement marginally; fast scintillators improve light collection speed and reduce timing jitter. The time resolution of 0.30 ns sigma must improve to ≤0.6 ns sigma—fast scintillators are essential for this 2× margin.

**2. Photomultiplier Upgrade**
- **Technology**: Replace 76 mm PMTs with fast phototubes (e.g., Hamamatsu R7600-series or similar with transit time spread <0.3 ns FWHM) or transition to silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) with gain ~10⁶ and timing resolution <50 ps
- **Why**: PMT transit time spread directly limits time resolution. Current specs suggest ~0.25 ns contribution from PMT alone; faster devices are needed to meet the 0.6 ns sigma requirement without degrading energy resolution.

**3. Light Guide Optimization**
- **Technology**: Replace 30 cm acrylic guides with shorter (20 cm) or graded-index (GRIN) guides; add wavelength-shifting (WLS) fiber coupling instead of direct contact
- **Why**: Reduces dispersion in light propagation time (currently contributing ~0.15-0.20 ns to timing resolution). WLS fibers also improve light collection uniformity across cell faces.

**4. Cell Depth Increase**
- **Technology**: Increase scintillator cell depth from 11 cm to 12-13 cm
- **Why**: The requirement for 3 cm minimum depth per cell (to absorb 3 MeV electrons) leaves limited margin in the current 11 cm design. Increased depth improves energy containment and reduces energy resolution degradation from edge effects.

**5. Magnetic Field Compatibility of Calorimeter Electronics**
- **Technology**: Redesign PMT/SiPM mounting and signal routing with mu-metal shielding; use radiation-hard preamplifiers positioned outside the 3 mT field region
- **Why**: Current design sits PMTs behind iron plates in a 3 mT field. PMTs are sensitive to magnetic fields; SiPMs perform better in-field but need rad-hard readout electronics. This ensures energy and timing performance is maintained.

**6. Readout Electronics Upgrade**
- **Technology**: Implement fast digitizers (sampling ≥1 GS/s, <0.5 ns jitter) with leading-edge and constant-fraction timing discrimination
- **Why**: Improved timing resolution requires low-jitter electronics. Current analog amplifiers/discriminators introduce timing walk; fast digitizers with CFD eliminate this systematic error.

**7. Temperature Stabilization**
- **Technology**: Install active thermal control (±0.5 K) for scintillator and PMT/SiPM boxes
- **Why**: Scintillator light yield and PMT gain both drift with temperature. Underground labs have stable ambient conditions, but local heating from PMTs requires active management to maintain the tight 18% energy and 0.6 ns timing specifications.

---

**TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace photomultipliers with fast SiPMs (e.g., Hamamatsu MPPC series) with transit time spread <50 ps and implement fast digitizer readout, as timing resolution is the critical path item and PMT transit time jitter dominates the current 0.3 ns performance, preventing achievement of the 0.6 ns sigma requirement needed for external background rejection.**

# Hardware Upgrades for the Planar Tracker-Calorimeter Detector

## Analysis of Current Performance vs. Requirements

| Parameter | Current | Required | Status |
|-----------|---------|----------|--------|
| Energy resolution | 20% FWHM @ 1 MeV | ≤18% FWHM @ 1 MeV | **FAILS** |
| Time resolution | 0.30 ns σ @ 1 MeV | ≤0.6 ns σ @ 1 MeV | Passes |
| Cell depth | 11 cm | ≥3 cm, fully absorbs 3 MeV | Passes |
| Cell face | 19×19 cm² | ≤6 cm separation → different cells | Passes |
| B-field operation | unspecified | Works in 3 mT | **Unknown** |

---

## Proposed Hardware Upgrades

### 1. Replace Photomultiplier Tubes with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) — *Critical*

**Problem addressed:** The 76 mm PMT is the dominant bottleneck for energy resolution. Standard bialkali PMTs have quantum efficiency (QE) ~25–30% at the polystyrene emission peak (~420 nm). The statistical photoelectron yield directly controls both energy resolution and timing.

**Energy resolution scaling:**
$$\frac{\text{FWHM}}{E} \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{N_{pe}}} \propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{\text{QE} \times \Omega \times \text{light yield}}}$$

A modern SiPM array (e.g., Hamamatsu S13360 series or FBK NUV-HD) achieves PDE ~50–55% at 420 nm, roughly doubling the detected photon yield relative to the PMT. For a resolution scaling as $1/\sqrt{N}$, this yields an improvement factor of $\sqrt{2} \approx 1.41$:
$$20\% \times \frac{1}{\sqrt{2}} \approx 14\%\;\text{FWHM} \ll 18\%$$

**Timing:** SiPMs have single-photon time resolution ~100–200 ps (σ), far better than PMT transit-time spread (~1 ns). The first-photon timing already satisfies the 0.6 ns requirement comfortably, providing safety margin.

**Magnetic field immunity:** SiPMs are entirely insensitive to magnetic fields — no electron drift trajectory is involved. The existing 76 mm PMTs, even with mu-metal shielding, may suffer gain degradation in stray fields beyond the iron plate (fringe fields from 3 mT across a large volume are non-negligible at the PMT face). SiPMs eliminate this concern entirely.

**Practical implementation:**
- Replace each 76 mm PMT with a ~4×4 array of 6×6 mm² SiPMs (total active area ~576 mm²) coupled directly or via short WLS fibers to the existing 30 cm acrylic light guide
- Use trans-impedance amplifier front-end boards mounted on the iron plate (SiPMs operate at ~25–70 V bias, low power)
- Temperature-stabilize bias voltage (SiPM gain is temperature-dependent at ~2 mV/°C): a simple RTD-based feedback circuit per cell or per sector

**Cost/complexity:** SiPM arrays at this scale (~few hundred cells per wall, two walls) are commercially available; readout ASICs (e.g., TOFPET2, TARGET) are mature.

---

### 2. Replace Polystyrene Scintillator with p-Terphenyl-doped Polyvinyltoluene (PVT) or Use BC-408/EJ-200 Cast Plastic

**Problem addressed:** Generic polystyrene scintillator (e.g., hand-cast or extruded) yields ~8,000–10,000 photons/MeV. Commercial high-performance PVT-based scintillators (Eljen EJ-200, Saint-Gobain BC-408) yield ~10,000 photons/MeV with better optical transparency (attenuation length ~380 cm vs. ~100–200 cm for polystyrene).

The larger attenuation length is critical for 19×19×11 cm cells: photons produced near the front face of the cell must traverse up to ~22 cm (diagonal) to the light guide. With polystyrene's short attenuation length, significant self-absorption degrades both yield and uniformity.

**Combined effect with SiPM upgrade:** The resolution improvement compounds multiplicatively with the PDE gain from SiPMs. Even a 20% increase in collected photons reduces resolution by ~10% relative.

**Implementation:** Machine or cast EJ-200 blocks to 19×19×11 cm³, wrap in Tyvek or VM2000 reflector foil for >95% reflectance, couple to existing 30 cm acrylic light guide with optical grease (n-matched).

---

### 3. Upgrade the Acrylic Light Guide to a Wavelength-Shifting Light Guide

**Problem addressed:** The 30 cm acrylic light guide attenuates ~420 nm polystyrene/PVT emission over its length. UV-transparent acrylic transmits >90% at 420 nm per 30 cm, but surface losses at the PMT/SiPM coupling are significant.

**Upgrade:** Replace plain acrylic with a WLS-doped acrylic rod (e.g., Y-11 dye, absorbs at 420 nm, re-emits at ~490 nm where SiPM PDE remains high and self-absorption is negligible). This can increase collected photons by 15–25% and improve uniformity of light collection across the cell face.

Alternatively, replace the fish-tail light guide geometry with a **compound parabolic concentrator (CPC)** in acrylic to better match the scintillator face area to the SiPM array area.

---

### 4. Add a Second-Layer Thin Scintillator Veto Paddle on the Outer Face of Each Calorimeter Wall

**Problem addressed:** Externally-entering electrons (cosmic muon daughters, gamma-induced electrons from rock/shielding) must be rejected. The current approach relies on timing (0.30 ns σ PMT timing is used to identify outside-in vs. inside-out). The requirement of ≤0.6 ns (σ) is already met, but a **hardware veto** layer provides rejection independent of calorimeter timing quality.

**Implementation:** A single layer of 1 cm thick EJ-200 scintillator tiles (or plastic scintillator strips) with SiPM readout, covering the outer face of each calorimeter wall, acts as an active veto for charged particles entering from outside. This directly suppresses backgrounds without relying solely on timing cuts.

---

### 5. Install Individual Cell High-Voltage / Bias Compensation with In-Situ LED Calibration Pulsers

**Problem addressed:** Cell-to-cell gain uniformity and long-term gain stability are essential for maintaining ≤18% FWHM. Gain drift leads to effective energy resolution degradation even if the intrinsic photon statistics are sufficient.

**Implementation:**
- Embed a blue LED (peak ~430 nm) + optical fiber per cell for daily gain calibration pulses
- For SiPM arrays: implement per-cell DCDC-converter-based bias adjustment with remote control, allowing online equalization
- Monitor with a dedicated DAQ channel that records LED pulse response; auto-correct gain drift via software threshold trim or hardware bias adjustment

This is standard practice in modern calorimeters (CMS ECAL, LHCb ECAL upgrades) and costs little per channel.

---

### 6. Replace Iron Plate Behind Photosensor with Non-Magnetic Equivalent (if SiPMs are Not Adopted)

**Problem addressed (contingency):** If PMTs are retained, the 3 mT field — even with an iron shielding plate — may allow fringe-field penetration at the PMT face sufficient to deflect the electron beam in the dynode chain. Iron plates are effective but add weight and may not fully attenuate the field along the plate edges.

**Upgrade:** Use **mu-metal** (Ni-Fe-Mo alloy, μᵣ ~ 20,000–50,000) cylindrical shields fitted around each PMT, plus a mu-metal end plate. This provides >99% attenuation of 3 mT to <30 μT at the photocathode. Alternatively, switch to **magnetic-field-tolerant mesh-dynode PMTs** (e.g., Hamamatsu R5924 fine-mesh type, operable up to 1 T transverse field), though these are more expensive than SiPMs at this scale.

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Addresses | Priority |
|---------|-----------|----------|
| PMT → SiPM array | Energy resolution (fails spec), B-field immunity, timing safety margin | **Critical** |
| Polystyrene → EJ-200/BC-408 PVT | Energy resolution, light yield, uniformity | High |
| WLS/CPC light guide | Light collection efficiency | Medium |
| Outer veto scintillator layer | External electron rejection (redundant with timing) | Medium |
| LED calibration + gain stabilization | Long-term resolution maintenance | Medium |
| Mu-metal PMT shields (if PMTs retained) | B-field immunity contingency | Low (superseded by SiPM) |

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the 76 mm PMTs with SiPM arrays (PDE ~50%), which simultaneously brings the energy resolution below the 18% FWHM requirement, maintains excellent timing, and eliminates all magnetic-field sensitivity of the photosensor.

Looking at this detector searching for neutrinoless double-beta decay of ¹⁰⁰Mo, I'll analyze the constraints and propose hardware upgrades:

## Current Performance vs Requirements

**Energy Resolution:**
- Current: 20% FWHM at 1 MeV
- Required: ≤18% FWHM at 1 MeV
- **FAILS requirement**

**Time Resolution:**
- Current: 0.30 ns σ at 1 MeV  
- Required: ≤0.6 ns σ at 1 MeV
- Meets requirement

**Spatial segmentation:** 19 cm × 19 cm cells adequate for 6 cm separation requirement

**PMT performance:** 76 mm PMTs + 30 cm light guides likely limit both energy and time resolution

## Proposed Hardware Upgrades

### 1. **Replace 76 mm PMTs with larger-area PMTs (127-200 mm)**
Larger photocathode area improves photon collection efficiency, directly improving energy resolution. The √N statistics of photoelectrons dominate energy resolution at 1 MeV. Modern 5" (127 mm) or 8" (200 mm) PMTs like Hamamatsu R1408 or R5912 series work well in low magnetic fields and would collect 3-5× more photons.

### 2. **Shorten or eliminate acrylic light guides**
30 cm light guides cause significant light loss and transit time spread. Replace with:
- Direct PMT coupling where possible
- Shorter (5-10 cm) light guides with better optical coupling
- Wavelength-shifting light guides to improve collection

### 3. **Improve scintillator optical coupling**
Add reflective wrapping (Tyvek or ESR) to maximize light collection. Optimize optical grease/gel at all interfaces.

### 4. **Upgrade to faster, higher-quantum-efficiency PMTs**
Modern bialkali or super-bialkali photocathodes (QE ~25-30%) versus older models (~15-20%) would significantly increase photoelectron yield. Fast timing PMTs with rise times <2 ns maintain excellent time resolution.

### 5. **Add magnetic shielding for PMTs**
Mu-metal shields around PMTs would allow use of high-performance PMTs that might otherwise be affected by the 3 mT field, enabling access to better models.

### 6. **Implement better HV distribution and stabilization**
Temperature-compensated, ultra-stable HV supplies reduce gain variations that degrade energy resolution.

### 7. **Upgrade to faster/better electronics**
Modern waveform digitizers (250-500 MSPS, 12-14 bit) would enable:
- Digital pulse shape analysis
- Better baseline subtraction
- Optimal filtering for energy resolution

### 8. **Segment cells into 2×2 subcells**
Subdivide each 19 cm cell into four ~9.5 cm cells using optical barriers, read by 4 smaller PMTs or one multi-anode PMT. Improves position resolution and energy measurement for events where both electrons hit the same wall.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace 76 mm PMTs with 127-200 mm diameter PMTs with higher quantum efficiency to improve photoelectron statistics and meet the 18% FWHM energy resolution requirement.

# Concrete Hardware Upgrades for the Next Phase

## 1. Calorimeter Scintillator: Replace Polystyrene with Yttrium-Doped Polystyrene or Pure PVT with Enhanced Light Yield

**Technology:** High-light-yield plastic scintillator (e.g., EJ-204 or BC-408 PVT-based, or anthracene-doped polystyrene), increasing photon yield by ~30–40% over standard polystyrene.

**Physics motivation:** Energy resolution scales as σ_E/E ∝ 1/√N_pe, where N_pe is the number of photoelectrons. The current 20% FWHM at 1 MeV must improve to ≤18% FWHM. A ~20% increase in light yield (∝ N_pe) reduces FWHM by ~10%, bringing resolution from 20% to ~18% or better. This directly addresses the stated energy resolution requirement. Higher light yield also improves the energy sum of both electrons near Q = 3.03 MeV, sharpening the signal peak against the background continuum.

---

## 2. Photomultiplier Tubes: Replace 76 mm PMTs with 76 mm Low-Radioactivity, High-QE Bialkali PMTs (e.g., Hamamatsu R6594 or similar)

**Technology:** High-quantum-efficiency (QE ~35% vs. ~25%) ultra-low-radioactivity PMTs, e.g., Hamamatsu R6594-MOD or ETL 9305 series with selected glass.

**Physics motivation:** Higher QE directly increases N_pe, improving both energy and timing resolution simultaneously (σ_t ∝ 1/√N_pe). The timing requirement is 0.6 ns σ at 1 MeV — the current tubes achieve 0.30 ns, so there is margin, but higher QE ensures this is maintained or improved even if the scintillator cell geometry is modified. Critically, low-radioactivity glass (selected for ²⁰⁸Tl, ²²⁸Ra content) reduces the internal background near the Q-value. PMT glass is a known source of high-energy gamma backgrounds in this energy range; standard borosilicate glass contains ~50–100 ppb Th, whereas selected low-background glass can reduce this by a factor 10, directly reducing accidental coincidences mimicking signal.

---

## 3. Light Guide: Replace 30 cm Acrylic Light Guide with a Shorter or Winston-Cone Coupled Direct Coupling + Reflective Wrapping

**Technology:** Shorter acrylic light guide (10–15 cm) with enhanced specular reflector (e.g., 3M Vikuiti ESR film replacing paint) or non-imaging concentrator cone, combined with optical coupling grease matched to scintillator emission (~420 nm).

**Physics motivation:** The 30 cm acrylic light guide is the dominant source of light loss (absorption + total internal reflection losses compound over length). Shortening it and improving reflectivity can recover 20–30% more photons at the PMT face. This simultaneously improves both energy resolution (direct N_pe increase) and timing resolution (less transit-time spread from long guide). The constraint that the PMT must sit behind an iron plate (for shielding) is maintained; the iron plate position can stay fixed while the guide geometry changes. This upgrade is mechanically straightforward and low-risk.

---

## 4. Tracking: Replace Geiger-Mode Drift Cells with Drift Cells Operating in Proportional Mode with Fast Readout

**Technology:** Proportional-mode drift cells with cathode-pad readout and TDC/ADC electronics (e.g., as used in DRIFT or NEXT-style trackers), or thin-gap drift tubes with ~100 μm position resolution.

**Physics motivation:** Geiger-mode cells fire along their entire length, giving only a yes/no hit, with no dE/dx information and limited 3D reconstruction. Proportional-mode cells provide both drift-time (position) and charge (dE/dx), enabling: (a) better vertex identification on the foil to confirm both electrons originate from the same decay point (key signal topology); (b) rejection of single electrons that scatter and appear as two tracks; (c) rejection of alpha tracks from foil contamination by dE/dx. At 3.03 MeV in a 3 mT field, track curvature is very slight (~1–2 mm sagitta over 50 cm), so the sign of charge determination is preserved; the upgrade does not interfere with this. Better track reconstruction also improves angular measurement, which matters for internal pair rejection and Compton electron rejection.

---

## 5. Shielding/Radon: Active Radon Monitor and Radon-Trapping System for Gas Supply

**Technology:** Electrostatic radon detector (e.g., Lucas cell with alpha counting, sensitivity ~1 mBq/m³) on the gas inlet/outlet, combined with activated-charcoal cold trap on the He-based gas supply loop, and positive-pressure nitrogen tent around the detector exterior.

**Physics motivation:** ²²²Rn → ²¹⁴Bi → ²¹⁴Po in the tracking gas produces electrons and alphas that can mimic the two-electron signal topology (BiPo events). Even at the sub-mBq/m³ level, Rn daughters plating out on the foil surface create a surface ²²⁴Ra/²²⁸Ra background. The gas flush already mitigates this, but without real-time monitoring one cannot correlate data quality with Rn level. Active monitoring allows offline rejection of data periods with elevated Rn, and the cold trap reduces the Rn activity in the circulated gas by a factor ~100. This is especially important for the ¹⁰⁰Mo Q-value at 3.03 MeV: the ²¹⁴Bi beta endpoint is 3.27 MeV, directly overlapping the signal region.

---

## 6. Calorimeter Cell Segmentation: Reduce Cell Face to 10 cm × 10 cm

**Technology:** Recut scintillator cells to 10 cm × 10 cm × 11 cm, read out by a single 50 mm PMT via a short tapered light guide, maintaining or slightly increasing total calorimeter coverage.

**Physics motivation:** The requirement that two electrons at least 6 cm apart deposit energy in *different* cells is marginal with 19 cm × 19 cm faces: two electrons 6 cm apart can easily enter the same cell and their energies cannot be separated. With 10 cm × 10 cm cells, two tracks separated by 6 cm much more reliably land in separate cells, as required by physics. Each electron in a double-beta decay carries on average ~1.5 MeV; measuring both separately improves the two-dimensional energy sum spectrum, providing much stronger background rejection. The 10 cm segmentation also improves position resolution for extrapolating tracks back to the foil vertex and for rejecting crossing electrons via timing. The 11 cm depth is unchanged, ensuring full absorption of 3 MeV electrons remains satisfied.

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Primary Benefit |
|---|---|---|
| Scintillator material | High-yield PVT | Energy resolution ≤18% FWHM |
| PMTs | High-QE, low-BG | Resolution + background |
| Light guide | Short + ESR reflector | Light yield, timing |
| Tracker mode | Proportional cells | Vertex & dE/dx reconstruction |
| Radon system | Cold trap + monitor | BiPo background rejection |
| Cell segmentation | 10×10 cm cells | Two-electron energy separation |

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Reduce calorimeter cell face size from 19 cm × 19 cm to 10 cm × 10 cm, because this directly enables the separate energy measurement of two electrons from the same decay — the fundamental observable of neutrinoless double-beta decay — which is compromised with the current coarse segmentation whenever the two tracks are only marginally separated, and no amount of resolution improvement in energy or timing compensates for the inability to distinguish two electrons entering the same cell.

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for the Tracker-Calorimeter Detector

## 1. Photomultiplier Tube → Silicon Photomultiplier (SiPM) Array Replacement

**Current:** 76 mm (3-inch) PMT behind iron plate, affected by 3 mT field (even at 3 mT, standard PMTs lose gain and resolution).

**Proposed:** Replace each PMT with a tiled array of **Hamamatsu S13360-6050PE or SensL J-series 6mm SiPMs** (e.g., 4×4 array totaling ~24×24 mm² active area, summed into one readout channel).

- SiPMs are **completely immune to magnetic fields** — eliminates the need for the iron shielding plate behind each calorimeter cell, reducing passive material
- Improved single-photon detection efficiency (~50% PDE vs ~25% for a standard bialkali PMT)
- The iron plate currently needed to shield the PMT from the 3 mT field absorbs backscattered photons and complicates calibration; removing it improves light collection
- Directly addresses the operational requirement that "every part of the calorimeter must work in the 3 mT field"
- SiPMs can be potted directly onto the rear face of the acrylic light guide, **eliminating the 30 cm light guide entirely** (see below)

---

## 2. Eliminate the 30 cm Acrylic Light Guide

**Current:** 30 cm acrylic light guide between scintillator and PMT.

**Proposed:** With SiPMs mounted flush against the scintillator rear face (or with a short <2 cm optical coupler), the light guide becomes unnecessary.

- The 30 cm light guide causes ~15–20% light loss per bounce and broadens the photon arrival time distribution, directly degrading time resolution
- Removing it increases photoelectron yield, improving both energy resolution (scales as 1/√Npe) and time resolution (scales as 1/√Npe for leading-edge timing)
- Estimated improvement: if Npe doubles, energy resolution improves by ~√2 and time resolution improves by ~√2, potentially bringing 20% FWHM → ~14% FWHM at 1 MeV (well within the 18% requirement) and time resolution from 0.30 ns → ~0.21 ns sigma (well within 0.6 ns)

---

## 3. Scintillator Material Upgrade: Polystyrene → PVT-based or PEN Scintillator

**Current:** Polystyrene scintillator (light yield ~8,000–10,000 photons/MeV, decay time ~3–4 ns).

**Proposed Option A:** **EJ-200 (PVT-based) plastic scintillator** — higher light yield (~10,000 photons/MeV), faster decay constant (~2.1 ns), better optical clarity, commercially available in large blocks.

**Proposed Option B:** **Polyethylene naphthalate (PEN) scintillator tiles** — intrinsic scintillator, ~10,000 photons/MeV, very low intrinsic radioactivity, being actively developed for 0νββ applications (demonstrated by LEGEND collaboration).

- PEN is self-supporting, radiopure, and can be machined to 19×19 cm² × 11 cm blocks
- Better time resolution from faster/brighter emission helps the 0.6 ns timing requirement for crossing-electron rejection
- Lower intrinsic radioactivity reduces background in the signal region near 3 MeV

---

## 4. Geiger-Cell Tracking → Drift-Cell Upgrade with Faster Gas Mixture

**Current:** Geiger-mode drift cells in helium-based gas.

**Proposed:** Transition to **small-cell proportional drift tubes** (e.g., 9 mm diameter, as pioneered in DRIFT or similar) operating in **He/isobutane (95/5)** or **He/ethanol** mixture with faster drift velocity and genuine drift-time position measurement.

- Geiger-mode cells fire along their entire length (Geiger discharge), giving only a hit position but **no drift-time information** for precise 3D vertex reconstruction along the wire direction
- Proportional-mode small drift cells give **true 3D hit coordinates** via drift time, improving vertex resolution on the foil from ~1 cm to ~1 mm
- Better vertex resolution suppresses backgrounds from electrons originating in the foil bulk vs. the foil surface (crucial for distinguishing signal from internal foil contamination by ²⁰⁸Tl, ²¹⁴Bi)
- He-based gas is retained (low Z, minimal electron scattering) but the mixture is optimized for speed
- Add **TDC readout at 1 ns resolution** (e.g., CAEN V1290 or similar) to each drift cell end

---

## 5. Radon Mitigation: Active Radon Trapping System

**Current:** Gas flushing to keep radon out of tracking volumes.

**Proposed:** Install a **dedicated radon-reduction unit** using activated charcoal cold traps at −40°C on the gas inlet, combined with continuous **online radon monitoring** (electrostatic radon monitors, sensitivity <1 mBq/m³).

- Radon daughters (²¹⁴Bi → ²¹⁴Po) plate out on the foil and produce high-energy electrons mimicking the 0νββ signal
- Simple flushing reduces but does not eliminate radon at the sub-mBq/m³ level needed
- Cold charcoal traps achieve **radon activity <0.1 mBq/m³** in the tracking gas (demonstrated by SuperNEMO collaboration)
- Pair with **electropolished stainless steel gas plumbing** (no plastic tubing that outgasses radon from ²²⁶Ra impurities)

---

## 6. Front-End Electronics: Waveform Digitization

**Current:** Implied analog readout with energy and time extracted by standard NIM/VME electronics.

**Proposed:** Replace with **switched-capacitor array waveform digitizers** such as the **DRS4 chip** (PSI) or **TARGET ASIC**, sampling at 1–2 GSa/s per calorimeter channel.

- Full waveform capture enables **offline pile-up rejection**: two electrons arriving within ~10 ns in the same cell can be separated in time
- Improved time-pick-off algorithms (constant fraction, matched filter) on waveforms can achieve **sub-100 ps timing** with high-Npe pulses, far exceeding the 0.6 ns requirement
- Pulse-shape discrimination can help separate electron signals from alpha or nuclear recoil backgrounds in the scintillator
- DRS4 is proven in low-background experiments (MEG, nEDM), consumes <50 mW/channel, operates at room temperature

---

## 7. Calibration System Enhancement

**Current:** Not explicitly described.

**Proposed:** Install a **UV laser fiber-based calibration system** with a single nitrogen laser or pulsed LED (e.g., 400 nm) distributed via optical fibers to each scintillator cell rear face through a small penetration in the light guide (or directly with SiPMs).

- Provides **cell-by-cell gain monitoring** at the 0.1% level continuously during data-taking
- Supplement with periodic **radioactive source deployment** (²⁰⁷Bi source wire, 1.064 MeV conversion electrons) inserted via thin tubes along the foil plane for absolute energy scale at the signal-relevant energy
- ²⁰⁷Bi gives conversion electrons at 0.482, 0.976, and 1.682 MeV — directly calibrating the resolution at 1 MeV as required

---
