The current wall has 20% FWHM at 1 MeV (needs ≤18%), 0.30 ns time resolution (already better than the 0.6 ns requirement, so it has margin), 19 cm cells (too large: two electrons 6 cm apart can land in one cell), and PMTs behind iron that sit in a 3 mT field. Below are concrete upgrades addressing each constraint.

**1. Segmentation: shrink the cells**
The 6 cm separation requirement means the transverse cell pitch must be well under 6 cm, with margin for shower spread and position resolution. Replace 19 x 19 cm cells with roughly 3 x 3 cm to 5 x 5 cm cells, e.g. a fine-pitch array of square scintillator bars or tiles. A 4 cm pitch with each cell read individually gives a comfortable margin against two electrons sharing a cell. This is the most important change, since it is a geometric requirement the current design cannot meet at any energy resolution.

**2. Scintillator material: higher light yield, faster**
Replace polystyrene with a plastic scintillator of higher light output, such as a PVT-based or PEN-based formulation with greater light yield and better transparency, or a loaded/wavelength-shifting plastic. Higher light yield directly improves the photostatistics term in energy resolution, which dominates for small sub-MeV-to-MeV deposits. Target a light yield gain of roughly 1.5 to 2 times to bring 1 MeV resolution comfortably below 18% FWHM.

**3. Light collection: wavelength shifting and direct readout**
Use wavelength-shifting fibers or WLS-coated light guides in place of the 30 cm acrylic guides, which lose light and add non-uniformity. Read small cells with fine-mesh or square-profile fibers coupled to the photodetector. Ensure optical coupling uses high-quality optical grease or a gel to minimize losses. Polish cell faces and wrap with a specular reflector (e.g. multilayer reflective film) to improve uniformity across each cell.

**4. Photodetectors: magnetic-field-tolerant SiPMs**
Replace the 76 mm PMTs behind iron plates with silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) or multi-pixel photon counters placed directly on the small cells. SiPMs are unaffected by the 3 mT field, can be mounted on the cell itself (removing the need for iron shielding and light guides), have high photon detection efficiency matched to the emission of the faster scintillators, and allow the compact fine-pitch geometry. Their gain is temperature-sensitive, so include a temperature-stabilized readout and per-channel gain calibration with LED or laser monitoring. Alternatively, if a PMT must be retained for its timing performance, use a compact fine-mesh or magnetic-shielded small-diameter PMT, but SiPMs are the cleaner solution.

**5. Timing: keep sub-0.6 ns**
The present 0.30 ns resolution is already adequate. Preserve it with the faster scintillator and SiPM readout, and add a fast digitizer (waveform sampling at several GS/s) with constant-fraction or leading-edge discrimination to maintain timing across the smaller cells. Check that the SiPM dark count and crosstalk do not degrade timing at the operating threshold.

**6. Depth**
Keep each cell at least 3 cm deep to fully contain 3 MeV electrons. The current 11 cm depth is more than sufficient, so retain it, or use a slightly shallower depth if needed to fit the fine-pitch layout within the existing wall envelope.

**7. Calibration and stability**
Add per-cell calibration with embedded LED or laser injection, and a radioactive source (e.g. 207Bi or 90Sr) calibration system, so that each of the many new channels can be energy-calibrated at 1 MeV to the required resolution across the full wall.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the 19 cm x 19 cm cells with fine-pitch segmented scintillator cells of roughly 3 to 5 cm read by SiPMs, since the 6 cm two-electron separation requirement cannot be met by the current cell size regardless of resolution improvements.

# Design Review: Calorimeter Upgrade Recommendations

## Executive Summary

The current calorimeter achieves 20% FWHM energy resolution and 0.30 ns timing at 1 MeV. The requirements are 18% FWHM energy resolution and 0.6 ns timing at 1 MeV. While timing is already satisfied with margin, the energy resolution requires improvement. I recommend the following hardware changes:

---

## 1. Replace PMTs with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)

**Specific Technology:** Hamamatsu S14160-6050HS or FBK NUV-HD SiPMs in tiled arrays

**Justification:**
- **Magnetic field compatibility:** The current 76 mm PMTs will experience gain shifts and trajectory distortion in the 3 mT field, even with the iron plate partially shielding them. SiPMs are completely insensitive to magnetic fields, eliminating this systematic uncertainty.
- **Higher photon detection efficiency (PDE):** Modern SiPMs achieve 50-60% PDE at 420 nm (polystyrene emission peak) versus ~25% quantum efficiency for bialkali PMTs.
- **Improved energy resolution:** The photoelectron statistics contribution to resolution scales as √N. Doubling the effective light detection improves this component by ~30%.
- **Compact geometry:** Eliminates the need for 30 cm light guides, reducing light losses (~15-20% in acrylic) and improving uniformity.

**Implementation:** Use 6×6 mm² SiPMs in a 4×4 array (covering ~6 cm²) directly coupled to the scintillator face, with temperature stabilization to ±0.5°C.

---

## 2. Replace Polystyrene Scintillator with High-Light-Yield Plastic Scintillator

**Specific Technology:** Eljen EJ-200 or Saint-Gobain BC-408

**Justification:**
- **Higher light yield:** EJ-200 produces ~10,000 photons/MeV versus ~8,000 for typical polystyrene, a 25% improvement.
- **Fast timing:** 0.9 ns rise time and 2.1 ns decay time maintain excellent timing performance.
- **Attenuation length:** >380 cm attenuation length ensures uniform response across 19 cm cells.
- **Energy resolution improvement:** Combined with SiPM upgrade, photostatistics contribution drops from dominant term to subdominant.

**Note:** Maintain cell dimensions (19×19×11 cm³) as 11 cm depth exceeds the 3 cm minimum and fully contains 3 MeV electron showers (range ~1.5 cm, but shower development requires ~5 radiation lengths ≈ 20 cm in plastic—recommend verification with GEANT4).

---

## 3. Redesign Cell Geometry with Direct SiPM Coupling

**Specific Technology:** Machined scintillator blocks with diffuse TiO₂-loaded reflector wrapping (Tyvek 1082D or ESR film) and direct optical coupling

**Justification:**
- **Eliminate light guide losses:** Removing the 30 cm acrylic light guide eliminates ~20% light loss and improves position uniformity.
- **Improved light collection uniformity:** With SiPM arrays on the rear face and high-reflectivity wrapping, position-dependent variations drop below 5%.
- **6 cm separation requirement:** The 19×19 cm² face dimension already ensures electrons >6 cm apart strike different cells (cell diagonal = 27 cm).

---

## 4. Upgrade Readout Electronics

**Specific Technology:** CAEN V1742 or custom waveform digitizers based on DRS4 chips (5 GSPS)

**Justification:**
- **Pile-up rejection:** Waveform sampling allows identification of overlapping pulses from different electrons or backgrounds.
- **Timing extraction:** Digital constant-fraction discrimination on stored waveforms achieves <0.3 ns resolution.
- **Energy integration:** Digital integration over optimized windows reduces baseline fluctuation contributions.

---

## 5. Add Segmented Light Collection for Position Sensitivity

**Specific Technology:** Dual-ended SiPM readout with position reconstruction from signal ratio

**Justification:**
- **Vertex correlation:** Allows correlation of energy deposit position with track extrapolation from drift chambers, rejecting backgrounds.
- **Uniformity correction:** Online position-dependent correction improves effective resolution by 1-2% FWHM.

---

## Expected Performance After Upgrades

| Parameter | Current | After Upgrade | Requirement |
|-----------|---------|---------------|-------------|
| Energy Resolution (1 MeV) | 20% FWHM | ~14-16% FWHM | ≤18% FWHM |
| Time Resolution (1 MeV) | 0.30 ns σ | ~0.25 ns σ | ≤0.6 ns σ |
| Field tolerance | Marginal | Complete | 3 mT |

---

**TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the 76 mm PMTs with arrays of silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) directly coupled to the scintillator, eliminating the light guides and providing magnetic field immunity with higher photon detection efficiency.**

# Proposed calorimeter upgrades

## Where the current design stands against the requirements

| Requirement | Current | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Energy resolution ≤18% FWHM at 1 MeV | 20% | **Fails** |
| Time resolution ≤0.6 ns σ at 1 MeV | 0.30 ns | Passes with margin |
| Two electrons ≥6 cm apart land in different cells | 19 × 19 cm cells | **Fails badly** |
| Cell depth ≥3 cm | 11 cm | Passes, but oversized |
| Operates in 3 mT | PMTs work only with iron/mu-metal shielding | Passes only because of the shielding |

The separation rule is the strongest constraint. Two points 6 cm apart must never fall in the same cell, so the largest distance across any cell must be under 6 cm. For a square cell the diagonal must be below 6 cm, so the side must be below 4.2 cm. The whole calorimeter must therefore be re-segmented. Large PMTs and 30 cm light guides cannot be used at that pitch.

## 1. Re-segment the walls into ~4 × 4 cm cells (mandatory)

- **Cell size:** about 4.0 × 4.0 cm faces, giving a 5.7 cm diagonal. A 3.5 cm pitch adds margin against dead space from wrapping.
- **Scintillator:** PVT or polystyrene, roughly 5 cm deep. This exceeds the 3 cm needed to contain 3 MeV electrons and keeps some margin for gamma tagging.
- **Optical isolation:** each cell wrapped in ESR or PTFE. The entrance face should use thin (~6 µm) aluminized Mylar to minimize electron energy loss and backscatter.
- **Channel count:** each wall is about 21 m². At this pitch that is about 13,000 cells per wall and about 26,000 for the detector.

## 2. Replace the PMTs, light guides and iron plates with SiPM readout

- **Mounting:** a 6 × 6 mm or 2 × 2 array of SiPMs per cell, coupled directly to the back face, or read through a few wavelength-shifting fibres.
- **Magnetic field:** SiPMs are insensitive to 3 mT, so the iron plates and mu-metal can be removed. This also removes their mass and radioactivity from the region near the source.
- **Radiopurity:** SiPMs are far less massive and far cleaner than 76 mm PMT glass. Gamma background from the calorimeter would drop substantially.
- **Timing:** SiPMs readily give better than 0.5 ns σ at 1 MeV in small cells, so the 0.6 ns requirement is kept.

## 3. Meet the 18% FWHM goal through light yield

- **Target:** 18% FWHM corresponds to 7.6% σ. Photostatistics alone then require more than about 170 photoelectrons per MeV; aim for at least 400 to leave room for non-uniformity.
- **How to get there:**
  - Small cells read on their full back face give high, uniform light collection.
  - SiPMs with 40–50% photon detection efficiency at the scintillator emission peak (about 420 nm).
  - Optimized fluors.
  - Per-cell calibration with ²⁰⁷Bi sources and LED monitoring.
- **Dark counts:** modest cooling (about 0 °C) or coincident multi-SiPM summing keeps dark counts negligible at a ~50 keV threshold.

## 4. Front-end electronics

- **Digitization:** multichannel waveform-digitizing ASICs (e.g. SAMPIC- or TOFPET-class), mounted on low-background PCBs behind the walls.
- **Per-cell measurements:** each cell gets its own charge and time.
- **Event-level use:** neighbouring-cell sums handle edge-sharing events, while the individual energies needed for single-electron spectra are retained.

## Alternative if SiPM channel cost is prohibitive

Use a 4 cm-pitch crossed-strip or fibre-readout scintillator with multi-anode PMTs placed outside the field region. This scheme has a weakness: two-electron ambiguity in crossed strips can violate the separate-measurement requirement. The direct per-cell SiPM design is preferred.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Re-segment both calorimeter walls into ~4 × 4 cm × 5 cm scintillator cells, each read directly by SiPMs (removing PMTs, light guides and iron plates), to meet the 6 cm separation rule and reach ≤18% FWHM.

This is an upgrade problem for the calorimeter walls of a NEMO-3-type tracker-calorimeter. The current design gives 20% FWHM at 1 MeV and 0.30 ns, so the needed improvements are a factor ~1.1 in energy resolution, a looser time requirement (which is already met), and a granularity change: cells must be small enough that electrons 6 cm apart land in different cells, which means cell faces must be well below 6 cm. The 19 cm faces are far too coarse. Each constraint is addressed below.

**1. Granularity (most fundamental change)**
Two electrons entering a wall at least 6 cm apart must be in separate cells. With square faces, a cell width of about 3 cm or less ensures this comfortably, since two points 6 cm apart can then never share a cell. Replacing the 19 cm cells with roughly 3 cm × 3 cm (or 2.5 cm) scintillator pixels increases channel count by about 40×. This is the change that drives everything else, because it forces a shift in readout technology.

**2. Readout: from large PMTs to multi-channel silicon photomultipliers or small-area tubes**
A 76 mm PMT cannot be used at 3 cm pitch and cannot sit behind an iron plate in a 3 mT field. Options:
- Silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) per pixel or per small group of pixels. They are compact, insensitive to magnetic fields, and can be mounted directly on the scintillator or light guide. Their dark-count rate and temperature dependence must be managed, and their radiation and radon-free operation are acceptable in the shielded environment.
- Alternatively, wavelength-shifting fiber readout coupled to multianode or small PMTs placed outside the field, with fiber lengths chosen to keep the field-exposed part short. This preserves a PMT's photon statistics but adds light-collection losses.
The iron plate and 76 mm tube are removed from the field region in either case, satisfying the magnetic compatibility requirement.

**3. Scintillator and light collection for energy resolution**
Achieving 18% FWHM or better at 1 MeV from 20% requires roughly 25% more photoelectrons per MeV, or equivalent reduction of non-statistical broadening. Measures:
- Upgrade to a higher light-yield scintillator (e.g., a plastic with higher light output or a PSD-free fast plastic with better light yield than standard polystyrene, or a dedicated high-yield formulation), or add a wavelength shifter to match SiPM peak sensitivity.
- Reflective wrapping optimized for small cells (e.g., specular reflector foil or diffuse reflector such as PTFE/Tyvek) to improve collection uniformity across each pixel.
- Smaller pixels with SiPM coverage on a larger fraction of the surface improve photon collection efficiency and reduce position-dependent light loss, which otherwise broadens the peak.
- Correct for light-yield non-uniformity and temperature drift via per-channel calibration with a light pulser and periodic radioactive calibration sources.

**4. Depth**
Each cell must be at least 3 cm deep to absorb 3 MeV electrons fully. The present 11 cm depth already satisfies this, so depth should be kept at 11 cm (or at least 3 cm plus margin for the new pixel geometry). Pixels can be long and thin rather than cubic; the depth requirement is met without change.

**5. Timing**
The existing 0.30 ns (sigma) is well below the 0.6 ns requirement. Smaller pixels and SiPM readout generally improve timing, and fast plastic with SiPMs can reach sub-ns resolution easily. Keep a fast front-end (constant-fraction discrimination or waveform digitization) and verify timing at 1 MeV for the final configuration.

**6. Magnetic-field and integration**
All active electronics (SiPMs, preamps) must operate in 3 mT, which SiPMs do without difficulty; any residual ferromagnetic material near the field volume should be removed. Cable routing, cooling, and bias distribution must be designed so the wall stays within the shielding and radon-control envelope. Calibration and monitoring hardware (LEDs or laser fibers, source deployment paths) must be included in the wall design.

**7. Channel count and electronics**
Roughly 6 m × 3.5 m of wall at 3 cm pitch on both sides of the foil plane means on the order of 10^4 channels, requiring multi-channel front-end ASICs, digitization, and data-acquisition scaling. Power, heat load, and cabling must be budgeted accordingly, and the cabling must not compromise radon control.

**Summary of the upgrade path:** shrink cells to about 3 cm pitch, replace the 76 mm PMTs and iron-backed mounting with SiPM-based or fiber-based readout inside the field, retain the 11 cm depth, improve light yield and collection, and verify that the resulting design reaches ≤18% FWHM at 1 MeV with ≤0.6 ns timing in every cell.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the 19 cm × 19 cm cells and 76 mm PMTs with ~3 cm pixels read out by magnetic-field-tolerant silicon photomultipliers, so that every electron pair ≥6 cm apart is resolved into separate, separately measured cells.

# Hardware Upgrades for the Next Phase of the ¹⁰⁰Mo Tracker-Calorimeter

## Where the present calorimeter stands against the requirements

| Requirement | Present cells | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Energy resolution ≤18% FWHM at 1 MeV | 20% FWHM | **Fails** |
| Time resolution ≤0.6 ns (σ) at 1 MeV | 0.30 ns | Passes, with margin |
| Hits ≥6 cm apart land in different cells | 19 cm × 19 cm faces | **Fails badly** |
| Cell depth ≥3 cm | 11 cm | Passes |
| Every part works in 3 mT | PMTs need iron shielding | Marginal |

**The granularity requirement sets the cell size.** Any two entry points at least 6 cm apart must fall in different cells. So no two points inside one cell face can be 6 cm or more apart, which means the face diagonal must be shorter than 6 cm. For a square face this gives a side below 6/√2 ≈ 4.2 cm.

A 19 cm cell, read by a 76 mm PMT through a 30 cm light guide, cannot be shrunk to about 4 cm. The PMT is larger than the cell. The whole calorimeter readout has to change.

## Upgrade 1 (main): fine-segmented scintillator cells read by SiPMs

**Cell design**
- Polystyrene or PVT cells with faces of about 4 cm × 4 cm (≤4.2 cm side, e.g. 4.0 cm on a 4.2 cm pitch including wrapping).
- Depth about 3.5–4 cm, which is ≥3 cm and contains 3 MeV electrons (range ≈1.5 g/cm²).
- Each cell wrapped in a high-reflectivity specular reflector (ESR) or PTFE.
- A SiPM array (e.g. 4 × 6 mm × 6 mm) coupled directly to the back face with optical grease. There is no light guide and no iron plate.

**Energy resolution**
- The present light chain loses many photons: large-cell attenuation, a 30 cm guide, and PMT quantum efficiency of about 30%.
- A small, compact cell has short optical paths and better light-collection uniformity.
- SiPM photon detection efficiency is about 40–50%.
- Reaching 18% FWHM (σ ≈ 7.7%) needs roughly ≥200 photoelectrons/MeV once non-statistical terms are included. With about 10⁴ photons/MeV produced, this is reachable with margin, aiming for ~12–15% FWHM.
- Better resolution narrows the 2νββ tail under the 3.03 MeV peak. This is the irreducible background, so it directly improves T½ sensitivity.

**Granularity**
- Cells of about 4.2 cm pitch mean each electron of the decay is measured separately, as the requirement demands.
- Each calorimeter hit can be matched unambiguously to its track.

**Magnetic field**
- SiPMs are insensitive to 3 mT, which removes the need for the PMT iron shields.

**Timing**
- SiPMs with fast front-end ASICs readily give about 0.2–0.4 ns σ at 1 MeV. This preserves time-of-flight rejection of crossing electrons.

**Radiopurity**
- Glass PMTs are a leading source of ⁴⁰K, ²³²Th and ²³⁸U gammas.
- SiPMs, together with low-mass PCBs, cut the calorimeter gamma background substantially.

**Channel count**
- The walls cover 2 × 6 m × 3.5 m = 42 m², giving about 25,000 channels.
- This is handled with multichannel SiPM ASICs of the kind used in TOF-PET and HEP calorimeters.

**Mitigations needed**
- *Dark counts:* use thresholds, and mild cooling (~10–15 °C) if needed.
- *Gain stability:* monitor temperature and bias.
- *Light-injection calibration:* calibrate each cell with an LED or laser.
- *Energy-scale calibration:* use ²⁰⁷Bi sources.
- *Electron backscatter and edge leakage into neighbours:* handle with tracker-guided reconstruction, adding a neighbour deposit only when it is unambiguously associated with the same track.

## Upgrade 2: tracker refinements

- Use finer Geiger cells or more layers near the foil to sharpen vertex resolution.
- This matches the finer calorimeter granularity and improves rejection of backgrounds from the foil surface and wires.

## Upgrade 3: radon and radiopurity

- Use an anti-radon tent with radon-free air or a gas trap, and seal the detector more tightly.
- ²¹⁴Bi from radon is the next-largest background after 2νββ.

## Upgrade 4: source

- Add more enriched mass, e.g. additional modules.
- Use purified foils with improved Bi and Tl contamination limits.
- Use thinner or more uniform foils, which reduce energy loss and improve resolution.

## Upgrade 5: magnetic field

- No change is needed. The 3 mT field is sufficient for charge-sign identification, and the new SiPM calorimeter tolerates it.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the 19 cm PMT-read scintillator blocks with ~4 cm × 4 cm × ~4 cm plastic scintillator cells read directly by SiPM arrays, which meets the granularity, energy-resolution and magnetic-field requirements.

**Assessment of the current calorimeter against the requirements**

- Energy resolution: 20% FWHM at 1 MeV versus a required 18% or better. Scintillator-plus-PMT with a 19 cm face and a 30 cm light guide is light-collection limited, and a 76 mm PMT behind an iron plate in a 3 mT field has poor photoelectron statistics and gain stability.
- Time resolution: 0.30 ns versus a required 0.6 ns or better. The current design is already comfortably better than required, so it is not the binding constraint. It does mean there is some room to trade time resolution for energy resolution or cost.
- Segmentation: 19 cm cells cannot satisfy the requirement that any two electrons at least 6 cm apart deposit in different cells. Two electrons from one decay entering a 19 cm cell would be summed, destroying the single-electron energy information that the sum-energy and angular analysis depends on.
- Depth: 11 cm of polystyrene is far below the 3 cm minimum for full absorption of 3 MeV electrons in the proposed design; this criterion is met on depth, but the depth is wasted if the readout is not optimized. Note that polystyrene's low density (~1.05 g/cm³) and low Z make it a poor absorber per unit depth; the 11 cm figure should be checked against the 3 MeV electron range, which in plastic is roughly 1.5 cm, so the depth requirement is comfortably met.
- Magnetic field compatibility: a 76 mm PMT with an iron plate behind it may be acceptable only with magnetic shielding; the iron plate must be re-examined because it perturbs the field in the tracking region.

**Recommended hardware changes**

1. **Finely segment the calorimeter.** Replace the 19 cm × 19 cm cells with cells no larger than about 5 cm × 5 cm (smaller than the 6 cm separation, with margin for the pitch and the readout). Options: extruded or cast plastic scintillator bars (e.g., 5 cm wide, read at both ends) arranged in crossed layers, or a pixelated array of small scintillator tiles. This is the single change needed to satisfy the two-electron separation requirement; without it the other requirements are secondary.

2. **Replace the readout with silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs).** SiPMs are compact (a few mm to ~1 cm active area), operate in magnetic fields of several tesla without performance loss, need no iron shielding, and have high photon detection efficiency (~40–50%) that improves light yield per MeV. Their compactness is essential for the small cells. Choose devices with low dark-count rate and cryogenic or temperature-compensated bias, as dark noise is the main downside.

3. **Improve light collection for energy resolution.** Use wavelength-shifting fibers embedded in the scintillator bars (or direct SiPM coupling with a reflective wrapper such as ESR or Teflon/PTFE), and eliminate or shorten the 30 cm acrylic light guides, which attenuate and add noise. Target a light yield that gives ≥ 3 photoelectrons per 100 keV-scale energy deposit after SiPM detection efficiency, to reach 18% FWHM at 1 MeV.

4. **Use a higher-light-yield scintillator if needed.** If the segmented, SiPM-read bars still fall short of 18%, switch from polystyrene to a higher light-yield plastic (e.g., PVT-based or a loaded scintillator) or consider a liquid or crystal scintillator in the thin cells. Crystal options (e.g., LYSO, CsI(Tl)) give much better resolution but cost more and may need the segmentation to be re-optimized; they should be evaluated as a backup.

5. **Remove the iron plates behind the PMTs and use non-magnetic, field-tolerant components throughout.** SiPMs and non-magnetic materials (aluminum housings, plastic light guides) remove the field-perturbation issue. Verify the residual field at the calorimeter with a map.

6. **Keep the time resolution budget in mind.** The planned SiPM readout with fast scintillator should comfortably achieve ≤ 0.6 ns; verify with a test-beam measurement at 1 MeV, since SiPM timing depends on the single-photoelectron jitter and the scintillator decay time.

7. **Validate with a prototype.** Build a small test module (a few segmented bars with SiPM readout) and measure energy resolution at 1 MeV, timing, and two-particle separation in a 3 mT field before committing to full production.

**Cost and risk notes**

Segmentation multiplies channel count substantially (the wall area of ~6 m × 3.5 m per side, divided into 5 cm cells, implies on the order of 10⁵ channels per side if individually read out). This is the principal engineering risk. Mitigation: read out bars at both ends and use position reconstruction along the bar, which reduces channel count by roughly the bar length-to-width ratio, or use multiplexed SiPM readout with front-end ASICs. The cost trade between channel count and cell size should be explicitly modeled.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the 19 cm × 19 cm polystyrene cells with finely segmented scintillator (≈5 cm pitch, bars or tiles) read out by silicon photomultipliers, since this is the only change that satisfies the two-electron separation requirement and it also enables the magnetic-field tolerance and light-collection improvements needed for 18% energy resolution.

# Hardware Upgrades for the Neutrinoless Double-Beta Decay Detector Calorimeter

## 1. Replace Photomultipliers with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)

**Technology:** Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs), also known as Multi-Pixel Photon Counters (MPPCs)

**Why:** The current 76 mm PMTs cannot operate reliably in the 3 mT magnetic field. SiPMs are solid-state devices completely insensitive to magnetic fields, eliminating the need for the iron plates currently shielding the PMTs. SiPMs also offer higher photon detection efficiency (40-50% vs ~25% for bialkali PMTs), which directly improves both energy and time resolution through increased photoelectron statistics.

## 2. Replace Polystyrene Scintillator with Higher Light-Yield Plastic Scintillator

**Technology:** Modern plastic scintillators such as EJ-200 or EJ-212 (Eljen Technology) or equivalent BC-408/BC-404 (Saint-Gobain)

**Why:** These scintillators offer ~10,000 photons/MeV compared to standard polystyrene. Higher light yield improves energy resolution (which scales as 1/√N) and time resolution. EJ-212/BC-404 specifically offers fast timing (~1.4 ns decay time) beneficial for the 0.6 ns timing requirement.

## 3. Reduce Cell Face Size to Meet Spatial Separation Requirement

**Technology:** Scintillator cells with faces ≤6 cm × 6 cm (or segmented readout achieving equivalent granularity)

**Why:** Current 19 cm × 19 cm cells cannot distinguish two electrons 6 cm apart. Reducing to ~5-6 cm cells ensures electrons separated by ≥6 cm deposit energy in different cells as required. This may require a modular design with individual SiPM readout per cell.

## 4. Replace Acrylic Light Guides with Direct Optical Coupling or Wavelength-Shifting Fibers

**Technology:** Direct SiPM coupling to scintillator faces, or embedded wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibers (e.g., Kuraray Y-11) routed to SiPM arrays

**Why:** The current 30 cm acrylic light guides cause significant light loss and timing degradation. With compact SiPMs (no magnetic shielding needed), direct coupling becomes feasible, dramatically improving light collection. For smaller segmented cells, WLS fiber readout provides efficient light collection with excellent timing.

## 5. Upgrade Scintillator Depth

**Technology:** Increase scintillator depth from 11 cm to at least 15 cm (or maintain at 11 cm if simulation confirms 3 MeV electron containment, but verify against the 3 cm minimum requirement which is already satisfied)

**Why:** The current 11 cm depth exceeds the 3 cm minimum, but full containment of 3 MeV electrons (range ~1.5 cm in polystyrene) should be verified. The current depth is likely adequate, but optimizing the geometry for the smaller cell size may require adjustment.

## 6. Implement Digital Readout Electronics with Waveform Digitization

**Technology:** Fast waveform digitizers (≥500 MHz sampling, e.g., DRS4-based systems or commercial FADCs) with FPGA-based triggering

**Why:** To achieve 0.6 ns timing resolution with SiPMs requires precise pulse timing extraction. Waveform digitization enables optimal timing algorithms and simultaneous energy integration, replacing legacy analog systems and improving both resolution parameters.

## 7. Temperature Stabilization System for SiPMs

**Technology:** Active thermal management (Peltier cooling or temperature-controlled water circulation) with feedback monitoring

**Why:** SiPM gain varies ~2-5% per °C. To maintain consistent 18% FWHM energy resolution across all cells, temperature must be stabilized to ±0.5°C or better, with gain correction in the DAQ.

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the 76 mm photomultipliers with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) to enable magnetic-field-compatible operation while improving energy and time resolution through higher photon detection efficiency.

# Hardware Upgrade Proposals for the Planar Tracker-Calorimeter Detector

## Analysis of Current Performance vs. Requirements

| Parameter | Current | Required | Status |
|-----------|---------|----------|--------|
| Energy resolution | 20% FWHM @ 1 MeV | ≤18% FWHM @ 1 MeV | **FAILS** |
| Time resolution | 0.30 ns σ @ 1 MeV | ≤0.6 ns σ @ 1 MeV | Passes |
| Cell separation | 19×19 cm faces | ≥6 cm separation → different cells | Passes (19 cm < 6 cm × 2 is marginal) |
| Depth | 11 cm | ≥3 cm, fully absorb 3 MeV e⁻ | Needs checking |
| Magnetic field compatibility | 76 mm PMT in 3 mT | Must work in 3 mT | **PROBLEMATIC** |

---

## Detailed Upgrade Proposals

### 1. Replace PMTs with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) — *Critical*

**Problem:** Conventional 76 mm PMTs are sensitive to even weak magnetic fields. At 3 mT, the electron trajectories inside the PMT are deflected, causing significant gain loss and non-uniformity, especially in large-diameter tubes. This directly degrades both energy and time resolution.

**Upgrade:** Replace each 76 mm PMT with an array of silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs), e.g., a 4×4 or 6×6 mosaic of 6 mm × 6 mm SiPM tiles (total active area ~15 cm²) coupled to the acrylic light guide exit face.

**Benefits:**
- Completely immune to 3 mT magnetic field (solid-state device, no electron drift paths)
- SiPMs achieve single-photon time resolution of ~100–200 ps, dramatically improving timing
- Photon detection efficiency (PDE) of modern SiPMs: 40–60% vs. ~25% for bialkali PMTs → more photoelectrons per event
- More photoelectrons → better energy resolution (scales as 1/√N_pe)
- Compact: eliminates the need for the iron shielding plate behind each PMT, reducing dead material
- Lower operating voltage (~30–60 V bias vs. ~1500 V for PMTs)

**Quantitative estimate:** If current yield is N_pe photoelectrons at 1 MeV, then:
- Resolution scales as ~1/√N_pe (for a scintillator dominated by photoelectron statistics)
- Doubling PDE from 25% → 50% increases N_pe by ×2, improving resolution by factor √2
- 20% FWHM / √2 ≈ 14% FWHM → well within the 18% requirement

---

### 2. Replace or Re-Optimize the Scintillator Material

**Problem:** Standard polystyrene-based plastic scintillator has light yield ~10,000 photons/MeV and relatively slow emission components. At 3 MeV electron energies, range in polystyrene is ~15 mm (CSDA), so 11 cm depth is adequate, but light collection uniformity across the 19×19 cm face is a limiting factor for resolution.

**Upgrade Option A — Higher light yield plastic:** Use PVT (polyvinyltoluene)-based scintillator such as BC-408 or EJ-200, which has:
- Light yield ~10,000 photons/MeV (similar to PS but with better spectral match to SiPMs)
- Fast decay time ~2.1 ns → excellent for time resolution
- Better optical clarity and longer attenuation length (~380 cm vs. ~250 cm for PS)

**Upgrade Option B — Add wavelength-shifting (WLS) coating:** Apply a p-terphenyl or bis-MSB WLS layer to cell walls to improve light collection uniformity, reducing position-dependent response and improving energy resolution.

**Upgrade Option C — BC-404 or EJ-232:** Even faster scintillator (decay time ~1.8 ns) if timing is to be further improved.

---

### 3. Upgrade the Light Guide Design

**Problem:** The 30 cm acrylic light guide introduces photon losses through total-internal-reflection inefficiency, absorption, and geometric dilution. The transition from a 19×19 cm scintillator face to a 76 mm (7.6 cm diameter) PMT already throws away most of the solid angle.

**Upgrade:** With SiPM arrays replacing PMTs, the light guide geometry can be redesigned:
- Use a **shorter, tapered Winston-cone-style acrylic coupler** (10–15 cm) matched to the SiPM mosaic area (~12×12 cm)
- This dramatically increases the fraction of photons that reach the photosensor
- Alternatively, **embed WLS fibers** in the scintillator slab and read out with SiPMs at the fiber ends, eliminating the light guide entirely (though this may sacrifice some time resolution)
- Apply **diffuse reflective coating** (e.g., Lumirror, 3M ESR film, or TiO₂ paint) to all non-readout cell faces to maximize light collection

---

### 4. Cell Geometry Refinement for Separation Requirement

**Problem:** The requirement states electrons entering the calorimeter wall at points ≥6 cm apart must deposit energy in different cells. With 19×19 cm cells this is satisfied for most configurations (a 6 cm separation will almost always straddle a cell boundary if randomly distributed), but events where both electrons hit near the center of the same cell would fail.

**Upgrade:** Reduce cell cross-section to **10×10 cm** or **12×12 cm** faces:
- A 6 cm minimum separation then reliably guarantees separate cells regardless of hit position
- With SiPM readout, there is no PMT-size constraint forcing large cells, so smaller cells become practical
- More cells also improves granularity for background rejection (single-electron vs. two-electron topology)
- Cell depth should be increased from 11 cm to **15 cm** to ensure full containment of 3 MeV electrons (CSDA range ~15 mm in PS, but accounting for straggling and shower tails, 15 cm provides comfortable margin and improves energy resolution by reducing leakage)

---

### 5. Front-End Electronics and Waveform Digitization

**Problem:** PMT-based analog electronics with standard ADC/TDC chains limit the achievable energy and time resolution regardless of the photosensor performance.

**Upgrade:** Deploy **waveform digitizers** (e.g., CAEN V1742 or similar, 5 GS/s, 12-bit) for each SiPM channel:
- Full waveform capture allows offline pulse shape analysis
- Enables pile-up rejection (critical for background suppression)
- Time pickoff via constant-fraction discrimination in software achieves better than 200 ps timing
- Energy extracted from integrated charge with corrections for non-linearity
- Enables pulse-shape discrimination if scintillator with PSD capability is used

---

### 6. Improved Magnetic Field Shielding for PMTs (Interim Solution)

**If PMTs cannot be immediately replaced**, as a lower-cost interim upgrade:

**Upgrade:** Install **mu-metal cylindrical shields** around each 76 mm PMT extending 10 cm beyond the photocathode face:
- Mu-metal (relative permeability ~20,000–100,000) provides attenuation factor >100 for the 3 mT field
- Residual field inside shield < 0.03 mT — negligible effect on PMT gain
- Low cost (~$50/tube), easily retrofitted
- Must verify no interference with the iron plate behind PMTs

---

### 7. Radon Mitigation in Tracker — Supporting Upgrade

**Not calorimeter-specific but critical for physics:** Even with the gas flush, radon daughters can plate out on foil and detector surfaces.

**Upgrade:** Install a **radon-free air supply** to the calorimeter region and scintillator surfaces (radon-free air has <1 mBq/m³ Rn vs. ~10–50 Bq/m³ in ambient lab air). Also consider:
- **Radon trapping system** (activated charcoal cold trap) on the gas supply line
- **Continuous radon monitoring** with electrostatic alpha detectors

---

## Summary Table of Proposed Upgrades

| Upgrade | Addresses | Priority |
|---------|-----------|----------|
| Replace PMTs with SiPM arrays | Magnetic field immunity, energy resolution, timing | **Critical** |
| Shorter/better matched light guide | Light yield, energy resolution | High |
| Higher-transparency scintillator (EJ-200/BC-408) | Energy resolution, timing | High |
| Reduce cell face to 10×10 cm, increase depth to 15 cm | Separation requirement, containment | High |
| Waveform digitizer electronics | Energy and time resolution, pile-up | Medium |
| Mu-metal PMT shields (interim) | Magnetic field immunity | Medium (interim) |
| Enhanced radon control | Background reduction | Medium |

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the 76 mm PMTs with SiPM arrays, since PMTs cannot operate reliably in the 3 mT magnetic field (causing gain degradation that directly causes the energy resolution to fail the 18% FWHM requirement), while SiPMs are field-immune, have higher photon detection efficiency that improves energy resolution beyond the requirement, and maintain or improve the already-passing time resolution.

This is a calorimeter upgrade problem for an NME-search tracker-calorimeter in a 3 mT field. Let me work through the requirements against the present hardware, then recommend changes.

**Diagnosis of the current design**

- Energy resolution: 20% FWHM at 1 MeV versus the 18% requirement. The gap is modest but real, and the current cells are large (19 cm faces), so light collection is nonuniform across the face and the 30 cm light guide adds attenuation and fluctuation.
- Time resolution: 0.30 ns sigma is already better than the 0.6 ns requirement, so timing is not the bottleneck. The margin is useful, though: it means we can trade some time resolution for segmentation or light yield.
- Spatial segmentation: 19 cm cells cannot separate two electrons that enter a wall at points 6 cm apart. Two electrons from one decay landing in the same cell would have their energies summed, destroying the single-electron energy information that the sum-energy analysis and the angular/energy correlation rely on. This is the most serious failure relative to the stated requirements.
- Magnetic field compatibility: the iron-backed photomultipliers and the iron shielding plate are not acceptable inside a 3 mT field without consideration. Iron near the tracking region distorts the field, and PMTs of the standard type suffer gain and collection changes in even small fields. Mu-metal shielding and/or a switch to magnetic-field-insensitive readout is needed.
- Depth: 11 cm of polystyrene is already more than 3 cm, so the absorption requirement is met; the problem is the 30 cm light guides and their interplay with segmentation.

**Recommended hardware changes**

1. **Segment the calorimeter into cells no larger than about 5 cm across, with the cell pitch chosen below 6 cm (preferably 4–5 cm) so that any two electrons 6 cm apart fall into different cells.** Practically this means replacing the 19 cm cells with a fine-grained array of plastic scintillator bars or tiles. Bars of 4–5 cm width, arranged in alternating layers (x and y orientations) with readout at both ends, give position as well as energy. Polystyrene is retained for cost and radiopurity, possibly with a PEN or a fast plastic for timing. Justification: this is the direct requirement; without it the physics channel cannot separate electrons.

2. **Replace the 76 mm PMTs and 30 cm light guides with silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) coupled directly or through short light guides.** SiPMs are insensitive to a 3 mT field, are compact enough for fine segmentation, and offer high photon detection efficiency with fast timing. Their dark-count rate and temperature dependence must be managed, and their gain depends on temperature and bias, so per-channel calibration with LED or radioactive sources is needed. Justification: solves the field compatibility problem and enables segmentation without the bulk of large PMTs.

3. **Remove the iron plate behind the photomultipliers and replace the front-end magnetic-sensitive elements with non-magnetic, low-mass readout.** Any ferromagnetic material within the field region should be eliminated or confined to places where its field perturbation is quantified and mapped. Justification: keeps the 3 mT field uniform in the tracking volume, which is what determines track curvature and charge sign.

4. **Improve light yield and uniformity: use wavelength-shifting fibers or direct-coupled high-light-yield scintillator (e.g., a loaded or doped plastic with higher photon yield), and wrap cells in a specular reflector (ESR or equivalent).** Justification: the 20% to 18% energy-resolution gap is a photostatistics and uniformity problem; more photoelectrons per MeV and reduced position dependence narrow the resolution. The stated 0.6 ns timing budget leaves room for the slightly slower wavelength-shifting path if needed.

5. **Calibrate and monitor the calorimeter continuously.** Include an LED or laser monitoring system for SiPM gain and a source or cosmic-ray calibration for each segment, and map the cell response across the wall. Justification: 18% resolution in every cell is demanding; cell-to-cell gain variation of a few percent would otherwise dominate.

6. **Radiopurity and radon control for the new materials.** SiPMs, fibers and reflectors must be screened for 40K, 232Th, 238U and 60Co, and the gas flushing already in place should be extended to any enclosed calorimeter volume. Justification: the 3 MeV region of interest is sensitive to background, and new components can reintroduce contamination.

**Summary of the plan**

Segmentation to cells below 6 cm, SiPM readout, removal of ferromagnetic material from the field, a higher-yield and more uniform scintillator and light path, and continuous calibration together meet all four requirements (18% FWHM, 0.6 ns, 6 cm separation, 3 cm depth in a 3 mT field), with the time resolution expected to remain well inside the budget.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Segment the calorimeter into cells of roughly 4–5 cm pitch (fine scintillator bars or tiles) so that electrons separated by 6 cm are measured in different cells, and read them out with silicon photomultipliers in place of the iron-backed 76 mm PMTs.

# Upgrade proposal for the next-phase 100Mo tracker-calorimeter

## Where the present design stands against the requirements

| Requirement | Present calorimeter | Status |
|---|---|---|
| ≤18% FWHM at 1 MeV | 20% FWHM | **Fails** |
| ≤0.6 ns (σ) at 1 MeV | 0.30 ns | Passes |
| Electrons ≥6 cm apart land in different cells | 19 × 19 cm faces | **Fails badly** |
| Depth ≥3 cm | 11 cm | Passes, with excess depth |
| Works in 3 mT | 76 mm PMTs need iron and light guides | Marginal |

The granularity requirement is the decisive one. Any square cell can contain two entry points as far apart as its diagonal. Guaranteeing that points 6 cm apart never share a cell therefore needs a face diagonal below 6 cm, i.e. a side of about 4.2 cm or less. Allowing roughly 1 cm for lateral spread from multiple scattering and backscatter in the plastic pushes the pitch to about 3 cm. A 76 mm PMT cannot read a 3 cm cell, so the photosensor has to change. This drives the rest of the redesign.

## 1. Replace the calorimeter with a fine-pitch scintillator array read out by SiPMs (core upgrade)

**Technology**
- Polystyrene (or PVT) scintillator cubes of about **3 × 3 cm face** and **3–4 cm depth**.
- Each cube wrapped in a high-reflectivity, optically isolating reflector (ESR film or PTFE) to suppress optical cross-talk between neighbours.
- Each cube read directly by a **silicon photomultiplier array** of about 6 × 6 mm, or several in parallel, with no light guide.

**Physics motivation**

*Separate energy measurement of each electron.* A 3 cm pitch meets the 6 cm two-electron separation with margin. Each electron's energy is then measured in its own cell. That allows:
- single-electron spectra and opening-angle studies,
- discrimination between decay mechanisms (light-neutrino versus right-handed-current exchange),
- checks of the two-neutrino double-beta (2νββ) spectral shape.

*Containment.* A 3–4 cm depth still exceeds the CSDA (continuous-slowing-down) range of 3 MeV electrons in plastic, about 1.5 cm, so full absorption is kept. Thinner cells also cut the γ-interaction probability, reducing the γ-induced single-electron background. This trades off some γ-tagging efficiency, which the outer cells and the shielding partly recover.

*Energy resolution.* With no 30 cm light guide and a small, highly reflective cell, light collection improves substantially:
- 18% FWHM corresponds to σ/E ≈ 7.7%, i.e. at least about 170 photoelectrons per MeV once non-statistical terms are allowed for.
- Small, well-wrapped plastic cells with direct SiPM coupling at 30–40% photon detection efficiency can reach several hundred photoelectrons per MeV.
- The target is about **12–15% FWHM at 1 MeV**. This narrows the 2νββ tail under the 3.03 MeV peak, which is the irreducible background for 100Mo, given its fast 2νββ rate.

*Magnetic field.* SiPMs are insensitive to 3 mT. This removes the PMTs' mu-metal and iron-shield requirement, and the whole calorimeter works in the field.

*Timing.* SiPMs on small cells give well under 0.3 ns σ at 1 MeV, comfortably inside the 0.6 ns requirement. This preserves time-of-flight rejection of crossing electrons. The finer spatial match between track and cell also sharpens the time-of-flight path-length calculation.

*Radiopurity.* PMT glass is a leading source of ²¹⁴Bi and ²⁰⁸Tl γ rays near the calorimeter. SiPMs are a few grams of silicon on low-background PCB or Kapton, so the γ background falls and the iron plate is no longer needed for the photosensors.

**Scale and readout**
- The two walls total about 2 × 21 m², giving roughly **45,000 channels** at 3 cm pitch.
- Readout uses multichannel SiPM ASICs with waveform or time-over-threshold capture. Candidates are TOFPET2-, PETsys- or CITIROC-class chips, chosen to keep about 0.1 ns time-to-digital-converter binning.
- Dark-count rate of about 50–100 kHz/mm² at room temperature is harmless at physics thresholds of about 50 keV (tens of photoelectrons). Mild cooling to about 10 °C lowers the rate further if needed.
- SiPM gain drifts with temperature, so continuous calibration is required. This can use an LED or laser light-injection system plus periodically deployed ²⁰⁷Bi sources, with per-channel bias compensation.

## 2. Low-radioactivity front-end and mechanics behind the calorimeter

**Technology**
- Radiopure PCBs (Kapton or PTFE), screened passive components and copper or PEEK holders.
- Electronics placed behind a thin copper backplate instead of the iron PMT plate.

**Physics motivation.** Once the PMT glass is gone, the next γ sources are readout boards and cables. Screening them with high-purity germanium (HPGe) detectors and ICP-MS to sub-mBq/kg levels in ²³⁸U and ²³²Th keeps the ²⁰⁸Tl 2.6 MeV line, the dominant γ background near Q, under control.

## 3. Radon suppression upgrade for the tracker

**Technology**
- An anti-radon tent around the detector, flushed with radon-free air from a cooled activated-charcoal trap.
- Tighter sealing and a higher flushing rate for the tracker gas.
- Radon-concentration monitoring at the ~0.1 mBq/m³ level.

**Physics motivation.** ²¹⁴Bi from radon daughters on the cell wires and the foil surface mimics two-electron events. With better calorimeter resolution, radon becomes a leading remaining background.

## 4. Tracker refinements (secondary)

Optionally, add more drift-cell layers near the foil to sharpen vertex resolution. This improves foil-surface versus wire-origin discrimination and reinforces the one-electron-per-cell assignment when tracks are extrapolated to the 3 cm calorimeter pitch. The 3 mT field remains adequate for charge-sign determination.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the 19 cm PMT-read scintillator blocks with ~3×3×3–4 cm plastic scintillator cells read directly by SiPMs, giving per-electron granularity, ≤15% FWHM resolution at 1 MeV, sub-0.3 ns timing and full magnetic-field immunity.

# Hardware Upgrades for the Neutrinoless Double-Beta Decay Detector Calorimeter

## 1. Photomultiplier Replacement with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)

**Technology:** Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs), also known as Multi-Pixel Photon Counters (MPPCs)

**Why:** The current 76 mm PMTs cannot operate reliably in the 3 mT magnetic field. SiPMs are solid-state devices completely insensitive to magnetic fields, eliminating the need for the iron plate shielding currently protecting the PMTs. SiPMs also offer higher photon detection efficiency (40-50% vs ~25% for bialkali PMTs), which directly improves both energy and time resolution through increased photoelectron statistics.

## 2. Scintillator Material Upgrade to Plastic Scintillator with Higher Light Yield

**Technology:** Modern high-light-yield plastic scintillators such as EJ-200 or EJ-212 (or equivalent BC-408/BC-404)

**Why:** Energy resolution in scintillator calorimeters scales as 1/√(photoelectrons). To improve from 20% to 18% FWHM requires ~23% more light. Higher light yield scintillators (up to 10,000 photons/MeV vs ~8,000 for standard polystyrene) combined with better photosensor efficiency will achieve this improvement.

## 3. Light Guide Redesign or Elimination

**Technology:** Direct optical coupling with wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibers or plates, or shortened non-imaging concentrators

**Why:** The current 30 cm acrylic light guides cause significant light loss and timing dispersion. SiPMs' compact size allows direct coupling to the scintillator or use of WLS plates for light collection, improving both light yield and time resolution. Reduced optical path length decreases timing jitter.

## 4. Cell Geometry Modification

**Technology:** Smaller cross-section scintillator cells (approximately 5 cm × 5 cm face) with individual SiPM readout

**Why:** The requirement that electrons 6 cm apart deposit energy in different cells cannot be met with 19 cm × 19 cm cells. Cells with ~5 cm faces ensure two electrons separated by 6 cm always hit different cells. The depth should be maintained at or above 11 cm (well above the 3 cm minimum) to ensure full containment of 3 MeV electrons.

## 5. Fast Digitizing Electronics

**Technology:** Waveform digitizers with ≥1 GS/s sampling rate (e.g., DRS4-based or CAEN V1742)

**Why:** To achieve 0.6 ns (σ) time resolution with the improved scintillator/SiPM system, fast waveform digitization is essential for precise timing extraction. This also enables pulse-shape analysis for additional background discrimination.

## 6. Temperature Stabilization System for SiPMs

**Technology:** Peltier-cooled mounting plates or temperature-controlled water cooling loops with feedback regulation

**Why:** SiPM gain varies ~2-4% per °C. To maintain consistent energy calibration across all cells meeting the 18% resolution requirement, temperature must be stabilized to better than ±0.5°C throughout the calorimeter.

## 7. Bias Voltage Distribution System

**Technology:** Multi-channel programmable low-voltage power supplies with individual channel monitoring (e.g., CAEN A1515 or MPOD-based systems)

**Why:** SiPMs require precise individual bias adjustment to equalize gain across thousands of channels, essential for uniform energy response meeting the 18% FWHM specification in every cell.

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace photomultipliers with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) to enable magnetic field compatibility while simultaneously improving photon detection efficiency for better energy and time resolution.

# Design Review: Hardware Recommendations for Next-Phase Calorimeter

## Systematic Assessment of Current Performance vs. Requirements

| Parameter | Current | Required | Status |
|-----------|---------|----------|--------|
| Energy resolution @ 1 MeV | 20% FWHM | ≤18% FWHM | **FAILS** |
| Time resolution @ 1 MeV | 0.30 ns σ | ≤0.60 ns σ | Passes (2× margin) |
| Cell transverse size | 19×19 cm² | ≤6 cm separation → need ≤6 cm granularity? | **Needs scrutiny** |
| Depth | 11 cm polystyrene | ≥3 cm, fully absorb 3 MeV e⁻ | **Needs scrutiny** |
| Magnetic field compatibility | Fe plate behind PMT | 3 mT throughout | Manageable but improvable |

Let me work through each issue carefully before making recommendations.

---

## Issue 1: Cell Transverse Size and the 6 cm Separation Requirement

The requirement states that two electrons entering the wall at points **at least 6 cm apart** must deposit energy in **different cells**. With 19×19 cm² faces, two electrons 6 cm apart will frequently hit the **same cell** — this requirement is **catastrophically violated** by the current geometry. The cell face must be small enough that 6 cm separation reliably maps to different cells. A cell pitch of ≤6 cm is needed; practically, cells of **5–6 cm transverse dimension** would satisfy this. This is the most fundamental geometric constraint and drives a complete redesign of the calorimeter segmentation.

---

## Issue 2: Electron Range at 3 MeV in Polystyrene

The continuous-slowing-down approximation (CSDA) range of a 3 MeV electron in polystyrene (ρ ≈ 1.06 g/cm³) is approximately **14 mm × (density correction)** — more precisely, the CSDA range of 3 MeV electrons in plastic scintillator is roughly **~1.4 g/cm²**, giving a physical range of about **13–14 mm**. The current 11 cm depth is therefore more than sufficient for range. However, electromagnetic shower containment (including bremsstrahlung) for a 3 MeV electron requires more consideration: at 3 MeV in polystyrene (radiation length X₀ ≈ 42 g/cm² → ~40 cm), bremsstrahlung is a small but non-negligible effect. The 11 cm depth (~0.28 X₀) means most energy is deposited by ionization and contained. The ≥3 cm minimum depth requirement is **easily met** at 11 cm. So depth is not a problem for the current design **if we keep similar depth in the redesign**.

---

## Issue 3: Energy Resolution — Why 20% FWHM, and How to Reach 18%

For a plastic scintillator + PMT system, the energy resolution is dominated by:

**σ_E/E = √[(σ_N/N)²+ (non-uniformity)² + (noise)²]**

where N is the number of detected photoelectrons. For a 1 MeV electron in polystyrene (~10,000 photons/MeV, typical light collection ~1–5%), one gets ~100–500 photoelectrons at the PMT photocathode. With N=100 pe, the **statistical term alone** gives σ/E = 1/√100 = 10%, or FWHM ≈ 23.5%. To reach 18% FWHM (σ = 7.6%), one needs N ≥ 150 photoelectrons, achievable by increasing light yield or collection efficiency by ~50%.

The current design uses a **30 cm acrylic light guide** between a 19×19 cm² scintillator face and a **76 mm (3-inch) PMT**. The geometric coupling is poor: the PMT face area is π×(3.8 cm)² ≈ 45 cm² versus the scintillator face of 361 cm² — a ratio of ~12%, and the light guide over 30 cm adds further losses. This is a major source of inefficiency.

---

## Issue 4: Magnetic Field Compatibility

The 3 mT field is weak (30 Gauss). Standard PMTs are sensitive to fields above ~0.05–0.1 mT without shielding; the iron plate behind the PMT provides some shielding, but the arrangement is not systematic. Any replacement photosensor must work in this field.

---

## Detailed Hardware Recommendations

---

### Recommendation 1: Replace 19×19 cm² cells with smaller cells (~6×6 cm² or similar) — **MANDATORY to meet the separation requirement**

**The Problem:** With 19×19 cm² cells, two electrons separated by 6 cm at the wall face can easily enter the same cell, making their energies **inseparable**. This directly violates an explicit physics requirement.

**The Solution:** Redesign cells to have transverse dimensions of approximately **5×5 cm² to 6×6 cm²**. At this pitch, two electrons 6 cm apart are virtually guaranteed to enter adjacent or separated cells. A pitch of 5 cm would give ~(600 cm × 350 cm) / 25 cm² ≈ **8,400 cells per wall**, versus the current ~(600×350)/361 ≈ **580 cells per wall** — roughly 14× more cells. This is a major engineering challenge but is non-negotiable.

**Practical technology:** Smaller cells can be constructed from **extruded polystyrene scintillator with TiO₂-co-extruded reflective walls** (as used in NOvA, MINERvA, T2K ECAL). Extruded scintillator is cheap, mechanically rigid, and can be made to any cross-section.

**Light readout for small cells:** A 76 mm PMT cannot be matched to a 5×5 cm² scintillator via a light guide without catastrophic light loss. This immediately motivates the photosensor change described in Recommendation 2.

---

### Recommendation 2: Replace 76 mm PMTs + 30 cm light guides with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs) coupled directly to wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibers embedded in the scintillator

**The Problem:** The current light collection chain (large scintillator → 30 cm light guide → 3-inch PMT) is geometrically mismatched and lossy. After cell size reduction to ~5×5 cm², a 76 mm PMT cannot be used at all.

**The Solution:** Adopt the **WLS fiber + SiPM** readout architecture, which is now the industry standard for small-cell plastic scintillator detectors (NOvA, MINERvA, CMS HGCAL, DUNE). Specifically:

- Embed one or two **1.2–1.5 mm diameter Y-11 Kuraray WLS fibers** running longitudinally through each 5×5 cm² × 11 cm cell
- Read each fiber end with a **SiPM of area 1.3×1.3 mm² or 3×3 mm²** (e.g., Hamamatsu S13360 series, KETEK, or FBK devices)
- The WLS fiber absorbs the blue polystyrene emission (peak ~420 nm) and re-emits at ~490–500 nm matched to the SiPM's peak efficiency

**Why this improves energy resolution:**
- Y-11 fiber has ~3.5 m attenuation length; in 11 cm cells, attenuation loss is negligible
- SiPMs achieve photon detection efficiency (PDE) of **40–60% at 500 nm** vs. ~25% quantum efficiency for a bialkali PMT
- Eliminating the lossy 30 cm light guide and poor geometric coupling recovers substantial light
- Typical yield with WLS fiber + SiPM: **~20–30 pe/MeV/fiber**, so with 2 fibers read from both ends (4 SiPMs), one gets ~80–120 pe/MeV, comparable to or better than the current scheme
- This should push the statistical contribution to resolution well below 18% FWHM at 1 MeV

**Why SiPMs are superior in this application:**
- **Fully immune to magnetic fields** — no electron multiplication in vacuum, no deflection by B-field. The 3 mT concern is completely eliminated
- Compact: SiPMs of 1–9 mm² sit directly on the fiber end, requiring no light guide and no iron shielding plate
- Operate at low voltage (~25–70 V bias) — simpler HV infrastructure
- Low power, good gain stability once temperature-compensated

**Concern — SiPM dark noise and cross-talk:** SiPMs have dark count rates of ~100 kHz/mm² at room temperature, and optical cross-talk of ~1–5% for modern devices. In an underground laboratory at stable temperature, these are manageable. The energy threshold is ~100 keV for the signal electrons, well above the noise floor. Temperature stabilization of the calorimeter at ±1°C would be recommended to control gain drift.

**Concern — SiPM radiation damage:** At 3000 m.w.e. overburden, the muon flux and resulting fast neutron flux are very low. Radiation damage to SiPMs is not a concern for the exposure expected in a double-beta decay experiment.

---

### Recommendation 3: Increase scintillator light yield — use **PEN (polyethylene naphthalate)** or **high-output doped polystyrene** rather than standard polystyrene

**The Problem:** Standard polystyrene-based scintillator (e.g., with p-terphenyl + POPOP dopants) produces ~8,000–10,000 photons/MeV. This limits the statistical photoelectron count at 1 MeV.

**The Option:** 
- **Polyvinyltoluene (PVT)-based scintillator** (e.g., BC-408/EJ-200): light yield ~10,000 photons/MeV, slightly higher than polystyrene, well-matched to WLS fiber absorption
- **PEN scintillator**: polyethylene naphthalate is a naturally scintillating polymer with ~10,000–15,000 photons/MeV and excellent transparency; it can be machined or thermoformed; recently demonstrated in AMoRE and LEGEND R&D
- **Alternatively**, standard EJ-200 (PVT) with **two WLS fibers read from both ends** is a mature, low-risk solution

**Recommendation:** Use **EJ-200 or BC-408 extruded scintillator** (which is well-characterized, cheap, and producible in arbitrary cross-sections) rather than introducing a new material like PEN. The light yield improvement from polystyrene to PVT is ~10–20%, worth having but not transformative. The bigger gains come from better photodetectors (Recommendation 2).

---

### Recommendation 4: Retain the cell depth at ≥10 cm but verify longitudinal containment with updated simulation

**The Current Situation:** At 11 cm depth, the current cells nominally contain 3 MeV electrons. However, with the new **5×5 cm² cross-section**, the scintillator volume is 5×5×11 cm³ = 275 cm³, and the light collection geometry changes. With WLS fibers running longitudinally, light collection is uniform along the depth, which actually **improves energy resolution** compared to end-face light guide coupling.

**Action:** Confirm via GEANT4 simulation that 11 cm of EJ-200/polystyrene (ρ ≈ 1.03 g/cm³) contains >95% of the energy from 3 MeV electrons including bremsstrahlung tail. If not, increase depth to 13–14 cm. The ≥3 cm minimum requirement is trivially met.

---

### Recommendation 5: If WLS fiber + SiPM is not adopted, consider replacing 76 mm PMTs with **metal channel dynode PMTs** (e.g., Hamamatsu R7724 or fine-mesh PMTs) with improved magnetic shielding

**Fallback for PMT-based approach (not recommended as primary):**

If the collaboration wishes to retain PMT technology (e.g., due to cost or familiarity), then:
- Replace round 76 mm tubes with **square-faced metal channel dynode PMTs** (e.g., Hamamatsu H8711 series) that can be tiled more efficiently against the scintillator back face without a light guide
- Use **fine-mesh PMTs** (Hamamatsu R5924 series) that operate in magnetic fields up to several hundred mT — more than adequate for 3 mT
- Increase photocathode coverage by eliminating the 30 cm light guide and butting the PMT directly to the scintillator rear face
- Apply mu-metal or Co-netic shielding sleeves around each tube

**However,** fine-mesh PMTs are expensive (~$300–600 each), and with ~8,400 cells per wall × 2 walls = 16,800 channels, the cost and channel count strongly favors SiPMs, which cost ~$5–20 per device at volume.

---

### Recommendation 6: Replace the iron shielding plate behind each PMT with a **distributed SiPM bias/readout board with on-board temperature compensation**

Since we are recommending SiPMs, the iron plates (which served to shield PMTs from the magnetic field) are **unnecessary** and can be removed. This saves mass, simplifies the mechanical structure, and reduces the material budget behind the calorimeter.

Replace with a **custom PCB** per cell or per group of cells carrying:
- SiPM bias circuit with temperature compensation (a simple NTC thermistor feedback loop maintains constant overvoltage as T varies)
- Trans-impedance amplifier (TIA) or voltage amplifier as first stage
- Signal transmission to ADC/TDC modules via coaxial or LVDS twisted-pair cable

This follows the design philosophy of CMS barrel HGCAL and Belle II TOP modules.

---

### Recommendation 7: Add a **second WLS fiber** per cell read from the **opposite end**, to improve timing resolution and provide redundancy

**The Timing Requirement:** Current performance is 0.30 ns σ at 1 MeV — already a factor of 2 better than the 0.60 ns requirement. With SiPMs, timing performance can be **further improved**, since SiPMs have single-photon time resolution (SPTR) of ~100–300 ps and rise times of ~1 ns. The main limitation in WLS fiber readout is the WLS fiber decay time (~2.7 ns for Y-11).

For the **0.60 ns requirement**, Y-11 + SiPM is marginal if only a few photoelectrons are detected early. However, with 20–40 pe detected, the **leading-edge** timing jitter scales as ~τ_decay/√N_pe ≈ 2.7 ns/√30 ≈ 0.5 ns, which satisfies the requirement. Reading both fiber ends doubles N and improves timing.

**Alternative for better timing:** Use **BCF-91A** (Saint-Gobain) WLS fiber with faster decay time (~2.7 ns vs. Y-11's ~2.7 ns — similar) or **direct coupling** via clear fiber to SiPM, and rely on the prompt polystyrene emission (~3–4 ns decay) rather than WLS re-emission. This is more complex optically but gives better timing.

**Verdict:** The timing requirement is met by the current design and will continue to be met with WLS+SiPM. No major change needed here, but reading both fiber ends (Recommendation 7) adds robustness.

---

| 1 | Reduce cell size to ~5×5 cm² | 6 cm separation requirement | **Critical** |
| 2 | Replace PMT+light guide with SiPM+WLS fiber | Energy resolution, magnetic immunity, enables small cells | **Critical** |
| 3 | Use EJ-200/BC-408 (PVT) scintillator | Light yield, energy resolution | High |
| 4 | Verify/adjust cell depth ≥11 cm | 3 MeV containment | Medium |

| 7 | Temperature-stabilize calorimeter ±1°C | SiPM gain stability | Medium |
