**Why:**
- Standard 76 mm (3-inch) dynode-chain PMTs are sensitive to magnetic fields well below 3 mT — a field of this magnitude misaligns the electron trajectories between dynodes and causes gain loss of 50% or more unless the tube is very carefully aligned with the field. This is a hard failure of the stated requirement that every part of the calorimeter must work in the 3 mT field.
- SiPMs are solid-state devices with no electron drift paths and are completely immune to magnetic fields of this strength.
- SiPMs have higher photon detection efficiency (PDE ~40–50%) compared to bialkali PMTs (~25–30%), improving both energy and time resolution.
- Removing the iron plate behind the PMT (which currently serves as magnetic shielding for the PMT) reduces passive material and potential backgrounds.
- The acrylic light guide can be retained or shortened; coupling geometry can be optimised for the SiPM array geometry.

---

## 2. Replace 19×19 cm Scintillator Cells with Smaller Cells (~6 cm × 6 cm face)

**Technology:** Polystyrene scintillator cells with face dimensions of approximately 5–6 cm × 5–6 cm, each read out by a single SiPM or small SiPM array, assembled into a modular wall.

**Why:**
- The requirement states that two electrons entering the wall at points ≥6 cm apart must deposit energy in *different* cells and be measured separately. With 19×19 cm cells, two electrons 6 cm apart will very frequently hit the same cell, violating this requirement entirely. The cell pitch must therefore be no larger than ~6 cm.
- Smaller cells also reduce the probability of two simultaneous electrons from a double-beta decay sharing a cell, which would bias the individual energy measurements — critical for the signal topology where each electron energy is measured separately.
- Smaller cells with SiPM readout have no light-guide length penalty for time resolution and can achieve better energy uniformity.
- The depth (11 cm of polystyrene, ρ ≈ 1.06 g/cm³, so ~11.7 g/cm²) is sufficient to stop 3 MeV electrons (range ~1.5 cm in polystyrene), so the depth specification is already met and need not change.

---

## 3. Improve Scintillator Material or Surface Treatment to Achieve ≤18% FWHM Energy Resolution

**Technology:** Replace standard polystyrene scintillator with either:
- **Higher-light-yield plastic scintillator** (e.g., EJ-204 or BC-404 polyvinyltoluene-based scintillator, ~10,000 photons/MeV vs. ~8,000 for polystyrene), with enhanced specular/diffuse reflective wrapping (e.g., VM2000/ESR multilayer film or PTFE tape); or
- **Improved polystyrene formulation** with higher dopant concentrations and better surface polishing.

**Why:**
- The current 20% FWHM at 1 MeV fails the ≤18% FWHM requirement. Energy resolution in a plastic scintillator cell is dominated by photoelectron statistics: FWHM = 2.35/√N_pe. Going from 20% to 18% FWHM requires increasing the number of detected photoelectrons by a factor of (20/18)² ≈ 1.23, i.e., ~23% more photoelectrons.
- The switch to SiPMs (item 1) already contributes a ~60–80% increase in detected photons from improved PDE alone, which more than covers the resolution requirement — but only if the scintillator and optical coupling are also optimised to avoid light loss that would otherwise negate the gain.
- Improved reflective wrapping (ESR film) increases light collection uniformity and total yield.
- Shorter light guide or direct coupling of SiPM to the small cell face (enabled by item 2) reduces attenuation losses in the light guide, which currently degrades both yield and uniformity.
- The combination of higher-yield scintillator + SiPM readout + better optical coupling should comfortably achieve ≤18% FWHM, with margin.

---

## 4. Retain and Optimise the Acrylic Light Guide (or Shorten/Remove It)

**Technology:** Reduce acrylic light guide length from 30 cm to the minimum needed for SiPM thermal/electronic isolation, or eliminate it entirely with direct SiPM coupling.

**Why:**
- The 30 cm light guide was needed to place the PMT behind an iron shielding plate to protect it from the magnetic field. With SiPMs, this iron plate and the long light guide are no longer necessary.
- Shorter light path reduces photon absorption and time dispersion in the guide, improving both energy resolution (more photons) and time resolution (tighter arrival time distribution).
- The time resolution requirement (≤0.6 ns σ) is already met by the current detector (0.30 ns σ), so this is an improvement with margin; however, with smaller cells the solid angle to the photosensor changes and the time resolution should be verified — shorter/no light guide maintains it.
- Direct SiPM coupling also eliminates the need for optical grease interfaces at the PMT face, reducing a source of optical loss.

---

## 5. Upgrade Front-End Electronics for SiPM Readout

**Technology:** Custom ASIC or FPGA-based front-end boards with low-noise charge-integrating amplifiers and fast timing discriminators (e.g., waveform digitisers at 500 MHz–1 GHz, or dedicated SiPM readout ASICs such as CITIROC or TARGET chips), with per-channel energy and time extraction.

**Why:**
- SiPMs present a very different signal impedance from PMTs (high capacitance, lower voltage, different dark-count characteristics) and require matched front-end electronics to extract their full performance benefit.
- The existing PMT-based electronics (high-voltage supplies, analog shapers tuned for PMT pulse shapes) will not work correctly with SiPMs.
- Fast digitisation allows offline corrections for SiPM saturation at higher energies (relevant for 3 MeV electrons near the Q-value), temperature-dependent gain drift, and dark-count subtraction — all of which are needed to achieve and maintain ≤18% FWHM uniformly in every cell over the lifetime of the experiment.
- Precise time-stamping in the electronics chain is needed to maintain the ≤0.6 ns time resolution at the system level.

---

## Summary Table

| Upgrade | Technology | Requirement Addressed |
|---------|-----------|----------------------|
| Replace PMTs | SiPM arrays | 3 mT field compatibility (hard failure) |
| Smaller scintillator cells | ~6×6 cm² polystyrene cells | 6 cm two-electron separation |
| Better scintillator/optics | High-yield plastic + ESR wrapping | ≤18% FWHM energy resolution |
| Shorten/remove light guide | Direct SiPM coupling | Energy + time resolution; remove iron plate |
| New front-end electronics | SiPM ASIC/FPGA readout | Enable SiPM operation; maintain resolution |

---

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the 76 mm PMTs with SiPM arrays, because the existing PMTs demonstrably fail to operate in the 3 mT magnetic field — making the entire calorimeter non-functional as specified — and the switch to SiPMs simultaneously resolves the field-compatibility failure, removes the need for the iron shielding plate and long light guide, and provides the higher photon detection efficiency needed to achieve the energy resolution requirement.

Based on the detector description and requirements, here are the hardware upgrades the proposal should include:

## 1. **Replace Photomultiplier Tubes with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)**

**Technology:** Large-area SiPM arrays (e.g., 6×6 arrays of 6mm SiPMs) matched to the 76mm diameter requirement.

**Why:** 
- SiPMs are insensitive to magnetic fields, eliminating performance degradation in the 3 mT field
- Better photon detection efficiency (~40-50%) vs PMTs (~20-25%) improves energy and time resolution
- Lower voltage operation (~50V vs ~1000V) improves safety and reduces noise
- More compact, allowing potential elimination of long light guides

## 2. **Eliminate or Shorten Acrylic Light Guides**

**Technology:** Direct coupling of scintillator to SiPMs with minimal (~5 cm) light guides or wavelength-shifting plates.

**Why:**
- Current 30 cm light guides cause significant light attenuation and time dispersion
- Removing them would dramatically improve both energy resolution (reducing 20%→15% FWHM) and time resolution (0.30 ns → 0.20 ns)
- Addresses the critical 18% FWHM energy requirement with margin
- SiPMs' compact form factor enables this change

## 3. **Upgrade Scintillator Material**

**Technology:** Fast plastic scintillator with higher light yield (e.g., EJ-200 or BC-408 with ~10,000 photons/MeV) or add wavelength shifters optimized for SiPM spectral response.

**Why:**
- More photons collected improves energy resolution (scales as 1/√N)
- Faster scintillation decay time improves time resolution
- Better spectral matching to SiPM peak sensitivity (~420 nm) maximizes efficiency

## 4. **Implement Improved Front-End Electronics**

**Technology:** Multi-channel ASICs designed for SiPM readout with low noise, fast digitization (≥250 MSPS), and individual channel calibration.

**Why:**
- Modern electronics reduce electronic noise contribution to energy resolution
- Fast waveform digitization enables advanced pulse shape analysis for background rejection
- Per-channel calibration maintains uniformity across all cells
- Lower power dissipation reduces thermal noise

## 5. **Add Temperature Stabilization System**

**Technology:** Active cooling/heating system maintaining calorimeter at constant temperature (±0.5°C).

**Why:**
- SiPM gain is temperature dependent (~3-5%/°C)
- Temperature stabilization ensures stable energy calibration
- Prevents systematic drifts that could degrade energy resolution
- Essential for maintaining <18% FWHM requirement over long runs

## 6. **Replace or Remove Iron Plate Behind PMTs**

**Technology:** Remove iron magnetic shielding or replace with aluminum structural support.

**Why:**
- Iron plates were needed to shield PMTs from magnetic field
- SiPMs don't require magnetic shielding
- Reduces radioactive background from iron (⁶⁰Co, ⁵⁴Mn activation)
- Reduces detector mass and cost

## 7. **Upgrade Cell Segmentation (Optional)**

**Technology:** Reduce cell face size from 19×19 cm to 12×12 cm while maintaining 11 cm depth.

**Why:**
- Improves spatial resolution for the 6 cm separation requirement
- Provides more granular energy measurement
- Better position reconstruction aids background rejection
- May require more readout channels but provides better physics performance

## 8. **Implement Real-Time Monitoring System**

**Technology:** LED pulser system with optical fiber distribution to each scintillator cell.

**Why:**
- Enables continuous gain monitoring and calibration
- Detects cell degradation or failures quickly
- Reduces systematic uncertainties
- Essential for multi-year data collection stability

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace PMTs with SiPM arrays and eliminate/shorten the 30 cm light guides, as this single change simultaneously solves the magnetic field sensitivity issue, dramatically improves both energy resolution (from 20% to ~15% FWHM) and time resolution (from 0.30 ns to ~0.20 ns), and creates margin beyond the required 18% FWHM and 0.6 ns specifications.

# Hardware Upgrade Recommendations for the Mo-100 Neutrinoless Double-Beta Decay Detector

## Current Bottleneck Analysis

The present cells achieve 20% FWHM energy resolution and 0.30 ns time resolution, but the detector requires 18% FWHM and 0.6 ns sigma (≈1.4% FWHM equivalent for timing). The energy requirement is marginally unmet; the timing requirement is easily satisfied. The real physics limitation is energy resolution for separating signal from background.

## Proposed Hardware Upgrades

### 1. **Replace PMTs with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)**
- **Technology**: Hamamatsu S14160-6050HS or equivalent (6×6 mm, 50 μm cell pitch) mounted directly on scintillator or after light guide
- **Rationale**: SiPMs provide superior photon counting statistics (effectively lower noise floor), better time resolution (sub-0.2 ns possible), and insensitivity to 3 mT magnetic field (unlike PMTs which require mu-metal shielding and may have field-induced gain shifts)
- **Benefit**: Energy resolution improvement to ~16-17% FWHM through reduced photoelectron counting variance and temperature-compensated gain stabilization

### 2. **Upgrade Scintillator to EJ-228 or EJ-260 (dual-output)**
- **Current**: Standard polystyrene (likely EJ-200)
- **Proposed**: Fast scintillator with wavelength-shifting fiber coupling for improved light collection uniformity and faster photon delivery (~1.5 ns rise time vs. 2.7 ns)
- **Benefit**: Reduces timing jitter and energy resolution by 15-20% through more uniform light transport

### 3. **Implement Dual-Photosensor Readout per Cell**
- **Technology**: Mount two SiPMs at opposite ends of each 19×19 cm cell (or corners for diagonal coupling)
- **Rationale**: Provides redundancy, improves light collection uniformity, allows charge-sharing analysis to correct for position-dependent response
- **Benefit**: Achieves ~16% FWHM and 0.4 ns sigma, and improves single-cell efficiency for identifying multi-electron events

### 4. **Add Wavelength-Shifting (WLS) Fiber Coating**
- **Technology**: Embed Y11 or similar WLS fibers in 5 mm grooves on cell faces, or apply thin reflective WLS coating
- **Rationale**: Shifts 425 nm scintillation light to 476 nm for better SiPM quantum efficiency (~35-40% vs. ~25% for direct coupling)
- **Benefit**: ~12-15% light collection improvement, translating to ~2% FWHM energy resolution gain

### 5. **Temperature and Bias Voltage Stabilization Electronics**
- **Technology**: Precision temperature controller (±0.1°C) for SiPM array; dynamic bias adjustment via ASIC (e.g., MAROC3 or CITIROC) with 12-bit DAC per channel
- **Rationale**: SiPM gain drifts ~0.3%/°C and ~0.2%/V; underground lab temperature stability is ~±0.5°C
- **Benefit**: Reduces gain-induced energy resolution degradation to <1%

### 6. **Replace Iron Shielding with Mu-Metal Inner Layer**
- **Technology**: 1-2 mm mu-metal (Cryoperm or Metglas) lining inside iron shield, oriented to cancel 3 mT field locally near PMT region (now less critical with SiPMs, but improves any residual sensor performance)
- **Benefit**: Minimal incremental cost if switching to SiPMs; removes field-induced PMT complications

### 7. **Upgrade Calorimeter Digitization Electronics**
- **Technology**: 14-bit, 1 GHz sampling ADCs with Wilkinson or successive-approximation architecture per channel; integrate into ASIC with programmable trigger
- **Current**: Likely 12-bit or lower
- **Benefit**: Reduces digitization noise from ~1% to ~0.02%, improving effective energy resolution by ~0.5% FWHM

---

## Expected Performance After Upgrades

| Parameter | Current | Target | After Upgrades |
|-----------|---------|--------|-----------------|
| Energy Resolution @ 1 MeV (FWHM) | 20% | 18% | ~15-16% |
| Time Resolution @ 1 MeV (sigma) | 0.30 ns | 0.6 ns | ~0.25-0.35 ns |
| Magnetic Field Robustness | Poor (PMTs) | Good | Excellent (SiPMs) |
| Single-Electron Detection Efficiency | ~95% | — | ~98% |

---

**TOP RECOMMENDATION:** Replace all 76 mm PMTs with arrays of Hamamatsu S14160 SiPMs (2-4 per cell, dual-ended mounting) integrated with 14-bit digitization ASICs and temperature-stabilized bias supplies; simultaneously upgrade to fast EJ-228 scintillator with WLS fiber coupling. This single coordinated change addresses the energy resolution shortfall, eliminates magnetic field complications, and provides superior timing as a bonus—making it the highest-leverage modification for both physics performance and detector robustness.

# Calorimeter upgrade proposal for the 100Mo ββ0ν tracker-calorimeter

## 1. Check the present calorimeter against each requirement

| Requirement | Present design | Status |
|---|---|---|
| ≤18% FWHM at 1 MeV, every cell | 20% FWHM | **Fails** |
| ≤0.6 ns (σ) at 1 MeV | 0.30 ns | Passes with margin |
| Electrons ≥6 cm apart land in different cells | 19 × 19 cm cells | **Fails badly** |
| Depth ≥3 cm | 11 cm | Passes |
| Works in 3 mT | PMTs need an iron plate and 30 cm guides; the guides themselves are fine | Marginal and costly |

**Granularity is the binding constraint.** Any two entry points inside one square cell of side *a* can be up to a√2 apart. For every pair ≥6 cm apart to be in different cells, a√2 < 6 cm, so a ≲ 4.2 cm. A pitch of about 4 × 4 cm (diagonal 5.66 cm) satisfies this.

A 76 mm PMT cannot read a 4 cm cell. That forces a change of photodetector, and the new photodetector is also the natural fix for the resolution and field problems.

## 2. Proposed hardware changes

### a) Re-segment the scintillator wall
- Use polystyrene (PVT-type) cells with about 4.0 × 4.0 cm faces.
- Make them about 4–5 cm deep. This is above the 3 cm full-absorption minimum and keeps the aspect ratio good for light collection. The 11 cm depth was mainly for γ efficiency; keep extra depth only if the γ-tagging channels need it.
- Wrap each cell individually in specular/diffuse reflector (ESR plus PTFE). This gives optical isolation, so there is no light cross-talk between neighbours.
- Use a thin, low-Z entrance window (aluminised Mylar) to limit electron backscatter and energy loss.
- **Channel count:** each wall is 6 × 3.5 m = 21 m², about 13,000 cells. Both walls total about 26,000 cells.

### b) Replace the PMTs with SiPM arrays
- Couple the SiPM arrays (e.g. 4 × 6 mm, ~45–50% PDE) directly to the back face of each cell, with no light guide.
- SiPMs are insensitive to 3 mT and to much larger fields. This removes the iron plate and the 30 cm acrylic guides, so every part of the calorimeter works in the field.
- **Resolution:**
  - 18% FWHM corresponds to σ ≈ 7.6%. Photostatistics then require at least 170 photoelectrons per MeV, and more like ~300 to leave room for non-uniformity and noise.
  - A small, well-wrapped cell read by high-PDE SiPMs can reach several hundred photoelectrons per MeV. That target is about 14% FWHM, comfortably meeting the requirement.
  - Removing the guide also improves light uniformity across the cell face.
- **Timing:** short light paths and fast SiPM signals keep σ well below 0.6 ns. The present value is about 0.3 ns, and comparable is expected.
- **Radiopurity:** SiPMs are far less massive and radioactive than PMT glass. This lowers the ²⁰⁸Tl/²¹⁴Bi γ background near the source.

### c) Readout electronics
- Use multi-channel SiPM front-ends, either ASIC or waveform digitisers, giving per-cell charge plus timing at ≥1 GS/s equivalent.
- Include temperature-compensated bias, since SiPM gain drifts about 1–2%/°C. This preserves per-cell energy-scale stability.
- If dark-count rate threatens the trigger thresholds, cool the electronics region modestly or set an appropriate per-cell threshold.

### d) Calibration system
- Install an LED/laser fibre-injection system to every cell for gain and timing monitoring.
- Deploy ²⁰⁷Bi sources through the tracker for absolute energy-scale calibration of each of the ~26,000 cells.
- Use radiopure low-background materials throughout the wall mechanics.

### e) Mechanics
- Build a modular support of radiopure copper or plastic holding blocks of about 8 × 8 cells.
- Keep the passive shielding outside the calorimeter. The iron plates are no longer needed as magnetic shields.

## 3. Summary

Segmenting the wall to about 4 cm cells read by directly coupled SiPMs fixes all three shortfalls at once:
- It satisfies the 6 cm two-electron separation.
- It gives better than 18% FWHM through high light yield and uniformity.
- It makes the calorimeter fully immune to the magnetic field.
- It keeps sub-ns timing and reduces radioactive background.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the 19 cm PMT-read cells with ~4 × 4 cm polystyrene scintillator cells read directly by SiPM arrays.

# Design Review Recommendations for Calorimeter Upgrade

## Current Performance Gap Analysis

The present calorimeter meets the time resolution requirement (0.30 ns < 0.6 ns) but fails the energy resolution requirement (20% > 18% FWHM at 1 MeV). Additionally, the current design has some inefficiencies that should be addressed.

## Recommended Hardware Changes

### 1. **Replace 76 mm PMTs with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)**

**Justification:**
- SiPMs are insensitive to the 3 mT magnetic field, unlike PMTs which suffer gain variations
- Superior photon detection efficiency (>50% vs ~20-25% for PMTs)
- Excellent single-photon resolution improves energy resolution
- Compact form factor eliminates need for iron magnetic shielding plates
- Can be mounted directly on light guides, improving light collection
- Time resolution of ~100 ps enables even better event discrimination

**Expected Impact:** Energy resolution improvement to ~15-16% FWHM at 1 MeV, well below the 18% requirement.

### 2. **Optimize Light Guides: Replace 30 cm Acrylic with Shorter (~10 cm) Tapered Designs**

**Justification:**
- Current 30 cm light guides cause significant light loss (~40-50%)
- Shorter guides with optimized geometry improve light collection efficiency by 30-40%
- Modern ray-tracing codes (ZEMAX, Geant4 optical) can optimize taper geometry
- Reduces dead space and material budget

**Expected Impact:** Combined with SiPMs, delivers the required energy resolution margin.

### 3. **Implement Dual-Ended SiPM Readout on Each Scintillator Cell**

**Justification:**
- Improves light collection uniformity across the 19 cm cell face
- Position-dependent response variations currently degrade energy resolution
- Redundancy improves reliability over 10+ year running
- Timing from both ends enables position determination along cell length
- Minimal additional cost given SiPM affordability

**Expected Impact:** Reduces position-dependent energy resolution variations from ~3-4% to <1%.

### 4. **Upgrade Scintillator: Use Extruded Polystyrene with Wavelength-Shifting Fibers**

**Justification:**
- Current bulk polystyrene likely has non-uniformities from casting
- Extruded scintillator (e.g., Eljen EJ-200) provides better uniformity
- Embedded WLS fibers (e.g., BCF-92, Y11) collect light more efficiently
- Well-established technology from NOvA, T2K experiments
- Better long-term stability and light yield uniformity

**Expected Impact:** Improves energy resolution uniformity across all cells to meet the 18% requirement reliably.

### 5. **Add Reflective Wrapping: VM2000 or ESR Film**

**Justification:**
- Current design likely uses less-optimal reflector (Tyvek or aluminum foil)
- 3M VM2000 or ESR provides >98% reflectivity vs ~85-90% for alternatives
- Direct impact on light collection: ~15-20% increase in photons reaching detector
- Proven in many calorimeter applications
- Low cost, high impact upgrade

**Expected Impact:** Additional 10-15% improvement in light yield translates to ~5% improvement in energy resolution.

### 6. **Implement Cell-by-Cell Calibration System with LEDs**

**Justification:**
- Required to maintain 18% specification across all cells over time
- LED pulsers (blue, 470 nm) can inject calibration light into each cell
- Monitors PMT/SiPM gain drifts, scintillator aging, temperature effects
- Essential for long-term stability in underground environment
- Automation enables daily calibration without detector access

**Expected Impact:** Ensures sustained performance at specification over multi-year data taking.

### 7. **Upgrade Electronics: Use Waveform Digitizing with 250-500 MSPS ADCs**

**Justification:**
- Enables optimal digital filtering for best energy resolution
- Pulse shape discrimination can reject backgrounds
- Better pile-up rejection
- Full waveform storage aids offline analysis and systematics studies
- Modern ASICs (e.g., CAEN DT5742, PSEC4) are cost-effective

**Expected Impact:** Extracts maximum information from scintillation pulses, contributing 2-3% to energy resolution improvement.

## Implementation Priority

**Phase 1 (Critical):** SiPM replacement (#1), optimized light guides (#2), reflective wrapping (#5)
- Directly addresses energy resolution requirement failure
- Total improvement: 20% → 15% FWHM expected

**Phase 2 (Important):** Dual-ended readout (#3), calibration system (#6)
- Ensures specification met uniformly across detector
- Provides long-term stability

**Phase 3 (Enhancement):** Scintillator upgrade (#4), electronics upgrade (#7)
- Further optimization if budget allows
- Consider for cells with marginal performance

## Cost-Benefit Analysis

The SiPM replacement is the single highest-impact change: it simultaneously solves the magnetic field sensitivity issue, dramatically improves energy resolution through better photostatistics, and enables removal of the iron shielding plates (reducing cost and radioactive background). Modern SiPMs (e.g., Hamamatsu S13360 series, FBK NUV-HD) cost $50-100 per channel vs comparable pricing for 76 mm PMTs, making this cost-neutral while delivering superior performance.

**TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace 76 mm PMTs with Silicon Photomultipliers and optimize light guides to achieve required 18% energy resolution while eliminating magnetic field sensitivity.**

## Current Performance Assessment

The existing calorimeter meets the energy resolution requirement (20% < 18% FWHM at 1 MeV) but fails the time resolution requirement (0.30 ns > 0.6 ns sigma at 1 MeV). However, the design has significant inefficiencies that should be addressed.

## Recommended Hardware Changes

### 1. **Replace PMTs with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)**

**Technology**: Large-area SiPM arrays (e.g., Hamamatsu S13361 series or FBK NUV-HD)

### 2. **Optimize Cell Segmentation**

**Technology**: Reduce cell face size from 19×19 cm to 10×10 cm

**Justification**:
- **Spatial resolution**: Current 19 cm cells with 6 cm separation requirement waste calorimeter capability. Smaller cells better match the tracking resolution
- **Energy measurement**: More granular energy deposition improves background rejection
- **Dual electron events**: Better separation for 0νββ topology with two electrons
- **Depth retained**: Keep 11 cm depth (>3 cm requirement) for full absorption

**Technology**: EJ-228 or EJ-230 fast timing plastic scintillator

**Justification**:

**Technology**: Thin wavelength-shifting film (e.g., Saint-Gobain BC-620) on scintillator surfaces

**Justification**:

- **Energy resolution**: Better photon statistics improves energy resolution toward 15% FWHM
- **SiPM matching**: Shifts blue scintillation light to green where SiPMs have better photon detection efficiency
- **Minimal cost**: Thin coating adds negligible mass and radioactivity

**Technology**: 250-500 MSPS waveform digitizers (e.g., CAEN DT5730 or equivalent)

**Justification**:
- **Pulse shape discrimination**: Enables identification of electron vs. alpha particles in scintillator for better background rejection
- **Precise timing**: Extract best timing information through digital filtering
- **Energy reconstruction**: Digital integration improves energy linearity and resolution
- **Diagnostic capability**: Full waveform storage for debugging and optimization
- **Future-proof**: Allows algorithm improvements post-deployment

### 6. **Light Injection Calibration System**

**Technology**: LED-based light injection system with optical fibers to each cell

**Justification**:
- **Monitoring**: Continuous monitoring of SiPM gain and scintillator performance
- **Stability**: Essential for maintaining <18% FWHM over multi-year running
- **Time calibration**: Regular timing calibration for 0.6 ns requirement
- **Minimal intervention**: Reduces need to open detector for calibration

## Implementation Priority

**Phase 1** (Critical): Replace PMTs with SiPMs and install waveform digitizers
**Phase 2** (High value): Upgrade to fast scintillator and add wavelength shifter
**Phase 3** (Optimization): Implement smaller cells and calibration system

# Hardware Upgrades for the Next Phase of the ¹⁰⁰Mo Tracker-Calorimeter

## Where the current design fails its own requirements

| Requirement | Present detector | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Energy resolution ≤ 18% FWHM at 1 MeV | 20% FWHM | **Fails** |
| Time resolution ≤ 0.6 ns σ at 1 MeV | 0.30 ns | Passes |
| Two electrons ≥ 6 cm apart land in different cells | 19 × 19 cm cells | **Fails badly** |
| Cell depth ≥ 3 cm | 11 cm | Passes |
| Every part works in 3 mT | PMTs work only behind iron plates and long light guides | Marginal |

The granularity requirement sets the cell size. For two entry points 6 cm apart never to share a square cell of side *s*, even along the diagonal, *s*√2 must be less than 6 cm. That gives *s* < 4.2 cm. With 19 cm cells, the two electrons of a decay often share a cell, so their energies cannot be measured individually.

## 1. Replace the calorimeter with finely segmented plastic cells read by SiPMs (main upgrade)

**Technology**
- Polystyrene scintillator cells of about 4 × 4 cm face and 3–4 cm depth.
- Each cell is wrapped in a reflector (PTFE or ESR film) for optical isolation.
- Each cell is read directly by a silicon photomultiplier array (e.g. 6 × 6 mm or a 2×2 tile), with no light guide.
- The PMTs, light guides and iron shield plates are removed.

**Physics motivation**
- **Granularity.** A 4 cm pitch satisfies the 6 cm separation rule in all directions, including the diagonal. Each electron's energy is then measured on its own, which is needed for:
  - the single-electron energy spectra used to separate 0νββ mechanisms;
  - the angular-correlation analysis;
  - rejecting events where one electron plus a γ mimics the signal.
- **Containment.** The CSDA range of a 3 MeV electron in plastic is about 1.5 cm, so a depth of at least 3 cm gives full containment. A thinner cell also lowers the γ detection efficiency, which reduces sensitivity to external γ background.
- **Energy resolution.** Small cells have short optical paths, so less light is lost. SiPM photon-detection efficiency (about 40–50%) exceeds the PMT quantum efficiency (about 25–35%), and removing the light guide removes a light-loss stage.
  - 18% FWHM corresponds to σ ≈ 7.6%, which needs at least about 170 photoelectrons/MeV (photostatistics only).
  - Well-reflected small cells with SiPMs can reach several hundred photoelectrons/MeV. That allows margin for non-uniformity, giving about 12–15% FWHM.
- **Magnetic field.** SiPMs are insensitive to the 3 mT field. Every component then meets the field requirement without iron plates.
- **Timing.** SiPMs plus fast plastic readily achieve 0.2–0.4 ns σ at 1 MeV. This comfortably meets the 0.6 ns time-of-flight criterion for rejecting crossing electrons.
- **Radiopurity.** PMT glass is a dominant source of ²⁰⁸Tl, ²¹⁴Bi and ⁴⁰K. Low-mass silicon sensors cut the external γ background considerably.

**Costs and mitigations**
- **Channel count.** About 42 m² of walls at 16 cm² per cell is roughly 26,000 channels. This is handled with ASIC readout (waveform or ToT plus fast timing).
- **SiPM dark rate.** Mitigations are:
  - a coincidence or threshold set at a few photoelectrons, against a signal of hundreds of photoelectrons;
  - mild cooling;
  - per-cell temperature and gain monitoring with an LED or laser calibration system.

## 2. Supporting upgrades

- **Isotope mass and source foils.** Add enriched ¹⁰⁰Mo in further modules. Use thinner, more uniform foils, or several thinner foils, to reduce electron energy loss and scattering in the source. This sharpens the peak at Q = 3.03 MeV and so improves the resolution gain.
- **Radon control.** Use a radon-tight tracker envelope and a radon-trapping (cooled activated charcoal) gas purification loop. ²¹⁴Bi from radon on the foils and wires is a leading background near Q.
- **Tracker.** Use more radiopure wires and cell materials, and possibly finer cells near the foil. This improves vertex resolution, so the two tracks can be tested for a common vertex.
- **Calibration.** Install a deployable ²⁰⁷Bi source system plus light injection, to track the absolute energy scale of every small cell.
- **Shielding and γ veto.** Add an active γ veto around the calorimeter edges and improve the neutron shielding. This suppresses external γ and (n,γ) events.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the 19 cm PMT-read scintillator blocks with ~4 × 4 × 3–4 cm plastic scintillator cells read directly by SiPMs, giving cells small enough to separate electrons 6 cm apart, better than 18% FWHM resolution, and full operation in the 3 mT field.

This is essentially the SuperNEMO demonstrator calorimeter problem. I'll go through each requirement against the present design and propose upgrades.

**Where the present design stands**

1. Time resolution (0.30 ns sigma) already beats the 0.6 ns requirement, so no change is needed. It must simply not degrade.
2. Energy resolution (20% FWHM at 1 MeV) misses the 18% requirement. This is the main deficiency.
3. Granularity: cells with 19 cm faces mean two electrons entering 6 cm apart will often hit the same cell. The requirement of separate cells for electrons at least 6 cm apart demands much finer segmentation.
4. Depth: 11 cm of plastic is acceptable (at least 3 cm needed), but it is not optimal. Depth drives light-guide length and collection.
5. Magnetic field: 3 mT with PMTs behind an iron plate and 30 cm light guides is already tolerant, but a finer-pitch design must still work in field.

**Proposed upgrades**

**1. Replace the large scintillator blocks with finer-segmented ones, with the cell pitch set by the 6 cm separation requirement.**
The cell face must be smaller than the minimum two-electron separation so that two electrons at least 6 cm apart fall in different cells. A cell width of about 5 cm (or less) in the transverse direction guarantees this. The readout must then be per-cell, with independent PMT, digitization, and calibration for every cell, since each electron energy is used individually. This raises the channel count considerably: roughly 2 walls × (6 m × 3.5 m) = 42 m², and with about 5 cm cells this is on the order of 15,000+ channels if one PMT per cell is kept, so the PMT size and cost matter.

**2. Use smaller, high-quantum-efficiency PMTs coupled directly to the scintillator (no 30 cm light guide).**
Replace the 76 mm PMTs and long acrylic guides with 3-inch (or smaller) PMTs with high-QE bialkali photocathodes (super-bialkali, 35–40% QE) coupled directly or via a very short guide. Removing the long light guide eliminates attenuation and the photon transit-time spread, improving both energy and timing. Higher QE improves photoelectron statistics, which is the dominant term in the 1 MeV resolution. The PMT diameter should be matched to the small face (about 5 cm cell versus 3-inch PMT; use a short tapered guide or a 2-inch PMT).

**3. Improve the scintillator and its wrapping.**
Use higher light-yield polystyrene (or polyvinyltoluene, PVT) with optimized dopants, polished surfaces, and a high-reflectivity wrap (Teflon/PTFE or aluminized Mylar) with a thin entrance window on the foil side. This raises light collection and uniformity, directly improving resolution. Keep thickness about 10 cm, which is well above the 3 cm minimum and fully contains 3 MeV electrons, while the thin front minimizes energy loss.

**4. Magnetic shielding and field compatibility.**
Surround each PMT with a mu-metal shield and maintain the iron plate shielding behind the PMTs. This preserves gain and timing in the 3 mT field and keeps the resolution gains from being lost.

**5. Electronics and calibration.**
Provide fast waveform digitization (about 1 GS/s) per channel for pulse-shape and timing, plus an LED/laser light-injection system and a radioactive source (207Bi) calibration for gain monitoring and energy-scale stability in every cell, so that every cell individually holds the 18% FWHM spec.

**Summary**
- The energy-resolution shortfall is fixed by a higher-QE PMT, direct coupling, and improved scintillator and wrapping.
- The granularity requirement is met by shrinking the cell face to below 6 cm.
- Timing already satisfies the requirement and is expected to improve with shorter light paths.
- Depth (at least 3 cm) and field operation are retained by the thick scintillator and mu-metal shielding.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the 19 cm × 19 cm scintillator cells with finer-segmented cells (face width below 6 cm, each read out individually) coupled directly to high-QE PMTs without the 30 cm light guide

# Design Review Recommendations

## Critical Issues & Recommendations

### 1. **PMT Replacement with SiPM Arrays** (HIGHEST PRIORITY)
**Issue:** 76 mm PMTs in a 3 mT magnetic field will suffer severe image distortion and gain loss. The Lorentz force deflects photoelectrons, degrading position resolution in the light guide and reducing light collection efficiency by ~30-50%.

**Solution:** Replace PMTs with **Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)** arranged in a 4×4 or 6×6 array (e.g., Hamamatsu or SensL 6×6 mm tiles). SiPMs are immune to magnetic fields, provide:
- Comparable quantum efficiency (25-40%)
- Excellent timing (inherent ~100 ps resolution)
- Compact geometry enabling placement directly behind scintillator
- Demonstrated 18-20% energy resolution at 1 MeV in similar geometries

**Justification:** This is non-negotiable for operation in 3 mT; PMTs simply cannot meet specs in this field.

---

### 2. **Acrylic Light Guide Elimination**
**Issue:** The 30 cm acrylic guides introduce:
- Optical attenuation (10-15% loss over 30 cm even in UV-transparent acrylic)
- Geometric complexity incompatible with tight SiPM coupling
- Difficulty maintaining timing resolution <0.6 ns over this distance

**Solution:** **Replace with direct optical coupling** (wavelength-shifting fibers or optical grease interface) from scintillator to SiPM array positioned immediately behind the cell. If iron backing plates are required for shielding, use 1-2 cm thickness and couple SiPMs through side-mounted fiber bundles.

**Justification:** Simplifies the optical path, improves light collection by ~20%, and ensures timing spec compliance.

---

### 3. **Scintillator Cell Depth Increase**
**Issue:** Current 11 cm depth is marginal for full 3 MeV absorption in polystyrene (radiation length ~42 cm). Only ~95% containment; ~5% of high-energy events leak, degrading energy resolution and risking misidentification of decay topology.

**Solution:** Increase depth to **15-18 cm**, or confirm via Monte Carlo that 11 cm achieves ≥99% containment for 3 MeV electrons at 45° incidence angles.

**Justification:** Ensures the 18% FWHM energy spec is met across the full energy range; 3 MeV electrons are at the Q-value edge and cannot be lost.

---

### 4. **Transition Edge Sensor (TES) Microcalorimeter Feasibility Study**
**Alternative consideration (not primary):** For ultimate energy resolution beyond 18%, investigate whether **cryogenic TES arrays** on small scintillator samples could be prototyped. However, this is likely over-specified given current scintillator+SiPM performance.

---

### 5. **Cross-Talk Mitigation in SiPM Array**
**Issue:** 4×4 or 6×6 SiPM arrays can suffer optical and electrical cross-talk, broadening the energy resolution.

**Solution:** Use **low-cross-talk SiPM variants** (e.g., Hamamatsu S13361 with trenches) and apply **Teflon reflectors** or black epoxy borders between individual SiPM elements to suppress inter-element crosstalk to <5%.

**Justification:** Essential to preserve the 18% FWHM target.

---

### 6. **Timing Specification Verification**
**Current status:** 0.30 ns sigma at 1 MeV must improve to 0.6 ns sigma—this is actually a *relaxation*, not a tightening. However:

**Action:** Confirm via test beam that SiPM + scintillator timing remains <0.6 ns sigma. SiPMs with <100 ps intrinsic jitter plus ~2-3 ns scintillation decay time should comfortably meet this.

---

### 7. **Iron Plate Behind Calorimeter**
**Issue:** Iron backing serves shielding but adds dead material and complicates light coupling.

**Recommendation:** **Minimize iron thickness to 1-2 cm** and move bulk shielding to the outer detector envelope. This reduces light path and improves timing.

---

## Summary Table

| Component | Current | Recommended | Justification |
|-----------|---------|-------------|----------------|
| Light detector | 76 mm PMT | SiPM array (4×4 or 6×6) | Immune to 3 mT field; meets energy & timing specs |
| Light guide | 30 cm acrylic | Direct coupling + WLS fibers | Improves light collection, simplifies geometry |
| Cell depth | 11 cm | 15-18 cm | Full 3 MeV containment |
| Iron backing | Thick | 1-2 cm minimum | Reduce dead material, improve timing |

---

**TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace 76 mm PMTs with SiPM arrays (4×4 or 6×6 configuration, low-cross-talk variants) and eliminate the 30 cm acrylic light guide in favor of direct optical coupling. The PMT is incompatible with the 3 mT magnetic field and is the primary blocker to meeting the energy and timing specifications.**

# Calorimeter upgrade proposal: required hardware changes

## Where the present calorimeter stands against the requirements

| Requirement | Present calorimeter | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Energy resolution ≤ 18% FWHM at 1 MeV | 20% FWHM | **Fails** |
| Time resolution ≤ 0.6 ns (σ) at 1 MeV | 0.30 ns | Passes with margin |
| Electrons entering ≥ 6 cm apart must hit different cells | 19 × 19 cm cells: two electrons up to ~27 cm apart (the cell diagonal) can share a cell | **Fails badly** |
| Cell depth ≥ 3 cm | 11 cm | Passes |
| Works in 3 mT | PMTs work only because of the iron plates | Passes now, but the shielding cannot be scaled to a fine-grained design |

The upgrade is therefore driven by **granularity** and **energy resolution**. Timing is not a driver. It only has to be preserved.

## Upgrades to include

**1. Re-segment the calorimeter into small cells (the core change)**
- **Technology:** square plastic scintillator cells of about 4 × 4 cm face. PVT-based scintillator gives higher light yield than polystyrene. Each cell is individually wrapped in a thin reflector (ESR film or PTFE) so it is optically isolated.
- **Why the size:** to guarantee that any two entry points ≥ 6 cm apart fall in different cells, the largest distance within one cell (its face diagonal) must be below 6 cm.
  - That requires a square side below 6/√2 ≈ 4.2 cm.
  - 4 cm cells give a 5.7 cm diagonal, which meets the requirement.
- **Why the depth:** about 5 cm is enough. It exceeds the 3 cm needed to fully absorb 3 MeV electrons, with margin for angled tracks, and it reduces material, cost and gamma background.
- **Packing:** keep the reflector and gaps thin to minimise dead area.

**2. Replace the PMTs and light guides with directly coupled SiPMs**
- **Technology:** arrays of silicon photomultipliers (for example 4 × 6 mm² devices, several per cell) glued or optically coupled directly to the back face of each cell.
  - This eliminates the 30 cm acrylic light guides.
  - It also eliminates the 76 mm PMTs and the iron plates.
- **Why — size:** a 76 mm PMT physically cannot read out a 4 cm cell.
- **Why — magnetic field:** SiPMs are insensitive to magnetic fields, so 3 mT needs no shielding.
- **Why — energy resolution:** SiPMs have higher photon detection efficiency (about 40–50%), and direct coupling removes the light-guide losses. Together these raise photoelectron statistics enough to bring resolution from 20% to below 18% FWHM.
- **Why — timing:** SiPMs keep sub-0.6 ns time resolution, and the shorter light path helps.

**3. Optical quality for uniform light collection**
- **Technology:** polished cells, a reflective wrap on all faces except the SiPM face, and possibly a sensor mosaic covering more of the back face.
- **Why:** the requirement holds *in every cell*. Non-uniform light collection across the face would broaden the resolution, so it must be controlled.

**4. Cooling and temperature control of the SiPMs**
- **Technology:** modest cooling (for example to 0–10 °C) with temperature-stabilised bias voltage.
- **Why:** this limits dark-count rate, which adds noise to low-energy measurements, and stabilises gain. Stable gain is needed for both resolution and energy-scale stability.

**5. High-channel-count front-end electronics**
- **Technology:** multichannel SiPM readout ASICs with waveform digitisation or time-stamping.
- **Why:** each wall is 6 m × 3.5 m, so 4 cm cells give about 13,000 channels per wall, or roughly 26,000 in total. The electronics must deliver an independent energy for each cell, plus sub-ns timing.

**6. Calibration system**
- **Technology:** an LED or laser light-injection system, plus deployable radioactive sources (for example ²⁰⁷Bi conversion electrons).
- **Why:** to verify the 18% FWHM and the timing requirement cell by cell, and to track SiPM gain drift across about 26,000 channels.

**7. Radiopurity screening of the new components**
- **Technology:** HPGe screening of the SiPMs, PCBs, reflector film and cables.
- **Why:** these components sit right at the tracking volume, so they must not add γ or radon backgrounds near Q = 3.03 MeV.

## Not needed in this proposal

- **Faster timing hardware:** 0.30 ns already beats the 0.6 ns requirement.
- **Changes to the field, tracker, foils or shielding:** none of the stated requirements calls for them.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Rebuild each calorimeter wall as ~4 × 4 cm scintillator cells read out by directly coupled SiPMs, replacing the 19 cm cells, light guides and shielded 76 mm PMTs.

# Hardware Upgrades for the 100Mo Planar Tracker-Calorimeter

## Requirement check against the present calorimeter

| Requirement | Present | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Energy resolution ≤18% FWHM at 1 MeV | 20% FWHM | **Fails** |
| Time resolution ≤0.6 ns σ at 1 MeV | 0.30 ns | Passes, with margin |
| Electrons ≥6 cm apart land in different cells | 19 × 19 cm cells | **Fails badly** |
| Cell depth ≥3 cm | 11 cm | Passes |
| Works in 3 mT | PMTs work only behind iron plates and 30 cm light guides | Marginal |

The granularity requirement drives the design. Two points inside one square cell can be as far apart as the face diagonal, √2·a. To guarantee that points 6 cm apart always fall in different cells, you need √2·a < 6 cm, so a < 4.2 cm. The 19 cm cells are about 4.5 times too large in each direction.

## Proposed upgrades

**1. Re-segment both calorimeter walls into ~4 × 4 cm scintillator cells (diagonal 5.7 cm).**
- This is the only way to meet the two-electron separation requirement.
- Each wall is 6 m × 3.5 m = 21 m², so this means about 13,000 cells per wall and about 26,000 in total.
- Depth can be reduced from 11 cm to about 3–5 cm of polystyrene (or PVT). This still fully absorbs 3 MeV electrons, whose range is about 1.5 cm, and it lowers gamma-ray background, mass and cost.
- Wrap each cell individually in PTFE plus aluminised Mylar. This isolates cells optically and maximises light collection.

**2. Replace PMTs and light guides with SiPM arrays coupled directly to each cell.**
- *Magnetic field:* SiPMs are insensitive to magnetic fields. This removes the iron plates and the field-distorting magnetic shielding.
- *Fit:* 76 mm PMTs cannot physically read out 4 cm cells; SiPM arrays of about 6 × 6 mm up to 4 × 4 cm can.
- *Energy resolution:* SiPMs have high photon detection efficiency (~40–50%). Removing the 30 cm light guide eliminates its light loss and non-uniformity. Together these raise the photoelectron yield. Reaching 18% FWHM (about 7.6% σ) needs roughly 200 or more photoelectrons per MeV, which is readily achievable in small, well-wrapped cells.
- *Timing:* SiPM timing stays well inside 0.6 ns σ.

**3. New multichannel front-end electronics and DAQ.**
- About 26,000 channels need ASIC-based or waveform-sampling readout that records charge (energy) and time per cell.
- Cell energies must be measured separately and summed per electron.
- Include SiPM bias and temperature stabilisation, because SiPM gain depends on temperature.
- Consider mild cooling to keep dark counts compatible with low thresholds.

**4. Per-cell calibration and monitoring system.**
- Use an LED or laser light-injection system plus radioactive source deployment (e.g. 207Bi).
- This tracks energy scale and uniformity across all cells, as required by "18% in every cell."

**5. Radiopurity programme for the new components.**
- SiPMs, PCBs, cables and the scintillator now sit close to the source foil.
- Screen all of them (HPGe, radon emanation) so that background stays at the level of the current low-activity PMT/iron design.

## Left unchanged

- Tracker, 3 mT field and charge-sign determination: these meet their purpose as they are.
- Shielding and radon flushing.
- Source foils.
- Timing: no timing-driven upgrade is needed. The new readout must only preserve ≤0.6 ns.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Re-segment the calorimeter walls into ~4 cm × 4 cm (≈3–5 cm deep) scintillator cells, each read out directly by magnetic-field-immune SiPMs instead of light-guided PMTs.

This is a NEMO-3/SuperNEMO-type demonstrator, and the requirements (18% FWHM at 1 MeV, i.e. about 7% at 1 MeV for the SuperNEMO goal, 0.6 ns timing, 3 mT field, cell separation of 6 cm or more) point to a calorimeter-focused upgrade. The present cells already meet the timing (0.30 ns vs 0.6 ns) and nearly meet the energy goal (20% vs 18%), so the work is mainly on energy resolution, with the constraint that nothing else is spoiled.

**Where the problem lies**

The 20% FWHM comes from light collection and photoelectron statistics. The 19 cm cells with 30 cm light guides lose light in the guide and in the large block, and the 76 mm PMT's quantum efficiency is modest (about 25%) with a bialkali photocathode. The main lever is the photoelectron yield: resolution scales as 1/sqrt(Npe), so going from 20% to below 18% needs only about 25% more photoelectrons, but a margin is wise, and every cell must meet it, not just the average.

**Proposed hardware upgrades**

1. **High-quantum-efficiency PMTs.** Replace the 76 mm tubes with super-bialkali or ultra-bialkali photocathode tubes (QE of about 35% at peak, versus about 25%). This alone gives roughly 40% more photoelectrons and an energy resolution near 17% FWHM at 1 MeV, before any other change. Choose tubes with low-radioactivity glass (e.g. low-40K borosilicate) and good single-photoelectron timing (transit time spread under 3 ns FWHM) to preserve the 0.6 ns requirement. Use 8-inch tubes with the larger cells only if a design with larger cells is chosen; keep the 19 cm faces, because the 6 cm separation requirement and the individual cell energy readout prevent enlarging or merging cells.

2. **Remove or shorten the light guide.** Couple the PMT directly to the scintillator through a short, optimized acrylic window (or a tapered guide) rather than 30 cm of acrylic. This reduces attenuation and reflection losses and cuts the geometric spread of light travel time, which also helps timing. The 11 cm scintillator depth satisfies the 3 cm minimum.

3. **Improved scintillator.** Use polystyrene-based scintillator with higher light yield (e.g. PS with loaded fluors tuned to the PMT spectral response), with a high-reflectivity wrapping (Teflon/PTFE plus aluminised Mylar, or ESR film), and reduce the block thickness to what is needed for full absorption of 3 MeV electrons (about 10 cm is already generous). A thinner block improves light collection uniformity. The cells must remain optically isolated for the individual energy measurement.

4. **Magnetic shielding and field compatibility.** A 3 mT field degrades large PMT gain and timing. Keep the iron plate behind the tube and add mu-metal sleeves around each PMT, and verify gain stability in-field for every unit. Test each PMT in a Helmholtz coil to reject those with poor performance at 3 mT.

5. **Calibration and monitoring.** Add a LED or laser light-injection system through optical fibres to each cell, tracking gain drifts, plus periodic 207Bi sources inserted on the foil plane for absolute energy calibration; this keeps every cell within spec over time. Use waveform digitizers (e.g. 1 GS/s, 12-bit) for pulse-shape analysis and good timing.

6. **Quality control.** Test every cell individually and reject or reassemble those not reaching 18% FWHM; the requirement is for every cell.

**What stays unchanged**

The tracker, the foil, the 3 mT field and the shielding are not limiting and need no change; the radon flushing is already in place.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the 76 mm PMTs with high-quantum-efficiency (super/ultra-bialkali), low-radioactivity, magnetic-field-tolerant tubes coupled directly (without the long light guide) to the 19 cm x 19 cm polystyrene scintillator cells to raise photoelectron yield and bring every cell below 18% FWHM at 1 MeV.

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for Next-Phase Detector

## 1. **Upgrade Calorimeter PMTs to Fast Photomultipliers (e.g., Hamamatsu R13435 or equivalent)**
**Physics Motivation:** Current time resolution is 0.30 ns (sigma) at 1 MeV, meeting the 0.6 ns requirement with margin. However, upgrading to faster PMTs (transit time spread ~0.15 ns) would improve time resolution to ~0.20 ns, significantly enhancing rejection of external backgrounds and cosmic-ray-induced events. This is critical for an underground experiment where cosmic-ray muon contamination, though suppressed by 3000 m water equivalent, can still produce secondary particles and Michel electrons. Better time resolution provides an independent veto.

## 2. **Replace Polystyrene Scintillator with Plastic Scintillator + Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)**
**Physics Motivation:** The current 20% FWHM energy resolution at 1 MeV in individual cells is marginal. SiPMs (e.g., Hamamatsu MPPC arrays) offer superior photon detection efficiency (~40–50% vs ~25% for PMTs), lower dark noise in underground setting, insensitivity to magnetic field (unlike PMTs), and faster timing (~40 ps intrinsic). A 3×3 or 4×4 SiPM array per cell would achieve ~15% FWHM energy resolution and ~0.3 ns time resolution, meeting the 18%/0.6 ns specs with substantial headroom. Magnetic-field immunity is essential since the 3 mT field degrades PMT gain.

## 3. **Increase Calorimeter Cell Depth from 11 cm to 15 cm**
**Physics Motivation:** Current cells already absorb 3 MeV electrons (requirement met at 11 cm), but increasing depth to 15 cm improves containment of edge-scattered secondaries and reduces light loss from photons escaping the cell side. This would improve energy resolution by ~2–3% absolute, helping reach the 18% target more robustly across all cells and angles of incidence. The trade-off (increased detector footprint) is minor for a 6 m × 3.5 m system.

## 4. **Upgrade Tracking Gas to Xenon-Helium Mixture with Increased Drift Field**
**Physics Motivation:** Current helium-based gas has modest ionization density, limiting track reconstruction fidelity near the foil vertex (critical for rejecting background). A 10% Xe + 90% He mixture (with radon scrubbing) improves dE/dx by ~30%, enhancing electron/positron separation and vertex localization. Higher drift field (now feasible with radon control) increases drift velocity and reduces diffusion, improving spatial resolution from ~mm to ~0.5 mm. This sharpens vertex identification on the 45 mg/cm² foil and reduces mis-reconstruction of external backgrounds.

## 5. **Add Thin Cherenkov Detector (e.g., FDIRC-style planar radiator) Between Tracking Volume and Calorimeter**
**Physics Motivation:** A 2–3 cm quartz radiator plate upstream of each calorimeter wall, read out by fast SiPMs, provides particle identification (electron vs. gamma, electron vs. positron via complementary track info). This helps distinguish signal (two electrons with unique vertex on foil, correlated energy ~3 MeV) from background (single electrons from external sources, uncorrelated energies). The ~50 ps Cherenkov timing is faster than calorimeter timing and provides an independent cross-check on acceptance timing windows.

## 6. **Implement Segmented Read-out of Light Guides and Position-Sensitive PMT Arrays**
**Physics Motivation:** Current single PMT per cell cannot localize energy deposition within the 19 cm × 19 cm face. A 2×2 or 3×3 array of smaller PMTs (or SiPM array subdivisions) per cell provides ~5 cm spatial resolution of shower position. This allows precise separation of closely-spaced electron deposits and better rejection of multiple low-energy background interactions mis-identified as a single electron. Critical for the "6 cm apart" requirement for two-electron events.

## 7. **Upgrade Iron and Water Shielding with Muon Veto Scintillator Plane**
**Physics Motivation:** While 3000 m overburden suppresses cosmic muons by ~10⁶, residual muons (and their induced neutron spallation products) can mimic decay signatures. A thin (5 cm) plastic scintillator plane wrapped around the outer detector volume, instrumented with SiPMs, detects muon transits with ~ns timing. Coincidence veto eliminates events within ~1 μs of a muon, removing backgrounds from muon-induced decays of stopped pions and neutron activation.

---

## TOP RECOMMENDATION: **Replace Polystyrene Scintillator with Plastic Scintillator + Silicon Photomultiplier (SiPM) Arrays per Calorimeter Cell**

**Justification:** This single upgrade addresses the detector's most stringent bottleneck—the energy resolution specification (18% FWHM vs. current 20%) and provides magnetic-field immunity lacking in the present PMT design. SiPMs also deliver superior timing (~0.3 ns), lower cost than PMT replacements, and enable segmented position sensitivity. The technology directly improves signal efficiency for genuine two-electron events while reducing background mis-identification, with implementation straightforward in the next-phase rebuild.

This is the NEMO-3 → SuperNEMO calorimeter upgrade. The current cells (19 cm blocks, 20% FWHM, 30 cm light guides, 5" PMTs) already meet the timing requirement (0.30 ns versus the 0.6 ns limit) and the 3 cm depth requirement (11 cm is far more than needed). The only gaps are energy resolution (20% vs 18%) and granularity (19 cm cells cannot separate electrons 6 cm apart). Every change should be judged against these two gaps, and against the 3 mT field.

**Analysis of the constraints**

1. **Granularity.** Two electrons from one decay entering a wall at points ≥6 cm apart must land in different cells. With 19 cm faces this fails frequently, so the face must shrink, or the readout must be segmented. A cell with a face of ~6 cm or less would work, but the natural compromise is a scintillator block of roughly 25 cm × 25 cm face? No: larger blocks make things worse. Smaller blocks (≤ ~6 cm pitch) would multiply the channel count by about 10 and require many more PMTs, so a different design is required. A reasonable resolution is to keep the optical readout but segment the scintillator into ~6 cm cells, each with its own light collection, with the choice of photodetector being the main decision.

2. **Energy resolution and the light guide.** The 30 cm acrylic light guide loses light, and the iron plate is only needed because of the field. Removing the light guide and coupling the PMT directly to the scintillator raises light collection and improves resolution, and it also makes a compact cell possible. Large photocathode area per cell face is needed, which is why a PMT matched to the scintillator face is preferable.

3. **Magnetic field.** The 3 mT field means conventional PMTs lose gain unless shielded (hence the iron plate). Options are mu-metal/iron shielding, or a photodetector insensitive to B (SiPM or similar). Silicon photodetectors would remove the iron shield and light guide altogether, but a 6 cm × 6 cm scintillator face needs sizeable photodetector area, and SiPM noise and timing at 1 MeV for such large faces are uncertain. Hence, the safer, proven choice is a low-radioactivity, high quantum efficiency PMT with shielding.

**Recommended hardware changes**

1. **Replace the PMTs with high-quantum-efficiency (super-bialkali, ~35–40% QE) low-radioactivity 8" PMTs, coupled directly to the scintillator block.** This delivers the energy-resolution gain (about 7–8% FWHM at 1 MeV is the best realised with such designs), with ample time resolution margin. An 8" tube on a ~25 cm face would conflict with the granularity requirement, so see item 2.

2. **Reduce the scintillator face size and use a PMT sized to it.** Use blocks with face and photocathode matched (e.g. 5" PMTs on ~13 cm blocks) are insufficient for the 6 cm rule. To meet the 6 cm separation requirement strictly, cells need faces ≲ 6 cm, meaning a pitch of order 6 cm with correspondingly smaller PMTs (e.g. 2–3" high-QE tubes) or segmented blocks, with the cell depth kept ≥3 cm (e.g. ~10 cm of polystyrene retained, or a shallower but still ≥3 cm block to reduce Compton/γ confusion and background).

3. **Eliminate the 30 cm acrylic light guides**, coupling PMT directly to the scintillator (with optical grease/pad and reflective wrap). This removes light loss, shortens transit-time spread, and shrinks dead space.

4. **Use plastic scintillator with higher light yield (polystyrene-based, e.g. high-light-yield PVT/PS with optimized dopants) and high-reflectivity wrapping (e.g. Teflon/Mylar).** Combined with items 1 and 3, this should push resolution to the 18% FWHM target or better with margin, and this must hold in every cell, so uniformity QC of each cell is needed.

5. **Magnetic shielding of each PMT** (mu-metal, plus the iron plate if retained) so gain is stable in the 3 mT field.

6. **Retain** the tracker, foil, gas flushing against radon, the shielding and the timing electronics, as these already meet specifications.

**Key trade-off:** the granularity requirement dominates. Going to ≤6 cm cells is the largest change in channel count and cost, while energy resolution is addressed by PMT QE, removal of light guides, and scintillator quality.

TOP RECOMMENDATION: Replace the 19 cm × 19 cm scintillator cells with finer-granularity cells (face ≲ 6 cm) read directly by high-quantum-efficiency, magnetically shielded PMTs without the 30 cm light guides.

This is a calorimeter upgrade problem for a NEMO-3-like detector. The current constraints are: energy resolution 20% → must reach ≤18% FWHM at 1 MeV; time resolution 0.30 ns → can be relaxed but must stay ≤0.6 ns (so the current value already meets this, and the requirement is really to keep it); cell size 19×19 cm² with 6 cm minimum separation logic; depth 11 cm must be kept ≥3 cm (already satisfied); everything must operate in a 3 mT field (standard PMTs are not magnetic-field tolerant at this level, and iron plates in the magnetic environment are a concern).

**Proposed hardware upgrades**

1. **Photodetectors: replace the 76 mm PMTs with higher-quantum-efficiency, larger-area or silicon-based readout that works in a magnetic field.**
- Option A: Replace the 76 mm PMTs with 8-inch or 3-inch-class high-QE bialkali PMTs with low-noise dynodes, mounted behind the existing light guides and shielded with a mu-metal or soft-iron cup. Higher photoelectron yield per MeV is the main lever on the energy resolution (resolution scales roughly as 1/√N_pe).
- Option B (preferred for field tolerance): Silicon photomultipliers (SiPMs) coupled to the light guides. SiPMs are unaffected by a 3 mT field and have high PDE, giving substantially more photoelectrons per MeV. Their gain temperature dependence and dark count rate must be managed (cooling or temperature compensation), and their dynamic range must be checked for the full energy range. The pulse shape and timing are also good for the 0.6 ns requirement.
- Rationale: The energy resolution gap (20% → 18%) is a photostatistics-limited problem. Increasing collected light is the most direct route, and SiPMs remove the field-sensitivity issue entirely.

2. **Light collection: improve light guides and wrapping.**
- Replace the 30 cm acrylic guides with optimised, higher-transmission guides (e.g., with a reflective wrap such as ESR/Vikuiti-type specular film or PTFE diffuse reflector around the scintillator), and optimise the guide geometry to reduce light loss at the cell–guide interface.
- Rationale: Raises light yield per MeV at essentially no detector-volume cost, contributing to the resolution target together with item 1.

3. **Scintillator: upgrade to a higher-light-yield scintillator.**
- Replace or supplement polystyrene with a higher-light-yield plastic (e.g., a PVT-based or polystyrene formulation with optimised dopants, or a fast liquid/plastic with higher photon yield), keeping the 11 cm depth so that the 3 MeV full-absorption requirement is preserved.
- Rationale: Intrinsic light yield is the fundamental input to resolution; combined with better photodetection it should comfortably reach ≤18%.

4. **Cell segmentation and readout electronics.**
- Keep the 19 cm × 19 cm faces, since the 6 cm minimum separation rule is satisfied by a 19 cm pitch, but verify that the readout of each cell is independent and that digitisation/electronics are low noise and have adequate dynamic range for 0–3 MeV deposits.
- Upgrade front-end electronics to fast waveform digitisers or low-noise shaping ASICs to preserve the 0.6 ns timing requirement and avoid pile-up.
- Rationale: Electronics must not degrade the improved photostatistics; timing must remain within the rejection requirement.

5. **Magnetic-field compatibility and shielding.**
- Assess whether the iron plates behind the PMTs are needed; with SiPMs they may be removed or reduced, which also reduces the local field distortion. Any remaining ferromagnetic parts should be checked in the 3 mT field.
- Rationale: Every component must function in the field; removing or redesigning magnetic-sensitive elements avoids gain loss or track-reconstruction distortion.

**TOP RECOMMENDATION:** Replace the 76 mm PMTs with silicon photomultipliers (or equivalent high-PDE, field-insensitive photodetectors) coupled to the existing light guides, since increasing collected photoelectrons per MeV is the single change that addresses the 18% energy-resolution requirement while remaining compatible with the 3 mT magnetic field.

**Energy Resolution Shortfall:**
- Current: 20% FWHM at 1 MeV
- Required: 18% FWHM or better
- The 2% gap suggests photon collection efficiency and/or scintillator light output are limiting factors

**Time Resolution Requirement:**
- Current: 0.30 ns sigma at 1 MeV
- Required: 0.6 ns sigma or better
- Currently EXCEEDS requirement by 2×, so time resolution is adequate

**Spatial Separation Requirement:**

- Cell depth must be ≥3 cm (currently 11 cm, adequate)

### 1. **Upgrade Photomultiplier Tubes (PRIMARY)**
**Change:** Replace 76 mm PMTs with larger format (89 mm or 3" tubes, e.g., Hamamatsu R12860 or equivalent)
- **Rationale:** Increases solid angle for light collection, improving photon collection efficiency by ~20%

**Change:** Increase cell depth from 11 cm to 13-14 cm
- **Rationale:** Improves light yield per MeV deposited; better photoelectron statistics
- **Impact:** ~2-3% improvement in energy resolution
- **Constraint:** Must maintain field uniformity in 3 mT magnet; manageable

- **Risk:** SiPMs require careful magnetic field mitigation; higher complexity

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for the Tracker-Calorimeter Detector

## 1. **Replace PMTs with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)**

**Current limitation:** 76 mm PMTs with 30 cm light guides cause significant light loss and timing degradation.

**Upgrade:** Replace with arrays of 6×6 mm² SiPMs (e.g., Hamamatsu S13360 series or FBK NUV-HD) tiled directly on the scintillator face, eliminating light guides.

**Benefits:**
- Improved photon detection efficiency (>50% vs ~25% for PMTs)
- Better time resolution (~100 ps intrinsic vs ~1 ns for PMTs)
- Excellent performance in 3 mT magnetic field (PMTs are field-sensitive)
- Compact design eliminates 30 cm light guides, reducing photon path length
- Expected energy resolution: 12-15% FWHM at 1 MeV
- Expected time resolution: 0.25-0.35 ns sigma at 1 MeV

## 2. **Optimize Scintillator Cell Geometry**

**Current issue:** 19 cm × 19 cm faces are large; 11 cm depth may be excessive for most events.

**Upgrade:** Redesign to 10 cm × 10 cm × 5 cm cells using faster plastic scintillator (e.g., BC-420 or EJ-228 with τ ~1.5 ns decay time).

**Benefits:**
- Better granularity for energy separation (6 cm requirement easily met)
- Reduced depth saves material/cost while still fully absorbing 3 MeV electrons
- Faster scintillator improves timing resolution
- More cells provide redundancy and better position resolution

## 3. **Upgrade to Wavelength-Shifting Fiber Readout**

**Alternative to SiPM arrays:** Embed wavelength-shifting (WLS) fibers (e.g., Kuraray Y11) in grooves on scintillator surfaces, read out by SiPMs at edges.

**Benefits:**
- Uniform light collection across cell face
- Cost reduction: 2-4 SiPMs per cell instead of 36+
- Proven technology in SNO+, T2K, and MINOS detectors
- Maintains good energy and timing resolution

## 4. **Implement Machine Learning-Based Energy Reconstruction**

**Current limitation:** Simple energy sum likely suboptimal with multiple photon reflections and position-dependent collection.

**Upgrade:** Deploy neural network algorithms (e.g., trained on calibration data) for energy reconstruction accounting for:
- Hit position on cell face
- Light collection non-uniformities
- Pulse shape analysis
- Multi-cell shower leakage corrections

**Benefits:**
- 10-15% improvement in energy resolution achievable
- Better handling of edge effects and shower leakage
- Can be implemented in existing DAQ/software with minimal hardware changes

## 5. **Enhanced Light Collection with Reflective Coatings**

**Upgrade:** Wrap all scintillator cells in specular reflector (ESR film, 3M Vikuiti) instead of diffuse reflectors (Tyvek).

**Benefits:**
- 30-50% increase in light collection efficiency
- Improved energy and time resolution
- Minimal cost, can be done during maintenance

## 6. **Digital DAQ with Waveform Sampling**

**Current limitation:** Likely using charge integration without full waveform capture.

**Upgrade:** Implement 250-500 MHz waveform digitizers (e.g., CAEN V1730, DRS4 chips) for each channel.

**Benefits:**
- Pulse shape discrimination for background rejection
- Offline optimization of timing algorithms
- Better pile-up rejection
- Precise energy reconstruction via fitting

## 7. **Upgrade Tracking Gas Mixture**

**Complement to calorimeter:** While not calorimeter hardware, switching to He:C₂H₆ (90:10) or adding quenchers could improve electron energy loss measurements and timing in tracking volume, providing independent energy validation.

---

**TOP RECOMMENDATION:** Replace the 76 mm PMTs and 30 cm light guides with tiled SiPM arrays mounted directly on the scintillator faces to achieve the required energy resolution (18% FWHM), improve time resolution to <0.4 ns sigma, eliminate magnetic field sensitivity, and enable more compact, reliable calorimeter operation.

# Proposed Hardware Upgrades for the Tracker-Calorimeter Detector

## 1. Calorimeter Photodetectors: Replace PMTs with Silicon Photomultipliers (SiPMs)

**Problem:** 76 mm PMTs are sensitive to the 3 mT magnetic field. Even this modest field can deflect photoelectrons within the PMT dynode chain, degrading gain and resolution. The iron plates behind each PMT partially shield this but add dead material and complicate the geometry.

**Proposal:** Replace each 76 mm PMT with an array of **SiPMs (e.g., Hamamatsu S13360 series or FBK NUV-HD, 6×6 mm² tiles)**, tiling a ~76 mm diameter active area (roughly 10–15 tiles per cell). SiPMs are completely immune to magnetic fields, eliminating the need for the iron shielding plates behind each module. This directly removes a source of systematic error and dead material.

- Expected improvement: energy resolution could reach **12–15% FWHM at 1 MeV** (better than the 18% requirement), since SiPM photon detection efficiency (PDE ~40–50%) exceeds that of bialkali PMTs (~25–30%).
- SiPM transit time spread is ~0.1–0.2 ns per pixel, so with averaging across the array the **time resolution can reach ~0.1–0.15 ns (sigma) at 1 MeV**, well within the 0.6 ns requirement.
- Operating temperature should be stabilized (e.g., ±0.1°C control) to manage SiPM gain temperature coefficient (~2%/°C), using resistive heater mats on the calorimeter walls.
- Use custom low-noise front-end ASICs (e.g., CAEN A5202 or IN2P3 SPACIROC3-style) for SiPM signal shaping and timing.

---

## 2. Scintillator Material: Replace Polystyrene with PVT-Based or Lanthanum Bromide Composite

**Problem:** Polystyrene scintillator has relatively low light yield (~10 photons/keV), which is a primary limiting factor for both energy and time resolution.

**Proposal (Option A – conservative):** Replace polystyrene with **PVT (polyvinyl toluene)-based scintillator** (e.g., Saint-Gobain BC-408 or Eljen EJ-200), which has ~20% higher light yield, longer attenuation length (~380 cm vs ~250 cm), and faster rise time. This is a drop-in replacement requiring no geometry change.

**Proposal (Option B – aggressive):** Use **undoped CsI crystals or GAGG(Ce) crystals** (Gd₃Al₂Ga₃O₁₂:Ce) for the cells closest to the foil where energy resolution is most critical. GAGG offers ~46 photons/keV, good energy resolution (~6% FWHM at 662 keV), is non-hygroscopic, and has no intrinsic radioactivity. However, its decay time (~90 ns) is slower; this is acceptable given the 0.6 ns time resolution requirement is met by the SiPMs on the faster BC-408 scintillator.

**Recommended practical choice:** EJ-200/BC-408 PVT scintillator with SiPM readout, targeting **~14% FWHM at 1 MeV**.

---

## 3. Light Guide: Replace 30 cm Acrylic Light Guide with Short Winston Cone + Direct Coupling

**Problem:** The 30 cm acrylic light guide causes significant photon loss through absorption and total-internal-reflection losses, worsening both energy and time resolution. It was designed to distance the PMT from the magnetic field — with SiPMs, this motivation disappears.

**Proposal:** Remove the acrylic light guide entirely and couple the SiPM array **directly to the back face of the scintillator**, separated only by optical grease (e.g., Saint-Gobain BC-630) or a thin (~2 mm) UV-transparent epoxy layer. If some geometric matching is needed between the 19×19 cm² scintillator face and the SiPM tile array, use a short (<3 cm) **compound parabolic concentrator (Winston cone)** in PTFE-coated aluminum.

- Eliminating 30 cm of light guide recovers an estimated 30–40% more photons, directly improving energy resolution by ~15–20% relative.
- Timing improves because photon path-length dispersion is reduced.

---

## 4. Tracking: Upgrade Geiger-Mode Cells to Drift-Mode Cells with 3D Hit Reconstruction

**Problem:** Geiger-mode cells fire along their entire length when a particle passes, giving only a 2D (x,y) hit in the plane perpendicular to the cell axis. Longitudinal (z) position is obtained only from two-end anode readout timing, with ~1 cm resolution. This limits vertex reconstruction on the foil.

**Proposal:** Replace Geiger-mode cells with **small-diameter (∅ ~6 mm) proportional drift tubes** operated in full proportional mode with **cathode strip readout** (e.g., as used in COMPASS or T2K TPCs). Use an **Ar/CO₂/isobutane** or **He/isobutane** gas mixture compatible with the low-Z requirement (to minimize electron scattering).

Alternatively, consider a **Time Projection Chamber (TPC)** architecture with a **GEM (Gas Electron Multiplier)** or **Micromegas** readout plane at each end of the tracking volume. This gives continuous 3D track reconstruction rather than hit-by-hit Geiger firing.

- Improved vertex resolution on the foil: from ~1 cm to **~1–2 mm** in all three coordinates.
- Better dE/dx measurement to aid particle identification.
- He-based gas (80% He, 20% isobutane) can be maintained; GEM foils work well in this mixture.
- Note: GEM foils must be validated in 3 mT; they are electrostatic devices and unaffected by this field.

---

## 5. Front-End Electronics: Waveform Digitization

**Problem:** The current system presumably uses charge-integrating ADCs and leading-edge discriminator TDCs, limiting pile-up rejection and timing precision.

**Proposal:** Instrument every calorimeter channel with **switched-capacitor array (SCA) waveform samplers** (e.g., **DRS4 chip** from PSI, 5 GS/s, 1024 cells, 11-bit resolution, or the **TARGET** ASIC used in IACT cameras). Full waveform capture at 1–2 GS/s allows:

- Offline pulse-shape discrimination to reject α/γ pile-up on individual cells.
- **Digital constant-fraction discrimination (dCFD)** in firmware, achieving time resolution independent of pulse amplitude — critical for the 0.6 ns requirement across the full dynamic range (0.2–3.5 MeV).
- Identification of multiple sub-threshold hits within the same cell integration window.
- Each DRS4 chip reads 8 channels; with ~500 calorimeter cells per wall, ~125 DRS4 chips per wall are needed — a manageable number.

---

## 6. Radon Mitigation: Active Radon Trapping System

**Problem:** Radon emanation from detector materials (especially the iron shielding and soil) can enter the tracking volume and mimic signal via ²¹⁴Bi beta decay (Q = 3.27 MeV, endpoint above the signal region). Gas flushing alone is insufficient if the emanation rate is high.

**Proposal:** Add an **activated charcoal cold trap** (cooled to −40°C with a Peltier system) in the He gas recirculation loop, with a **radon monitor** (electrostatic collection + alpha counting, sensitivity <1 mBq/m³) on the return line. This is the technique used by SNO, GERDA, and nEXO.

- Supplementary: re-coat all inner iron surfaces with **Mylar film** or **Lumirror** to reduce radon diffusion from iron grain boundaries.
- Target: radon activity in tracking gas < **0.5 mBq/m³**.

---

## 7. Foil Upgrade: Thinner Molybdenum Foils

**Problem:** At 45 mg/cm² thickness, two electrons from a double-beta decay each lose ~20–30 keV in the foil before entering the tracker, smearing the energy sum and degrading signal efficiency near the Q-value endpoint.

**Proposal:** Reduce foil thickness to **~25–30 mg/cm²** while compensating mass loss by increasing foil area (the foil plane can be extended slightly, or a second parallel plane added). This requires improved mechanical support (carbon fiber frames) since thinner Mo foils are more fragile.

- Optionally, test **Mo-loaded scintillating foils** (Mo dissolved in PVT at ~50 mg/cm² equivalent), which would allow the foil itself to contribute scintillation light as a first-stage energy trigger — a technique explored by the MOON collaboration.
